Build quality and stiffness is excellent, but it's a little small for use with bass trombone mutes.

It's strong enough and rigid enough to hold a jo-ral bass trombone cup mute stably (which is a feat in itself) but:
 - the small ring is too small for trombone mutes (maybe a pixie would fit).  You can maybe balance a plunger on it but it didn't seem particularly stable.
 - the medium and large rings are small enough that you're likely to bonk one or two of the corks on the way out.
 - the arms attached to the rings are short enough that you can't use all the rings (not enough wingspan to fit the jo-ral bass cup next to a jo-ral bass straight mute and have any room left).

If they created a different model which added an inch to the length of the arms and half an inch to an inch to the ring diameters and it would be much better for trombone.

My kids, 2.5 and nearly 1, both love playing with these things.
They jump around shaking them, and the oldest likes to shake them while singing the Shake the Sillies Out song.

One problem... the 10 month old nearly gets the whole thing in his mouth.
I've been watching him, but If he pushed a little harder he'd get the egg in his mouth and then it would likely get stuck.

These eggs are a little small, so with kids under 18 months you need to be careful,and watch them carefully.

I ordered 4 sets of these LED strips to run around the perimeter of my family room. Overall I am quite happy with the purchase with a couple of small complaints.
3 of the 4 strips appear identical in color, however 1 of the strips is slightly off, particularly in the blue and white range. Not a big difference but slightly annoying.
The tape adhesive is fairly weak. It appears to be a standard 3M acrylic based adhesive but I had trouble getting it to stick long enough to fully cure. I would prefer to see a high tack foam tape. In their defense this is the same for most of these strip LEDs. Just plan on using additional fasteners if the surface is inverted or otherwise not pristine.
Finally...and most annoying... one of the strips has a section of 3 LEDs that has the red diode out. I didn't notice until everything was mounted so even though it's not that noticeable... its driving me a little nuts!

So why 4 stars with all these negatives? Because of price. I have spent much more on other strips with similar characteristics. These arrived promptly and well packaged in clam shells. Test them before you install and you'll be fine. Keep in mind you need to by a power supply and controller! They are not included.

If you've been afraid to drop $399+ on double pedals these will get you down the road for a few years+.  Within a few months one of the springs on the main pedal broke.  I was training my legs so with a bit of tension I think it gave out.  I was able to fix it easily.  After a couple years the glue gave away on the beater felts.  Again not the end of the world since they had another side.
I've used these for 3 years on a Electronic Drum kit and aside from the above they've been reliable.  They have fairly intelligent design with the onboard drum key, and accessibility.  These were not gigged or really transported much.  Pretty much sat in my office/studio.  I used them heavily for double bass training prior to upgrading to something more expensive.

The Alesis Q49 is about the best choice you can make if you are looking for a compact budget priced keyboard controller that you can play with both hands.

The Q49 is very spartan in its feature set - 49 full size keys, full size pitch & mod wheels, octave up/down buttons, sustain switch input and just 1 dedicated data entry slider - note that it has no assignable data entry knobs or controller (drum) pads.

It can be powered either by a USB port on your computer (there is a USB cable included - it's tucked into one of the foam endcaps in the carton) or it can be powered by a 9V power adapter (NOT included). As most people will probably be using this device with a computer, please be aware that the Q49 USB connection may not work with a USB hub - i.e., you may have to plug it directly into a free USB port on your computer - Alesis mentions this in their trouble shooting guide, and that was my experience.

That said, I really like this keyboard - First, it's pretty much plug & play - you don't have to mess around with loading a pesky hardware driver (although of course, you do have to configure your software apps to recognize it - I got it to work with Reason 4, FL Studio 9 and all my stand alone software synths with no problems).

It's fairly lightweight and doesn't have a lot of excess plastic, so if you want, you can kick back in your easy chair and rest the Q49 on your lap. The keys do not have aftertouch, but they respond well to velocity changes. Pitch and Mod wheels are the same size as what you find on full-size controllers.

The octave up/down buttons light when they are activated, a nice little feature.

Note that if you are into editing/designing sounds or tweaking parameters on your soft-synths while you play, then this keyboard probably isn't for you because there are no assignable rotary controls - this is where those little two-octave units come in.

As an added bonus, you also get a "Lite" version of Ableton Live.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Nice no frills budget performance keyboard -  needs a free USB port (no hubs)

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I purchased these for a tenor saxaphone mouthpiece.  The product description says these are size L for tenor saxaphone, but the product packaging states that large is used for barritone saxaphone and you should purchase the M for tenor.  I went ahead and used these on the tenor mouthpiece and they were slightly large, but worked well and I would not hesitate to buy them again.  I think I would try the reccommended size M next time, but I these still worked very well.

After years of going back and forth over whether or not to get a violin, I finally decide to go ahead and do it. Honestly I'm glad I did. The set is great and the violin itself is beautiful. The pegs are a little difficult to keep tight at the moment, but nothing some peg drops/rosin/compound shouldn't fix. The violin arrived well within its estimated delivery time (earlier than I expected in fact), and I couldn't be more pleased.

Been playing guitar for 30 years now, and strings are always hit or miss,  especially as you and your guitar changes over time,  I have a bottom feeder Alvarez regent six string as my main guitar over all these years, that being said, I thought I would try some silk and steel, and step away from the bronze and phosphors,  I like the feel, as I do not use a pick, and these have a nicer feel, the volume is muted some, and so is the resonance.  I play  old  American folk, acoustic blues, classic country and gospel music,  and these work fine for me, I don't need to project much volume as I play these days as a solo act at mostly retirement and nursing homes and sing with no microphone.  They have a warm , mellow  cozy sound.  I think if I had these a few years ago when I played in an classic country band they would not have worked well as they are a quieter string by design.

First what I got was a software disk for a program that cleans digitized files. I cannot use the provided program to capture phono or line in data by itself. I used audio cleaning lab 2005 ( not provided with this package ) on XP to capture files and parse into tracks. You must use an external power supply as the circuit (Gemsound)is ill designed to work well with a powered USB line as far as the headphone jack. I tried a laptop and desktop with noise. I used a 9V 500ma DC radio shack power supply wall wart to do the job with much better audio quality as well as no noise. That is the cure for a poor design job. I don't know if the digitizing quality will suffer for USB powered task. It depends if the eq is active or passive. You use cleaning lab to capture and parse, export to files then massage files. This thing is good for having the DA isolated and better analog components. I got it for $80 new. Good deal for me. I just want to clean records and tape stuff. I guess the driver was installed with the provided software as my computer sound card is now bypassed. My sound card was failing so this is my solution and portable for other computers. Even though the input says ac it just has a dc converter inside. The task is redundant and should not harm it. The noise might not affect DA conversion. Don't care as I will run external supply.
Musical_Instruments.summary: works if you isolate problem area design flaw.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: A really great practice amp that can actually be pretty loud. The only reason I give it 4 stars is because its distorted channel is kinda hard to work with. If you don't have the drive all the way up it lets some of the clean shine through with the digital distortion (if that makes sense) and it sounds odd for my tastes. If you want to dirty up your cleans a little I suggest a pedal with this one. But if you want all clean or heavily distorted this amp is great by itself. Couldn't believe the clean tone out of this amp.

Overall, I am really pleased with the Scarlett. The physical interface itself is beautiful and it's intuitive to use. I like how the ring around the gain will light up red if it detects you are clipping. Most importantly, with a good microphone, a decently quiet room, and a simple audio recorder, the audio quality is really superb. I am very happy with this purchase.

I want to clarify a few things for future buyers, though, and don't take this as a warning to stay away from this product. It is excellent if you can set it up right.

#1 - MICROPHONES V. INSTRUMENTS. The Scarlett has a very nicely designed combo jack, which allows you to plug in both an XLR connector and a 1/4" TRS jack plug. The Scarlett is automatically configured to recognize any XLR connector as a microphone and any 1/4" TRS jack plug as an instrument. So if you intend to use microphones I urge you to get an XLR cable to connect them. It is basically necessary you use XLR for condenser microphones to utilize the 48V phantom power. Even with a dynamic microphone, I really recommend you use an XLR connection. A dynamic microphone using a 1/4" TRS will be much quieter than one using an XLR, and can hardly be heard through a headphone monitor even with the gain turned up 100%.

#2 - MONITORS. If you intend to use headphones as a monitor (to listen to yourself as you record), you will need headphones ending in a 1/4" jack (6.35mm). Most headphones rarely end in anything other than a 1/8" jack (3.5mm), so it is 99% likely you will need an adapter. Get yourself a 1/8" female to 1/4" male TRS adapter if you want to use headphones. You can find these easily at Wal-Mart, BestBuy, etc. As a side note, on the back are two line outputs that also require 1/4" TRS jack plugs - these are for loudspeakers, not headphones. There is only one jack for one pair of headphones. (I am pretty sure you can use a headphone splitter if you need more headphones.)

#3 - DRIVERS. The package insert for this product will tell you to register your product on their website so you can download a USB driver. Go ahead and register because there are other free downloads, but DO NOT install the USB drivers from focusrite.com if you are using Windows. If you already installed it, you must uninstall it by going to Control Panel > Uninstall a Program. Go to http://beta.focusrite.com/releases/focusrite_usb2_drivers/ and download/install the latest USB2 driver (last I checked, there was only one available). You will know the driver is working if Line Output and Line Input appear and are enabled in Control Panel > Sound when you plug in the interface.

#4 - Find, download, and read the manual for this product. It will save you from any disappointment or surprises.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Intuitive interface and great audio quality. You'll need the right drivers and connections, though.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
The Yamaha MD-BT01 is a well-engineered product that works mostly as advertised, with the exception that you have to jump through a few hoops to get it working at all on iOS device.  I should start out by saying that this a $50 Bluetooth adapter that functionally performs the same task as a $10 5-pin DIN MIDI cable...it just does it wirelessly.  Therefore, I consider it more of a convenience item than a true necessity.  One exception to that argument might be that you can have several of them running at once (five, I believe).  So you could imagine having an interface with only 1 MIDI connections, and now you could have MIDI running (wirelessly) to several different hardware units, which is pretty cool.

The two important "issues" for you to be aware of before buying the MD-BT01 are: (1) It requires MIDI power and both the IN and OUT jacks; and (2) iOS Bluetooth doesn't recognize it natively, so Yamaha has engineered a software workaround.  The device runs off the power of the hardware you plug it into IF your device offers MIDI power.  There are more units than you'd think that do not have MIDI power.  This would include all of the Korg Volca series, which only has a MIDI in jack.  By contrast, the Korg Minilogue and Roland Boutique series do provide MIDI power to run the device.

Once powered up, you can't just go to your Bluetooth menu in "Settings" and find the MD-BT01.  You have download Yamaha's utility app to find the device and connect to it.  You can also rename the unit or do firmware updates from that utility.  As several reviewers have pointed out, I think you also have to identify it as a MIDI destination in an app that supports it.  There are several of these, but I found that if I skipped this step, I couldn't just load up a sequencer app (like Inifinite Looper or Xequence) and make the connection.  But once it works, it generally works.

I should point out that my primary concern prior to buying the device - latency - really isn't much of an issue at all.  The latency seems pretty minimal, and if you're just using the MIDI connection for sequencing or to mess with control parameters on a synth, it's basically a non-factor anyway.

The device is a little bulky, and maybe a little expensive for what it does.  I suspect that this is the type of device that will seem archaic in 5-10 years, but then again, MIDI is still with us, and has been since around 1983.  The primary reason I like and wanted the MD-BT01 is to connect my iPhone or iPad to a hardware synth with needing to use a MIDI interface.  If you're willing to deal with a few steps along the way, it works pretty well for that objective.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Works well and with low latency, but not exactly "plug and play"

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: This is a nice compact all in one unit.  This is a multi-day multi-season machinge.  It has the largest reservior for ice I have seen yet. When compared with standard for machines the fog it puts out stays much lower to the ground.  However the 400 watt is a bit on the low side so the volume of it's output is medium to low.  The picture of the fog comming out of the machine is greatly exagerated.  The amount of fog juice it can hold is small, so be careful.  When it runs out of juice you can easily burn up ANY fog machine.  When done and it is time to store clean it with fog machine cleaner.

This is a beautiful guitar.  The workmanship is excellent.  The finish is flawless. The chambered mahogany body makes it extremely light at 5 lbs or so.  The floating bridge, harp tailpiece, and P90 style single coil pickups give it a sound that is thicker, woodier, and creamier than my Telecaster can make.  It comes with 11-49 strings.  I love the sound.
I was unpleasantly surprised to find that the guitar arrived very poorly set up.  The neck was warped.  The intonation was far off.  The action was way high.  Each of these are easily fixed by a knowledgeable owner or tech (the truss rod tool is included) but are inexcusable in a $1,000 guitar.  The $300 Fender guitars from Asia are much better set up.

I had read reviews of many ukeleles and more than once read comments that the Lu-21 was a comparable instrument for a lot less money. So, I thought this was a good value for my first uke and took a chance.  I am well pleased.  The sustain is not great, but the action and frets are fine and it stays in tune. I'm having fun with it and the price was nice.

This pitch pipe is great for individual practice.  It's really nice to have such a great range of tones.  The volume is loud enough to hear when I am singing to make sure I am not losing pitch.  I had hoped my chorus could use it in place of the ones which are falling apart.  Unfortunately, the pause button does not keep the pipe silent while changing pitches and makes it unsuitable for that use.  Otherwise, the pipe is great and nicely priced!

I was introduced to these strings by a man who owns a fine violin shop about 5 years ago.  They are by far the best strings for my violin.  They produce a rich tone that no other string could produce on my violin.  I agree that the Gold E is the best but the G, D, and A Evahs are amazing.  I feel like my bow is moving through butter!  When I can afford them, these strings are my first choice!

I tried every brand of string for my Heritage Custom Eagle with Benedetto S6 pickup except Thomastik Infeld ( because I'm cheap) and nothing sounded right... until now. These strings are about as close as you'll ever get to perfection; rich, smooth, and acoustically vibrant. Go ahead and let the moths out of your wallet. They're worth every penny and will save you a ton of experimentation and wasted strings. Nothing works better for for my jazz box .

I got this when I was twelve. I thought it was the coolest thing ever after having a First Act electric for the longest time and a 12 string acoustic with a half broken bridge I got at a yard sale for $20.

Don't get me wrong, she's a great little concert body with a nice bright tone.

It's been four years now and I can honestly say that you have no need for a electric/acoustic; unless you play live shows and if thats the case you deserve better than this.

All in all the guitar itself is a solid beginners instrument but this package deal is nothing more than a novelty. For $200 you can buy a much nicer full body acoustic (Non electric) that you'd be much happier with.

Worth checking out: Yamaha FS700S  $199
  Yamaha F335  $159
  Washburn WD100DL  $124
  Fender FA-100  $119

*Prices are from Musicians Friend . com
Musical_Instruments.summary: Don't make the same mistake as me.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: AThe Makala Ukulele is fabulous!  It has a great sound and I like the concert size because it's larger than the soprano making it easier to make chords.  The case is very sturdy so I have no problem traveling with it.  I also love the tuner.  It works perfectly and clips right to the top of the ukulele making it very easy to use.  I've already recommended it to friends as a  wonderful way to get a new instrument to try that is definitely affordable.
Musical_Instruments.summary: If you're looking for a great starter ukulele, try the Makala!  You'll be happy you did!

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
First, the disclaimer.  The KLIQ! people gave me a discount on this product in return for agreeing to write a review.
However, after using the capo for a week or so, I can say without embarrassment that it this best capo I have owned so far.  I also have, and have used, a basic Shubb capo and and spring-loaded one from Keyser, as well as the cheap elastic kind, and the KLIQ K-PO is he best--really.  You don't have to worry about getting the right pressure (like the Shubb) or having to have hands like a gorilla to place it (as with the Keyser).  It goes on easily and quickly and you can move it almost effortlessly from fret to fret.
I recommend this capo very highly--and I would do so even if I had not been given the price break on it.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Best Capo I've Owned So Far

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I did a lot of research to find the perfect mixer for my internet radio station.  I needed multiple lines, good construction, reliability, and performance.  This mixer was just what I was looking for.  Allen & Heath are the industry standard when it comes to broadcast consoles, but I wasn't going by name alone.  It by far met my expectations and more!  If you are putting together an internet radio station or small terrestrial station, this is the mixer for you.  I specially like the 2 TELCO lines with off air talk to the callers.  I highly recommend this mixer!

style.Color:: Dusk Sun Red w/ Hard Case

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: We love this little guitar. My wife is learning (or relearning) the guitar, and the old box she was using had some issues. This made a perfect Christmas gift, and even the few accomplished guitarists who have played with it in our living room are impressed with its initial quality. Time will tell if Yamaha's claim to quality is warranted, but for now, at least, this was one very nice package.

I've used this bag with a Roland XV 88 that weighs in at 60 pounds.  It handled the weight without ripping apart.  The bag was just the right size.  Zippers are heavy duty, had no problems zipping open or closed.

This bag is a keeper.

Although I kinda of pushed it to the max carrying a 60 lb keyboard, I'd recommend this keyboard bag to anyone.  Gator makes some of the best cases and bags out there.

I have put this bag through the wringer recently by moving twice and having to pack it away around other stuff. Not to mention taking it with me either in my car or on my bike more often than not when leaving my house. This case looks new still. It's easy to clean, as I found out the hard/funny way. The pocket can accommodate quite a lot of gear to pack along with and has enough cushion to keep me from worrying about it's impact on the body of my guitar. Lastly, it's easy to modify and customize. I added a separate pouch in the neck (where most hard body cases have a pocket). It was so easy in fact that I plan on inserting plastic around the body of the guitar. All in all, soft body cases are pretty general but this one makes me feel a bit safer that I'm putting my guitar in a case with some cushion that helps keep it more secure.
Musical_Instruments.summary: I have nothing but good things to say about this case. Quality bag.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
I'm very happy with my G3X. It's definitely built really strong and feels like it can stand quite a beating. The sound quality is great and doesn't have that digital computerized 'fake amp' sound. I also own a Line6 PodXT (which is still one of my most favorite modellers), a BOSS GT-8, Digitech GNX3 (which sounds very digital). So i have a lot of different references to compare it with. This little baby does an outstanding job at amp modelling and the various FX. It's very easy to operate this device and finding the sound you're looking for shouldn't take you long at all.

Operating the G3X with a set of Eneloop rechargeable batteries offers you many hours of running it without the need of the (included) power brick. I prefer the Eneloops since they will hold their charge for a much longer time than regular rechargeable batteries when leaving it in the device without using it for an extended period.

The LCD screen is nice and bright and the foot switches and knobs feel very solid and work very responsive and smooth.

I decided to get the version with the expression pedal. Even with the pedal it's still really nice compact and less than half the size of my other full size (floorboard) modellers. This thing is great for traveling for sure and will easily fit in a small case or backpack.

The sound of the built-in rhythm patterns isn't bad at all. I like it a lot better than the sound of the drums in my Digitech GNX-3 or my Boss DR-5 drum computer. The looper works great too, it has a nice long recording time and operates easy and smooth. I only wish it would record and playback the guitar sound in stereo instead of mono.

Hooking it up to a PC with USB is super easy as well. It's great that the computer will power the device through USB when you don't have the power hooked up to it or no batteries inserted. And using the included library software on your computer makes presets even easier to (re)organize. The visual representation of all the built-in amps and stomp boxes makes it a breeze to set up a preset real fast.

I have the G3X for a few months now and am very impressed and happy with the overall value of this product. I would highly recommend this for the traveling musician but also for the beginning player that just likes to play in the privacy of his own room and try out many different sounds and effects without breaking the bank. This bad boy is an absolute joy to play around with.

Two metal horns way up!
Musical_Instruments.summary: Great quality sound and built like a tank

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: This is a great intermediate guitar and great for people who don't want to spend $1000+ to get a great sound.  I started off playing for about a year and a half with a Yamaha FG700s and this was definitely an upgrade.  The sound is very crisp, but beware, it is a little higher than some other guitars and may not particularly suit certain types of music (depending on what you like to play).  I'm not positive, but I'm pretty sure it comes equipped with Elixir strings that seem to sound a little brighter than some other strings.  Overall, great guitar for the money and I'd highly recommend  for anyone who wants a step up from the beginner models without emptying their pockets.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Great Sound, Awesome Guitar for the Money

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I was prepared to be disappointed. I was not. 30 years ago, one of my ambitions was to learn how to play the electric guitar. I bought a used 79 Ibenez LesPaul. I loved the guitar. The amp was a Crate. I was not enthusiastic about the sounds I was getting, and my interest waned. I read all the reviews, and most every review was correct. GREAT guitar. Than I got the Fender Mustang Amp, and the two combined revived my enthusiasm. If I had this guitar and this amp 30 years ago, I would probably still be playing.

I bought this guitar for my daughter's birthday, and later, when we got her in guitar lessons, found out the one we received had a problem with how it played.  Even though it had been well over 30 days, we received a new guitar in the mail, in great shape.  I was really impressed at their customer service.  For a guitar at this price, its a great deal and would recommend it to others.

What a lame name and color for such a unique pedal. Oh well.  This thing should cost more than $100 so I won't complain.

It really boils down to a set of DS-1 and SD-1 circuits tied together with the "color" knob to blend them along with other essential tweaks too lengthy to go into here.  I've owned a Boss Blues Driver for a while now and have found it limited for creamier tones.  It's a great pedal don't get me wrong but it really just sounds like a blackface Fender cranked.  I'm currently running a modded Blues Jr. with a Cannabis Rex which gives me good basic blackface tones.

Here's where this pedal shines IMHO.  i.e., PROS

With a Tele with Fender OV pups and the pedal tone @ 7, drive @ 9, and color @ 2 o'clock, respectively, this thing sounds almost exactly like a Vox AC-15 on the top boost channel with the gain and master at around 10 o'clock.  I actually tried this pedal with the above settings on my brothers AC-15 and couldn't believe how similar it sounded.  That chimey natural sweet breakup is here in spades, pretty amazing since I wasn't necessarily looking for a Vox simulator! This tone sounds like nothing you'd get from a DS-1 or SD-1.

With a Les Paul studio and pedal tone @ 9, drive@ 3, and color @ 2 o'clock, respectively, this thing sounds similar to a cranked Marshall.  Crazy pinch harmonics and chunky fatness and sustain for days.  It handily slapped the Rat 2 all over the room with the sheer gutsiness of harmonic complexity and killed it in dynamics as well at lower gain settings. Think of the raspy guitar tone from GNR's Paradise City and you'll get the idea.  This tone sounds like nothing you'd get from a DS-1 or SD-1.

CONS

1. The tone knob seems pretty useless to me anywhere above 9 o'clock.  I haven't played it on stage or in a band though so maybe it would be useful in such scenarios.

2. It's not a transparent pedal but nowhere near as bad as a lot of other stuff out there cheap and/or expensive.  In a live situation I doubt you'd notice it but sitting in front of the amp in a quiet room you'll hear some of your highs go bye-bye.  I bet the tone knob could be tweaked to adjust the top end sparkle but honestly the pedal is so fun to play you'll get over it..

3. The color knob is tricky.  I could not find a use for it anywhere below 12 o'clock.  It started to sound a lot like an SD-1 which isn't a terrible pedal.  I guess if you were recording you'd find this useful for getting compressed singing lead tones.

4. It's an ugly orange/yellow pedal that looks like it was marketed by the engineering department.

Manager: Hey you Mr. Smart Engineer with mismatched clothes. Come up with a name and look for the pedal by next week.  I was slacking off reading articles about golf clubs so you need to hurry up and get this done even though you've designed a totally awesome and unique sounding pedal in the minimal time/budget we provided you.

ENGINEER: Call it the Overdrive / Distortion because that's what it is.

Is it?  I don't think so. But what do I know? I'm just an engineer who loves to play guitar and build pedals sometimes.

While I did not purchase this from this vendor, I am so pleased with this light so far that I wanted to write a review.  Super excited that it is programmable, but even on it's own, the music activation is impressive as it syncs almost perfectly with whichever track is currently playing.  While there are moments I get worried that it isn't doing what I would expect it to, I've learned to trust the built in program and it seems to make sense in the end.  Excited to add another in the near future to my array.  Looks great with a fog machine too!

I am in the broadcasting profession, and had been searching for a microphone to use in my own voice-over business.  Over the years there were recommendations given from people with whom I worked about different mics.  Having been a victim of the economy, I needed a really good microphone that wouldn't bust the budget.  There were many options from which to choose.  The MXL brand has a good reputation among voice-over artists, so that is the route I chose.  But which model?  I chose the MXL 770 for it's features, of course, but one factor that drew me back to it was it's appearance.  It just has that 'quality' look about it plus I really like the coloring.  It is so different from other mics  which I have used over the years.  It has a warmth and fullness to it.  In the proper setting, it works like a charm.  And you can't beat the value.  If you want something that will give you a quality sound without breaking the bank, then I would give the MXL 770 a solid go.

I ordered this package because I wanted a playable violin with all the necessary accessories at the lowest price.  I was able to open the case, rosin the bow, position the bridge, tune up the violin and start playing.

If you buy a violin from a shop, they will set it up for you.  Setting up is the process of making final adjustments to the violin so that it functions smoothly and suits the musician.  Those of us who buy online have to either complete the setup ourselves or find someone to do it for us.  The Merano violin comes with an instruction sheet called "How to Set Up a Violin".  It tells how to install the bridge, how to tune the violin, and how to rosin the bow.  At the very end, the instructions mention that you might also want to sand the bridge down one millimeter at a time until you are satisfied with the way the violin plays.  The instructions also mention that you can put rosin on the tuning pegs to keep them from slipping.

If you're not comfortable and happy with the way the violin plays after the basic setup, you need to go back to the Internet and find out how to do the more advanced adjustments.  You may want to adjust the string height above the fingerboard, the separation between strings, and the curve of the top of the bridge.

The default setup of the Merano violin didn't suit me.  The strings were too high for my taste, which means extra force must be applied by the fingers to press strings down to the fingerboard.  Also, the strings were set too close together for my big blunt fingers.  The default setup might be okay for someone with long thin fingers.  I lowered my strings by sanding down the bridge and filing down the nut of the violin.  I increased the separation between strings by filing new notches in the nut with a triangular file.  It took me about two hours.

One thing I really like about this inexpensive violin is that if I drop it or make some mistake adjusting it, the maximum possible damage is still less than $100.  My other violin is a professional grade instrument and I'm afraid to do any adjustment on it myself for fear of making a mistake.  I think the Merano will probably become my favorite violin for casual playing.

Update: After six weeks I'm still pleased with the violin.
Musical_Instruments.summary: A good value package but you have to set up the violin yourself.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I love this! Before purchasing this, I had been researching and reading so many reviews of different guitar humidifiers. This is the only guitar humidifier I could find that did not have any history of it leaking inside guitars. This was very important to me. I would be devastated if it were to leak inside my guitar. I currently own a single unit humitar, as well as a humitar/humireader package. I really do trust that this will not leak into my guitar. It is very simple, all you have to do is soak distilled water into the sponge every week. The sponge holds a lot of water! I recommend purchasing the humitar/humireader package first. The humireader is pretty accurate, I have another humidity monitor in my room, and they are about 1-2% off. The humidity in the guitar case is going to be different then the humidity inside the guitar. It is a good idea to monitor the humidity levels because you do not want to over or under humidify your guitar. There have been a few instances where the humireader in my guitar read 65%, which proves that this product is effective but that is way over the recommended humidity level. I would not have otherwise knew I that the humidifying levels where too high without the humireader. It is cheaper to buy the humitar/humitar package together, rather than buying the only the humireader. The only thing that would make this product better is if it didn't stretch the guitar strings so far apart. Just would like if the product was a little thinner. I hope this was helpful. Definitely recommended!
Musical_Instruments.summary: Very effective, easy/cheap to maintain, and trustworthy.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
This is an interesting product.

At first I was confused with the setup, but make sure to look for the folder for the usb drums.  There are other downloads in there for stuff to download on your computer (example, keyboard and so on), which is nice so you can download other things for your kids to play on.

When you connect this to your computer and download using the included cd, it was have a screen that comes up (see my photo) that shows you the sounds and you can change up the type of drum used.

My son has really taken to it.  I personally wish that it just made noise without being connected to anything, but still a cute idea.

It was an excellent purchase for me!  I received this item at a discount in exchange for an honest review.  My review is absolutely true to my experience and in no way reflects any sort of promotion incentive. My opinions about this product are honest and are my own in an attempt to help other buyers like me make educated purchases. I reserve the right to change my review at any time if I find the product to not be as I thought before.

Overall the set is definitely worth it for any beginner to intermediate drummer. The hi-hats are definitely the best out of the set and sound close to some higher end cymbals. The crash is what you would expect for the price, not the best but still quite nice. The splash is slightly better than the crash with a nice sharp sound. Overall this was definitely worth the purchase and has made a fantastic addition to my set.

These medium duty speaker stands are probably the best speaker stand deal available on Amazon right now.  They're replacing a pair of light duty Sampson speaker stands.

The Sampson stands lasted me quite a while but, to replace them would have been more expensive than to buy these Hola stands and I'd still need to purchase a bag for them.

Haven't used the new stands live yet but, the materials are high quality and the construction seems good.  A VERY worthwhile upgrade from light duty speaker stands.

Used them for the first time last night.  Good and solid.  Don't expect any problems.  Don't waste any more time comparing prices, ust buy these and be done with it!
Musical_Instruments.summary: Got more than I bargained for

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: My husband loves musical instruments and was shopping around for banjos. Unfortunately they are a bit more than we wanted to shell out at the moment. I found this canjo, read through the reviews and had a good laugh with my husband....it's a can on a stick! The reviews have many who've said they got it as a gag gift but ended up loving it....so I got it for his birthday. WONDERFUL! I agree with all the other positives! My husband enjoys playing it, it's easy for him to carry around, he loves showing it off, and it's fun for the whole family. I completely recommend one of these for everyone!
Musical_Instruments.summary: read through the reviews and had a good laugh with my husband

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I really, REALLY like this pickup. I put it in a project strat. It came with the wrong springs and screws so make sure to have your own to put in. The pickup was actually a little under 7.5k but is plenty loud to match my H/S/S setup. I love the tele pickup sound. This is definitely a cool addition to any strat. The wiring is solid and well insulated. The ground an hit lead are wound in the same cable which is nice. As someone who takes risks buying generic pickups, I can't tell oh how many times I've been disappointed. But I can tell you now, I am NOT disappointed.

This is a very well-built bag and should have no issues with offering protection for the drums to be stored within. The V-shape design of the main compartment zipper may seem a little odd at first, but makes sense in that it is easier to place/remove toms with brackets or mounts protruding from their side (rather than wrestle them all the way into regular snug-fitting bags). The zippers are pretty heavy gauge, making them hold strong and be less prone to jamming. Also, the shoulder pad strap latches are of solid metal construction.

I purchased the 10x12, 11x13, and 12x14 models, and here are a few features that these bags came with that weren't listed in the product description.

-A luggage-type identification tag is included that you can attach
-In addition to the rubber-padded shoulder strap, there are three carrying handles around the bag, making it easier to find a grip when fumbling around with it.
-On the bottom there are four rubber feet to add to the durability of the base and to reduce skidding.

This contents of this review are based on that fact that this keyboard costs under $200.  Just knowing that it costs under $200 should tell you right off the bat this is not for a professional musician, nor will it have professional quality and tone.
However,  if you are like me and just beginning or even perhaps an intermediate musician looking for a practice keyboard, this is probably the keyboard you want to buy.
I tried out many many keyboard in the $200 price range and this is the ONLY one I would buy.  If it were not for this keyboard, I would have spent over $500 on a Yamaha.
What I like about this is the keyboard has a semi-weighted feel to the keys and the piano tones are very lush and nice. The organ tones as well are awesome.
After using it for a few months the keys are starting to 'crackle' a little and realistically this keyboard could probably only stand about 3-4 years of use before it breaks down.
I have no regrets at all about purchasing this.  If I continue to play and enjoy playing, I will probably go out and buy a $700 range professional digital piano or keyboard down the road and sell this one or give it away.
Also, you do need to purchase an a/c power supply (so add another $20) and probably a simple stand ($25).  So make sure you factor in another $45 for accessories.
If you are the type of person who likes to buy once and have a product for life, this may not be what you are looking for.  I would recommend a higher quality instrument.
If you just want to start playing right away and don't have a big budget, this is the ONE keyboard to get.  Quite frankly, almost any keyboard under $200 is a piece of junk!
Musical_Instruments.summary: Has a nice feel to it and nice sound; recommended

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: So my boyfriend and I live in tiny condo, he plays the saxophone and uses one of those tall stands. It kinda got in the way - that one square foot of precious real estate being taken up by a black metal, toe stubbing eye sore.  Anyway, this little portable stand is great, doesn't take up floor space like the old one did. We usually keep it on a half wall ledge thats about 5" wide and it doesn't get in the way at all now. If only it would double as a sound shield for when he plays......wishful thinking

This is an amazing electric guitar!  I know these are made in South Korea but they're incredibly well-made. They just have a nice solid feel  to them. I love the set neck it helps with sustain. The frets are perfect size the tuners  hold tuning great and the active EMG pick ups are awesome!  They are really hot pick ups I like how this model has the push pull  coil tapping so you can still get a good clean signal on that bridge pick up by running only one .  I kick myself in the butt because I had one of these guitars and I sold it. But now I bought it back again and instead of having the trans parent red I have this nice purple burst which is beautiful !

NOTE - I bought these headphones from Status Audio direct during the Black Friday sale and received them a couple days ago, hence why this is not a verified purchase.
These are definitely the best closed back headphones I've owned to date [you can just my head-fi username conquerator2 for a complete list of gear that I've owned and tried]. They are a bit V shaped, with a deep punchy bass response and a broader 5.5 - 7K treble rise but they aren't nearly as recessed in the midrange as most V shaped headphones. On the contrary, these headphones are surprisingly detailed, with very good soundstage and imaging and a surprisingly open sound, without hints of a closed-in feel, which closed back headphones usually have. They are pretty comfy too [great pads] and the build quality is surprisingly decent! You can use any slim profile 3.5mm or 1/8' cable with these; I wasn't a big fan of the tangly straight or coiled cables that were included, so I use a nuforce cable. In conclusion, I am fairly impressed at what these headphones can achieve, considering the price. I enjoy listening to music on them and they can be a good commute headphone too, and why I wouldn't say they'd be my first pick if I were looking for a completely flat monitoring headphone [open headphones usually have an edge here], these will find a permanent staple in my productions as a great closed back for testing aspects like soundstage, bass and highs. These absolutely trounce Beats and would be my current recommendation in this price range.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Hard to nitpick for the money!

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I used this with an old Kawai K5000W and a new Akai Miniak on a new Windows 7 PC and a 3 year old Win-X workstation.  Worked without a hitch with stand alone virtual instruments and through Cubase.  Latency was low enough to be unnoticeable.  I think any keyboard made today should have a USB MIDI port but for those that don't (like the Akai) or for older synths (like my ancient Kawai) this works great and costs less than a single normal MIDI cable.

I recently purchased an LPB-1 because I had a need for a straight "booster" on my pedal board.  Boost pedals, as a concept, are an extremely straightforward concept, but the way they impact tone through an amp depends quite a bit on placement in the signal chain, settings, and the type of amp.  With these issues in mind, I struggled a bit to decide between a 4- or 5-star review, since the LPB-1 has some limitations conveying clean, "transparent" boost.  But given that EHX has made it extremely affordable ($40) and it functions very well for a particular type of boosted sound, I decided that there was enough "function for value" here to warrant 5 stars.

Boosts raise the amount gain in your signal, so the assumption by many is that this makes the audio "louder".  While this can be true, particularly if the boost is used later in the signal chain, boosts can just as much increase the saturation of the input signal, and hitting the preamp of a tube amp (or perhaps some modeling amps) may also cause it to overdrive.  The EHX LPB-1 has a single knob for adjusting the amount of added gain - there are no tone controls or additional parameters.  But, used with other pedals (and the settings on your amp), tone control in a booster is more of a luxury than a necessity.

Choosing between boosters can be difficult because you really won't know how they function until you use them with your own rig.  I opted for the LPB-1 instead of the MXR Micro Amp (itself a single-knob industry standard) because the LPB-1 tends to be warmer and fuller sounding.  On a large, bassy amplifier, this may not be desirable.  But on a 10" bright combo amp, such as my Fender Super Champ X2, this is a desirable quality.

Some critics of the LPB-1 have noted that the LPB-1 will get "dirtier" more easily than other boost pedals.  Some have even noticed that there is a mid boost with overdrive, almost like a Tubescreamer.  However, this was a sound I actually wanted, and if you have a amp that can stay clean at high enough volumes, the LPB-1 should add additional saturation and "fullness" to that tone, without making it sound like an overdrive pedal.

I think the LPB-1 may make sense for a lot of players who use smaller, brighter amps since it is affordable and pairs well with that type of sound.  If your are looking for a boost to stack in front of other overdrive pedals to emphasize for lead work, you could consider the Micro Amp, or something with tone controls like the Micro Amp+ or Blackstar LT Boost.  In my case, I have the Soul Food (also made by EHX), which offers a lot of clean boost at low overdrive settings, but is considerably brighter than this LPB-1.  Between the two, I should have most of my needs covered.  The LPB-1 is a tested and proven classic and a great value for a blues/crunch sound, or to emphasize other pedals by giving them "just a little more".
Musical_Instruments.summary: Warm, affordable boost great for pairing with bright amps

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I started on Tenor when I was in sixth grade, but I never got to try the Bari until Seventh! After the first try, I've fallen in love with it and played it ever since. So recently, when I entered highschool and the marching band, I of course had to play the Bari. Being the 14-year old, 5'5, 105 pound girl that I am, this harness does the job but I have to crane my neck even after the highest it can be tightened. I absolutely adore the Bari sax, but I'm having some serious back pain! Is it weird to have a soul-instrument? Like a soul-mate? Parting with the Bari isn't even in consideration, but now this is the third harness I've bought, and I don't know what to do!

This karoake never worked properly, that is-the screen never displayed words at all. We hooked it up to the tv and used it that way. It's a bit more of a hassle and I hate that it didn't work as described right off the bat but we are happy with the way it has been working hooking it up to the tv. It was a gift to my kid and we didn't open in time to return it-so I didn't even bother with that route. But if you are looking to buy this for someone else you should test it before gifting it.
Musical_Instruments.summary: screen never worked-but we made it work

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
I've owned two of these and both were junk.  The battery compartment doors failed on both, rendering them useless.  The cheaper G-30 has received bad reviews for the exact same reason.  LINE 6 has absolutely zero customer service and support.  Don't buy anything from this company.

The above was my original review, written in haste and anger out of frustration.  While the battery doors continue to be a problem with this unit, it does perform fairly well as long as the rubber bands hold the doors closed!  I hope LINE 6 watches for reviews like this and remedies the problem for other future buyers.

I loved the look of the abalone picks which I bought a couple years ago, which are shown correctly in the photo, but the new formula looks really bad.  This batch has the newer packaging.  There is too much black and white, and it almost looks like zebra stripes, not like a shiny shell color.  I am hoping I just got a bad batch, and they are not trying to cut cost.  Otherwise, the picks seem to perform the same playing wise.

I received these headphones as a Christmas present.  Within two days they'd broken, but I was able to return them quite easily and comprehensibly.  I was sent a replacement pair, and have been using them since.
I have found two main problems with these headphones.  The first is that they aren't really constructed all that sturdily.  They're almost cheap in construction.  The second is that they don't quite fit.  The description says 'good for kids and adults' so I thought they would have a much greater range of adjustment than they do.  These headphones are just too big to fit comfortably - I currently have to fold a paper towel and wedge it between the band and my head in order to wear them without my ears hurting.
One should also note that the coloring is different than that in the image.  The colors are not as vibrant as shown, and there is not as much blue in the actual design, they're mostly pink.
On the plus side, I love the sound quality of these headphones.  While they are not sound cancelling, they are noise isolating.  My music sounds really good through these; I'm hearing all sorts of new layers in songs I thought I knew like the back of my hand!

Overall, the headphones sound great, but are not constructed all that well.  They're not worth 30 dollars, but I'm not regretting my purchase of them either.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Good sound, but a lot of hassle

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: This stand is heavy duty and seem well made. It is fine for dynamic mics and works well for all but the heaviest large condenser mics. Unfortunately that is exactly what I wanted it for. The issue is that you cannot extend the 16" boom past about about 4 inches with these heavy mics. A larger base would probably solve this problem but then it would take up a lot of desktop real estate. I secured the base to my desk with a clamp and that solves the problem. Other than that this is a worthwhile addition to my studio gear.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Long enough boom for desktop use

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: fits on top of my Zoom H4N just fine, took it out on a mildly windy day in the city about 20 min from the beach to record a short film outdoors. it does noticeably reduce wind noise but will not remove it altogether. still got some wind crackling in my recordings, so if you've got professional work you might as well just charge a professional price in your invoice and pay for something a little better to be safe, but in an indoor setting with a few fans running this thing does just fine.

I've never used this type of product before and I don't think I ever will again. I used it the way it states on label one should use it. Run the lubricant before you play and after. My strings are still pretty dirty on the first three fret and they surely don't sound like new strings anymore. What I do like about it is that it does help your fingers from getting stuck to the strings and making that annoying screeching sound when you run your fingers across the strings to play different chords. But it hasn't kept my stings looking new and it didn't help keep the tone of new strings. So I would rate this item as a 3.

Returned it. I got this because I wanted something with 88 preferably weighted keys that we can put in my kid's room so she can practice in her room. But the keys have a horrible feel. They would spring back at you with a cheep plastic feel. One of the other reviews called it a toy and this is what it is. I ended up getting the Yamaha P71 which was more but the keys feel incredible after the Alesis. I'm not sure why anyone would get this. It is too expensive for a toy and you can't call it a piano. I guess they call it a beginner piano but I can't imagine someone using this more than a few months and given the price difference to the P71, one would be much  better off getting something more expensive to begin with.

Yahama is normally a pretty good value. In the music world they make good quality stuff but not great quality. Not the bottom rung by any change but certainly not top-notch.
Probably for the price this is the best quality you're going to find, with Ibanez maybe being a close second. The guitar will do the job and fit & finish is quite good for a cheaper guitar, but like any cheaper guitar its not going to have incredible acoustic volume.
If money is not an object and you like Yamaha, check out their flamenco versions which are normally a couple hundred dollars more. Those are nice guitars.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Its ok, you get what you pay for

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
I had hoped this pageflip would have been sturdy, reliable and supported.  However this has not always been the case.

First off, it's made out of a cheap plastic and long term durability is questionable.

Secondly, It had intermittent sync with my ipad.  It just disconnect when it feels like it.  Like in the MIDDLE OF A SONG DURING A GIG!!!

Thirdly, When my gigging partner has his pageflip on, my sync just quits. What is that about?

Unreliable would be the bottom line here.  I've emailed tech support and have not yet received an adequate reply.

I had hoped this would be better than the AirTurn BT-105 @ $119, but it has it's share of issues too.  Perhaps all these devices are ineffective.

I bought these for my home studio.  Looked good online.  When I received them I was disappointed.  The microphone clips are so big they do not accommodate the most common sizes of microphones.  The stands are light weight, but very rickety.  One of the post head/threads is already loose.  They will be ok in a studio situation, but not a good choice for live gigs.  Once I used my other mic clips and retired one as a coat stand, I ended up with 4 ok stands.

I needed a stand and was attracted to this 1) because of the price and 2) because of the reviews.  I think the stand is ok but nothing to rave about.  I almost returned it because it just does not seem super stable to me.  My alto sax does fit but the setup has a bit of a wobbly feel to me even with all the screws firmly tightened.  The support arm slips into the middle socket and then there is a thumb screw at the base you use to tighten that arm inside the base.  Since my only intention with this is for a home stand where I will not be subjecting the sax to much toppling risk I decided to keep it rather than deal with returning it and then find a different stand.  If I was playing out and wanted a really safe stand I would probably do more research and find the most stable and protective stand out there.  For less than $13 including tax and free Prime shipping however, I will keep this.  It does get the job done but does not leave me with a feeling of complete security for my sax.  3 stars from me - ok but if something should happen to it I would look to upgrade to a higher stability model.

An OK universal case with some drawbacks: It needs TWO handles rather than one in center--keyboards that fit this are too heavy for 1 handle.  It does not have enough cushioning in the base where the wheels and back sleds drag over steps; There is not enough storage for pedals and chords.  The back "sleds" are made so that they CATCH on stairs and door jambs when being rolled! Need some angle skids to fix this and another handle horizontally at the foot so a follower can help lift the unit when it is towed on wheels.  Look for a different case.

The installation and setup of this device on a mac is literally plug and play. My mac picked up the device right away and I was able to use it using garageband. I bought this device to use with my electronic drum set, but it didn't really pick up the snare and toms well. For the price, I really can't complain about the usb-to-midi device, but if you want something that records well I suggest you invest a bit more and get something better.

I purchased this guitar because it had a Telecaster body and was cheaper than a Fender or the Squire version of Fender. A guitar's a guitar right?
Well, the reason it's cheaper is because cheaper parts were made to put it together.

The black paint on the body picks up the slightest scratch. Picture a cheap paint job on a car compared to a really well done paint job on a car. The well done paint job is going to cost more.

The pickups are adequate. I changed the pickups to Fender pickups and there was a significant difference in tone and volume.

I like the guitar for the reasons I purchased it, it wasn't expensive and had a Telecaster body. But I dislike the guitar because, well, it's cheaply made in comparison to the Fender or Squire models. If I had to do it all over again, I'd invest $80 more dollars and get the Squire.

If you're not a guitar fanatic and just want a cost efficient Telecaster body, this is an adequate guitar but if you're looking for a guitar to gig with or actually take it outside of your house, you'll need to change the pickups and expect the paint to be lacking in quality.

Fairly good sound from the stock humbucker pickups, but if you put on some aftermarket ones, the sound will be even better.  The tuners don't seem to slip, but aftermarket ones would help.
Distortion and sustain perfect for some hard rock or metal music, but with volume turned down it is so-so.
The 'black satin' finish is flat black, like unfinished carbonfiber, but its easy to keep fingerprint-free.
As a first electric guitar for the metal guitarist or future shredder, this will beat a cheap Squier Bullet or Affinity Strat, or the cheaper Epiphone Les Paul models.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Good value for a first electric guitar

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: Shipping was prompt and the price was nice and low for a full size violin.  Obviously this is a low quality instrument made in china so don't expect it to be amazing.  The wood is a nice color and the craftsmanship is not bad.  It's certainly not made for kids learning considering it's full size.  It works fine for an adult to learn on and as long as you're careful it shouldn't fall apart or anything.  Just to comment on some other reviews, the bridge isn't supposed to be glued to the body, most string instrument parts are held in place by the tension of the strings.  First of all I'd recommend getting better rosin for this, after I got better rosin it played much better.  If you purchase a good set of strings this would also greatly improve the sound.  The tuning pegs on it don't work the best so I recommend getting it in the ballpark range with the pegs and then use the fine tuners the rest of the way.  Be sure to reset the bridge after tuning.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Sometimes you get slightly better than what you pay for.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I love the purple violin that i purchased for my daughter. And the seller shipped it to me and it was received overseas in around two weeks. But i was disappointed with the bow that came with the instrument. I had to go buy a usable bow in order for her to play the pretty purple violin. The cotton hair fiber that the bow was strung with would not even pull a sound. By 110lb American Bull dog named enjoyed finishing ripping it up.

The case is nice looking. My high-school daughter was/is pleased with it. I am the one who knows the quality of the hardware used is sub-standard. The handle, hinges, rivets and buckles are woefully cheap. The buckles do not move smoothly and have already bound up a few times in the case's brief and occasional use with us. I don't have confidence the hinges will last.  When they break or otherwise malfunction, there will be challenges replacing them because rivets were used instead of screws. The same issue of rivets also prevents the quick swapping out of the cheap looking plastic molded handle, which, I would do just because how bad the handle looks against the beautiful outer case. The inside is ok. I haven't looked at it closely.
So there you have it.
Again, you get what you pay for. And I would have been willing to pay more if I were assured of better quality hardware on this case.
Musical_Instruments.summary: You Get What You Pay For... I would have paid more

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
The sound is fine. I'm not an expert in this area, but I'm satisfied with the sensitivity and ability to capture rich base tones for the limited sort of voiceover and screencast work I very occasionally need to do. I have had ZERO connectivity issues within OS X and apps like ScreenFlow and GarageBand....to borrow an old clich, it just works.

The place where this mic fails to impress are on both the design and build quality fronts.

Design: First, a small head's up - the mic is probably much larger than you expect. I am not deducting points for this, as obviously, the dimensions are available and I should have looked into it more closely before ordering - but I still think it's fair to warn you, it's oddly large, garish, and frankly just not very nice to hold or look at in person.

Aesthetics aside, I would have liked that the mic head could be panned vertically as you really need to lean down to speak directly into it when having it on a desk. The design of the mount and the stand that accompany it don't allow for this. Prepare to stoop a bit to get good vocal contact. The lack of a mute button, or an off switch of any kind was also disappointing.

Janky Construction: The LED light in mine that sits front and center is mounted about 20 degrees off of flush. The silver band that divides the axis of the orb is a sticker made to simulate the look of brushed metal. Because mine was sloppily applied and has air bubbles in it, the effect is ...not achieved. The small desk stand that ships with it is made of a very cheap alloy, the lock threads on the telescopic function barely work, and the black rubber feet are also prone to marking up your desk if you move it around. The "Blue" logo front and center is a horribly chromed plastic. All in all... a major bummer quality wise. Assembled in China, and without care or oversight from anyone with an eye for detail.

The design eccentricities (large size, garish chrome grill) might have worked if the materials used had been quality. Then again, maybe I'm asking too much of a 100 dollar piece of hardware. Still, based on this experience, I don't think I will buy a mic made by Blue again. They should have toned down the ambitious design flourishes if they didn't have the money to execute them with good materials.

I would have given it one star, but only because I have young kids and they would rather blow it like a whistle than actually learn a tune on it. The extra two stars are for the cuteness of a 5yo who finally learns to skreetch out "Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star"

Product wise, it's hard to make a crappy tin whistle, so Clarke is the best.

To sum it all up: 5 stars for Clarke, 1 star for the kids for a total of 6 stars. Minus 3 stars for the learning curve for young children.

I bought a Bigsby B7 from Amazon several months ago.  I attempted to install it directly on my Les Paul traditional and one of the two screws that hold the Bigsby down broke.  I thought my guitar was ruined for life (since one piece of the screw stayed in the guitar).  Recently, I found out about Vibramate.  Let me tell you, this allowed me to finally install the Bigsby on my guitar with zero hassle!  I was able to cover up the previous holes.  My guitar looks stunning once again!

My point: You may struggle with the installation but it's a good product once installed.  You may want to consider Vibramate (works like a charm and keeps you from drilling holes in your guitar).
Musical_Instruments.summary: Flimsy screws but good product once installed

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: The most desirable feature of this unit, he VSL zero latency software, no longer works with more recent versions of Mac OSX. The VSL software has been discontinued as has this piece of hardware and therefore is no longer supported by Presonus. I have this unit and its very nice,  study and reliable but no longer offers the feature I wanted. Also the newer ones cost less than this one here on Amazon.
Musical_Instruments.summary: This unit has been discontinued and no longer supported by Presonus. The VSL software feature no longer works.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
I bought this unit from another outlet. I thought 15 dollars was worth the gamble to see if a flanger would be useful to me. It's a fine effect when used sparingly. The plastic case some people complain about is not that big a deal. It's pretty sturdy. I don't see it breaking just because you drop it, or even throw it, on the ground.
  The bad news is that 5 days after I would have been able to send it back, day 50 of ownership, it seems to have taken a turn for the worse. It developed an annoying hiss/buzz when it reaches the apogee of its sweep. I tried to figure out some way of isolating the problem hoping it would be one of the cables (Why would that be better? The cables cost more than the pedal!)but it turned out to be in the flanger itself.
  I'm going to replace it for sure with a more reliable pedal but this thing served its purpose and hopefully I can adjust the setting and take the noise out of it and use it on my practice amp.

I myself have not used it, i inspected it when it arrived to make sure it looked alright and nothing was damaged or missing, however I do not play. string was broken but it came with another so was easily replaced.

My 17 year old wanted this. she has played one before and has a fair grasp of how to use it from school and choir. according to her nothing she does can make this thing sound like it should. she would attempt to play it almost every night for the first month or so but has become so frustrated now a few months later that she rarely to never pulls it out.
Musical_Instruments.summary: writing this as a parent of a teenager so keep that in mind.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
Zipper pull broke - replaced with a keychain ring - then the other zipper pull disintegrated.  Now must use one zipper for the whole case. Outer pocket zipper pulls are broken - paperclips in place for those.  Case stays shut with latch if all else fails.  Lid gapes about 1/4 inch when using only the latch.

Both bow holders broke - the plastic base for the twist-lock broke away leaving two screws each holding a tiny amount of plastic.  Could buy replacements.

All new lightweight cases are made of styrofoam.  It's cheap and almost weightless, but it has little to offer construction-wise.  Expect the fabric to come away from the case and any screws to loosen and fall out.

This case was eleven dollars from Amazon Warehouse.  I cannot complain at that rate because the handles work and the violin is protected.  Even with the faults it has developed in one year of use, this case is better than 90% of the lightweight cases I've had to repair.

As a teacher (and handyman for many students' cases), I think the best choice is still a thermoplastic case.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Do not expect wonders - it's still styrofoam with poor zippers.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I ordered this product to eliminate a ground loop when recording my guitars through a line 6 audio interface. I purchased a new HP Pavillion laptop with a three prong power supply and that apparently is the cause of the loop. This product did eliminate the ground loop noise, but it also sacked out most of the high end of all my guitars and basses. Basically it's just a high pass filter to cut out the very top end and presence of the instrument connected through it. Luckily I was able to connect an mxr eq pedal in the loop to bring some of the high end back. But using this device alone is not really a good solution if your having the same problem I was.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Not bad, but sucks out the presence of the guitar

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
So this is my second review of Gibson Melody Makers. I am completely satisfied with my first Les Paul version. I ordered 2 more of the SG version and will describe what I recieved.

The first one was perfect. No issues, but it was noticeably heavy. More about this later.

The second one had some of the same issues that sgbuyer describes. The pick guard was warped or had bubbled up in the exact same spot as his, near the bridge and jack. Mine also has lifted up at the point near the bottom cut away. Some of the pick guard screws are install at an angle and not perpendicular to the guitar surface. It looks sloppy. The headstock, fingerboard and frets also show a lack of attention. The back of the headstock where the serial # is stamped was not finished completely. It was not sanded flat so the first and last number of the serial number are very faint. The "made in" stamp is barely discernable. Yes these are cosmetic, but it show a lack of quality control for this guitar. How hard can it be to sand it flat and not have the surface have "rolling hills" which prevent the stamp from working properly. The fingerboard is missing a chunck at the nut in the first fret at the bottom e string. It looks like the corner edge splintered off. The surface between frets show unsanded wood blothches, that would have disappeared had a hair more wood been sanded off. The frets have some kind or residue on the sides, corrosion or wood stain which will not scratch off.

I find it weird that one instrument can have so many issues especially in light of the personally signed quality inspection check list Gibson provides with the guitar. One of these cosmetic issues would be acceptable to me. All of them together is just not right.

These guitars may have a wide spec variance because of the cheap price, understandably. The SG model had the lighter colored maple fingerboard, the les Paul I bought has a darker wood with a different grain. Another example of this variance is the difference in weight between the 2 SGs. One felt as heavy as a real Les Paul when I pulled it from the box. One weighed 6.4 lbs (as did my MM LP). The other weighed 7.4 lbs! A full pound heavier. Both sound and play fine though.

EDIT: I also contacted Gibson. The Customer service guy was not very patient but did issue me a RMA#. He said they might just send me another if it can't be repaired. I was told I would need to pay for return shipping. That was the deal breaker. I just returned it to amazon.

Pros:
Great Bass
Vibrant color (not as bright lime green as picture shows but still awesome)
Great Price

Cons:
Amazon.

The bass is great. I've played a lot of basses, this is the first dean bass I've played however I really enjoy it. It's lightweight, sounds good, nothing wrong with it and overall great price. The only problem I had with it is the shipping. I'm an Amazon Prime member and it took twice as long (and a whole other order) to get the bass delivered. This is the second package they've had to re-ship. This generally wouldn't be a big deal however you can find the bass cheaper at Guitar Center. I was willing to pay more to get it shipped fast, however I wish I would've just drove or ordered it from Guitar Center.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Great bass. Love it. Would be perfect if it didn't take twice as long as it was supposed to.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: I've had these pickups for about a month. They installed quickly and easily and they sound great. However there is a design flaw. The pickups connect to a wiring harness on the bottom of the pickup. The connection for that harness abruptly fell off the pickup and the pickup went dead. Now I have to play games to get them replaced and there is no guarantee that the replacement pickups will be better.

Seller is great, Product is garbage, Wiring diagrams are Teeeny weeeny,The ones that you down load from their web site is totally wrong, The one their tech sent me didn't work either Product does not work at all, Cannot ever get dimarzio support on the phone so I have an expensive lesson, Then I'm going to rip them out and throw them at cars on the highway, Really the MIM stock were better,, They worked! So save your money, Buy a nice set of anything but these, Pure crap and no customer support, Unless you enjoy wasting your money then your gonna love these.

I was very excite when I ordered this bench.  I have a Yamaha keyboard and a Yamaha keyboard stand, both of which are of exceptional quality.  Not so with this bench.  When I took the bench out of the box, it looked sturdy and well made.  I was a little disappointed at the mechanism that was used for raising and lowering the bench.  As mentioned in other reviews, the mechanism is cumbersome.  You have to remove a screw and some washers, do the adjustment and then put the screw and washers back. I've ordered some replacement 3W SMD LEDS and proper thermal adhesive, I'm hoping that will solve the problem. Eyourlife support was laughably bad and chose to send out replacement controllers instead of the LED board, even when this same issue has been reported in these reviews. Avoid these lights if you can! Pictures are of the LED board lit full red as is; the faulty LED in the outer red ring shorted (increases brightness in outer ring), and the faulty LED in the inner red ring shorted (inner ring actually lights up)

Musical_Instruments.reviewText: Yes, this is the cheapest, but unless you compare to the other products that Froggy's Fog makes, you won't realize how truly poor this fog looks outdoors.  We use three 400w foggers and this juice just makes dull, grey "smoke" that quickly dissipates.  Spend a few more dollars and don't waste your money on this.  If you upgrade to their Backwood Bay, or Bog Fog (which needs a higher wattage machine), you will get nice white FOG that actually hangs around.  We tested all of these and are going with Backwood Bay for our 400W machines (approved by the Froggy's website juice finder for 400W machines). The other thing is that this cheap stuff gets sucked up and used at a faster rate by the fog machines; the Backwood Bay and Bog Fog make more and better white fog, and they get used up more slowly by the machines.  So, that offsets the higher prices.  I wish I could return this gallon of weak fog juice that I wasted money on!  Oh well.
Musical_Instruments.summary: Not cost effective!  Get the other, real fog juice that Froggy's sells.

Musical_Instruments.reviewText:
To give you a bit of background, I bought this product about 6 months ago when I started building my recording studio and was very excited about the build quality and the looks of the thing. It is built like a tank and looks gorgeous. It was going to be the centerpiece of my studio.

Then I kept running into issues with pops and crackles even on my incredibly fast computer (4.5 Ghz overclocked with 8 gb of ram and no bottlenecks). I thought it must be some sort of issue with how windows 7 is dealing with this usb audio interface because latencymon kept telling me that my computer was unsuitable for real-time audio. So I went on several google marathons trying to figure out the issue and played with every setting imaginable both in windows and in my bios. I updated every driver and opened my pc countless times trying to reconfigure hardware.

I kept being defeated by this little box, but I noticed the vast amount of forum threads where people were having problems with this product on windows computers. And it seemed Native Instruments was just completely ignoring the community. So today I ran across a thread that just had a lot of information pointing to the fact that this might just be a faulty product with bad drivers for windows. It made so much sense because I tried disconnecting the device and running latencymon, which showed a totally health system and right after I plugged it in the problems immediately came back. I cannot believe I wasted 6 months of my time to figure this out!

http://www.native-instruments.com/forum/threads/komplete-audio-6-clicks-dropouts-cpu-spikes-every-15-seconds. 217813/

I will be getting rid of this product as fast as I can and buying the cheaper focusrite scarlett 2i2, which nobody is having problems with.

TL;DR: Don't buy this product if you own a windows computer. All the optimization in the world will not fix the faulty drivers that come with this audio interface and you won't be getting any help from the manufacturer.
