When I see a book listed in the mystery/thriller/suspense genres and it has a somewhat creepy sounding book description, once I open the book I'm expecting a few goosebumps somewhere along the way, a bit of a shiver down my spine or at least some twists I didn't see coming.  I didn't get that from this book which I found disappointing.

What I did get was a very well written, straight forward, solid story.  It just wasn't very exciting.  It was kind of like when you ask someone how they are expecting a response of fine and they instead proceed to basically tell you fine, but it takes them over 20 minutes to do it so that you tend to zone out somewhere along the way.

I was right there with Fred with every step he took along the way in this story until the last couple of pages when I realized nothing much was going to happen.  I kept waiting for the suspense to creep up on me, some unexpected thing to happen, something to shake things up, but it never did.  Unfortunately a short story that sounded so filled with promise ended with a whimper instead of a bang.  It just stayed bland.

3 stars because what you got truly wasn't bad, just a bit boring and maybe not what you were expecting...

First of all, I really like Dragos Roua's posts at his website. He's an extremely intelligent guy with excellent writing skills. However, His definition of "living off the grid," is not the standard definition. I hadn't caught up with Dragos lately and thought, based on this ebook title and subtitle, that he had truly gone OFF the grid. His definition is living without socially accepted descriptions of a regular job, basically just not following traditional social and work rules. He describes it as living, "...outside a normal grid of rules."

What does "Off The Grid" really mean? It's a pretty accepted definition. For example, from Wikipedia: "Off-the-grid homes are autonomous; they do not rely on municipal water supply, sewer, natural gas, electrical power grid, or similar utility services. A true off-grid house is able to operate completely independently of all traditional public utility services."

I was expecting to read about his life off the electrical grid, no public utility services of any kind - the traditional definition of "living off the grid." He doesn't do any of this. He's still comfortable, just unorthodox and definitely living an unconventional lifestyle.

The 3-stars are for what he wrote with HIS definition. Even though it's not the accepted definition, it was fascinating and I learned some interesting things. I obviously have an early Kindle version of the book and had to get past lots of grammar and spelling errors, but the content was fairly new to me and pretty interesting.

But, if you're expecting a book about someone truly living off-the-grid (as it's normally defined) and expecting ideas and tips for a real, nitty gritty life off the public electrical/utility/sewage/water grid, you might be very disappointed.

Great title, great cover, and yet...

I came very close to not reviewing this. Why? Because I only review books I like and this teetered on the edge. But, I decided to review it because it had some really good points and I think a lot of people will like it.

What worked for me: This is so witty and fun, right from the first page. The voice is funny and captivating. If you enjoy quirky main characters and a story that hasn't been told before, this may be fore you. The futuristic world is unique and interesting. The different take on dragons was a blast. While our main character Myrna's sense of humor is a bit dark, I liked it for the most part. She started out spunky and independent and I instantly liked her. There is some great tension between Myrna and Trian that held a lot of promise. The romance took a very, very long time to start to take center stage but once it did it was well worth the wait.

What didn't work for me: The info dump all across the first fifty pages drove me crazy and nearly made me stop reading. All that information would have been much more interesting if the author would have 'shown' us with action and scenes instead of simply 'telling' us. I understand that this is a hard temptation to fight when writing in narrative first person, but it can be done and has been often to great effect. Unfortunately, the 'telling' instead of 'showing' never stopped. Then there is Myrna's odd, complete insensitivity to watching animals being devoured alive. While I'm an animal lover, I'm also a realist with a tough skin, but this callousness started to get to me after a few scenes of it. I get where the author was going with this, but it didn't exactly make me like that aspect of Myrna.

Not everything is what it appears to be. Amanda gets kicked down in the dirt by her ex-fiance Ross but won't let it keep her there. Deciding she needs to regroup and make some serious changes, she packs up and moves back home, finding a place that can be remodeled into perfection with just a little bit of elbow grease. What she didn't expect to find was the sinfully attractive contractor Brax who not only will help her rebuild her new home on budget, but happens to be her little brother's best friend. The connection is instantaneous but Ross has taught her to be more careful with her heart. Can she get over the past to move on to a brighter future, or will all of those doubts and fears hold her back from finding true love?

I'm pretty torn on this book. The premise was great, and it was easy to fall into in the beginning. Amanda is understandably cautious while Brax is an honestly sweet man with a gorgeous smile. The pacing between the two coming together was wonderfully done. It eased into the romantic aspects with tastefully down intimate scenes. But I felt the conflict was a little over played to keep the story on edge. After the first plot twist I knew immediately where things were headed and sort of dreaded reading the rest. Thankfully our woman Amanda has an amazing best friend Kara to defuse most of the problems and keep her head on straight. It really helped her to see that not everything is what it seems, and honesty is the best policy.

This story was well written and jumped from Amanda's point of view to Brax's- which was something I truly enjoyed. However the ending felt rushed and left me a bit unsatisfied. We never really got to see Amanda over come her personal demons. Maybe it was the epilogue that makes me feel this way. I don't really know for sure.

Getting down to it I did enjoy reading this book and I could see myself buying more from this author in the future.

Heloise and William have danced around each other for a long time. As his bestfriend's little sister, William has tried to distance himself from Heloise while she has decided after once being rejected by him to protect her heart. They both have their share of scars, both internally and physically, but staying apart might be hurting them more than helping.
With Heloise in danger, William can't let her out of his sight. As they are forced together and their walls start coming down, it starts to become clear that the only way they can truly heal is with the love of the other.

"thou shalt not covet thy best friend's little sister."

Second in the Secrets and Spies series, A Raven's Heart can be read as a standalone. It's obvious that there is a continuous story thread involving the spy aspect but I never felt lost or confused, in fact it only made me curious about the first book in the series and future ones. I thought this started off very strong with the tension between our two leads. I will show up every time for the brother's friend, little sister trope and I thought that dynamic was portrayed very well here; a little less involvement with her brother's approval/disapproval and more shared history and emotional ties. As the story went on though, I thought the hero had disconnect between him continuously spouting (this was brought up a bit too much) about how he wasn't good enough for Heloise but still engaging physically with her. It was disorientating because I'm supposedly supposed to buy into his torment over not feeling good enough for her but at the same time he's constantly kissing on her and pushing their physicality. His reasoning for not feeling good enough for her was already a little murky, we are told he was kidnapped when he was younger and had to fight his way free but not given a clear enough picture to understand why he would demonize himself because of his actions. As the story goes on we learn he is a spy where he has to kill people occasionally, which fits better into the not feeling good enough narrative. If their intimate situations hadn't been ramped up so quickly in the beginning, I would have been able to follow along and connect with William's gradual breaking down and inability to stay away from Heloise.

"You want to pretend this scar isn't there, but it's what makes you you."

I was quite fond of Heloise as she was the little too smart for her own good, word loving, and scared bluestocking. Her personality quirk of etymology spouting was cute but I have read a heroine or two who could be her twin sister. Which is the main problem I had with this story, I've read it before. Again, I've read a ton of books from this sub-genre, which could maybe the problem in itself, but there was nothing new here. The writing is good and there are many crowd pleaser moments and lines, but maybe too many. It almost felt like the writer wrote what she thought a romance should be by taking good tropes, scenes, and lines and creating a story around that instead of having characters and story emerge from her. There was a kissing in the rain scene that should have felt emotionally powerful but all I could do was think about other scenes like that I have already read and compare them; this story was full of moments like that for me. Someone newer to the genre would probably not have the same problem I did. I've read Joanna Bourne's Spymasters series, which utilizes the same tropes and ideas as this but adds enough intrigue and emotion to distance itself from the similarities and be completely compelling.

She gave a watery laugh, "I might want to kill you, Ravenwood, but I'd never want you dead."

Heloise and William have a very back and forth relationship with them challenging each other that was fun to read. I just ran into the problem of having read it done better, I can read the same tropes over and over but I need fresh spins and/or deep emotional connections to the characters that I just couldn't seem to get here; there was a lack of "it" factor. Secondary characters stayed fairly close to the sides but there were a couple that I wouldn't mind knowing more about. This is also true for the spy ring the author has set up, there's enough there to grab your attention. I will say there were some comments made by Heloise regarding other women, former mistresses/courtesans and generally beautiful women, which felt mean spirited. There was a little bit of all those women are man hungry airheads; I could do without women on women hate and more female friendships. (Not suggesting Heloise would be friends with these women but less generalized superiority comments)

K.C. Bateman looks to be a newer author and I definitely see some promise in her writing, I would just like to hear more of her individual voice. There was good story plot progression and natural flowing interaction between the characters. I'll be going back and reading the first in the series and be on the lookout for the next in the series. If you're looking for a sweet "I'm not good enough for you but I can't stay away" with some road adventure, you might want to try this new author.

This is a story about love and death.  You've got the Deputy Prime Minister, Charles, who is in love with a young girl, Lorna, who isn't his wife; his wife, Elaine who was groomed to be a politician's wife and all that entails from a young age.  It was a marriage of compatibility; Faye, his devoted secretary who knows everything; Lorna's twin sister, Laurie.

Laurie comes to town to try and get an internship with the Deputy Prime Minister like her sister did.  She knows in her heart that her sister didn't commit suicide like the official report says.  But, who, why and how?  When everyone sees her they think they are seeing a ghost.  Laurie is determined to find the truth and there are so many people who could have done it.

Draw You Near #3 Savannah Sweethearts series by Jan Thompson
Last year while on vacationing in Savannah Lars Cargill bought a small watercolor painting of a woman called, Lady and the Sea, for his estate in England. There is something about the woman in the painting that captivates him. Determined to locate the woman, he returns to Savannah and approaches the artists. But Abilene Dupree insists there is no such woman, she made her up. Lars does not believe her and won't leave her alone. Does the elusive woman exist or just an artistic rendering?
Artist Abilene Dupree loves painting and is busy making a living as an artist and art teacher as well as selling her commercial art but not her personal life stories within her paintings. Her peaceful days are shattered when the handsome and charming Britisher admires her workflattering to be surebut then he becomes a bit irritating. Over time they form a friendship of sorts and she lets her guard down a tiny bit. They actually share some things in common, their faith for one thing, which was surprising at first. However, something from the past may break that fragile friendship when Lars must leave Savannah suddenly and return to England. Will he return or is their budding love over before it really began?
I enjoyed watching as Lars and Abilene got to know each other and their love grew. There was a few surprises that Abilene was not expecting which opened her eyes to Lars' true character. But then another shocking surprise that left doubts and fears for both Abilene and Lars. I like how they turned to God and prayer for guidance. A heartwarming story.

McKinsey & Company is a world-famous strategic consulting company, also known as "The Firm". Ethan Rasiel worked at McKinsey & Co. for several years and provides a quick, clear introduction into management consulting firm's problem solving methods. "I wrote this book with the goal of communicating new and useful skills to everyone who wants to be more efficient and effective in business. ... In addition, this book will give any executive woho works with management consultants, whether McKinsey or elsewhere, some insight into how these strange beings think."

The book is split up into five parts. In Part I, Ethan Rasiel explains the McKinsey-way of thinking about business problems. The author explains that the solution of the problem needs to be fact-based (facts are friendly), rigidly structured (MECE = mutually exclusive), and hypothesis-driven (solve the problem at the first meeting - the initial hypothesis). In addition, the author explains how McKinsey-ites approach business problems and apply the McKinsey problem-solving process to maximum effect. There is also a short introduction into a number of rules which McKinsey-consultants use for problem-solving purposes: the 80/20-rule, find the key drivers, the elevator test - sell in 30 seconds, make a chart every day, look at the big picture, say "I don't know", and don't accept "I have no idea".

In Part II, the author introduces the McKinsey-way of working to solve business problems. The author explains the selling process at McKinsey (the Firm does not sell, it markets), how to structure an engagement, and assembling of a team. Then the author comes to the most important part of the book, doing research, conducting interviews (the author insists on reading Chapter 8 - Conducting Interviews - "If you read no other chapter of the book from start to finish, read this one."), and brainstorming.

In Part III, the author, and the McKinsey-way of selling solutions. This part discusses the way McKinsey makes presentations, which is one of the strongest parts of McKinsey according to the author, displays data with charts (read Gene Zelazny (1985), 'Say it with Charts'), and the way to work with clients.

In Part IV, Rasiel gives some lessons how "McKinsey-ites" have learned for coping with the stresses of life at the Firm, and in Part V, the author recounts the lessons he learned at McKinsey and shares memories of various ex-McKinsey-ites. Both Part IV and V are 'a waste of paper' in comparison to the first three parts, but gives a little insight into what goes on behind the scenes at McKinsey & Co.

Yes, I can understand that some readers are disappointed by this book as it gives just an introduction into management consultancy (and McKinsey & Co). The author introduces the various problem-solving methods and tools, but does not discuss them in great detail. The author has responded to these criticisms by publishing The McKinsey Mind in 2002, which addresses this issue somewhat. However, for more details on the problem-solving methods and tools you will still have to read some other literature. I recommend you purchase The McKinsey Way if you want an introduction into management consultancy, and The McKinsey Mind if you want an introduction into problem-solving methods and tools.
Kindle_Store.summary: Short, clear introduction into management consultancy

Kindle_Store.reviewText:
Tod Goldberg has skillfully written these three mind-blowing short stories which incite introspection, and draw upon submerged memories. He writes about places he has lived, descending deeply into his psychic to dredge up old emotions, sounds and tactile impressions of long forgotten, but deeply moving sensations. Sensations so deeply felt they must be hidden in a locked closet. Why do we do the things we do?

Tod carefully examines the stories and motives of convoluted lives. A golf pro, King of the Fairway, who cannot hit a straight ball, and cannot climb out of the sand trap of his own creation. Another, haunted by the ghost of his brother. Still another man, who is compelled to revisit the pain of his childhood home. How did these places affect their lives? Or, is memory simply a trickster lurking, designed to lead all down wayward paths? These are forceful interludes. The realistic characters linger to remind us of our own hidden mistakes, and agendas.

Tod Goldberg's rich voice is well known through the ever popular "Burn Notice" T.V. series. His darkly comic voice compels, and taunts, those prone to self-deception, and yes, self-destruction. This is a quick read. One you won't want to put down until the final pages is turned. The effects will linger. It is well worth your attention.

Michael Shaughnessy's second novel (and I do recommend his first, The Archangel of Westminster, if you can find a copy) is a well-crafted page-turner that quickly hooks the reader into its `what-happens-next?' plot-line.  For the first two-thirds of the book, the situation confronting the priest-hero of the story, Fr. Michael Reilly becomes progressively more dire, and the reader wonders how it could possibly get any worse; which, of course, it unfailingly does.  I don't want to spoil the ending, but Fr. Reilly finally triumphs by means of a stunning gambit of humility and integrity.

The real strength of the book, for my money, is its character development - its depth of insight into the sundry and self-contradictory motives of each of the main characters kept me engaged, even more than the plot-line.  The Archbishop, stuck between concerns over public perception and pastoral care for one of his priests, and Adelia (the Red Madonna of the title, although by the book's end, it isn't yet quite apparent what, if any, significance attaches to the moniker), caught between concerns for Truth and Compassion, on the one hand, and her own vast ambition on the other, were the most intriguingly-drawn characters, for my part.

If the book has a weakness (and it is far from a fatal one), it is that the `good guys' are REALLY good, and the `bad guys' are REALLY bad - it could seem a tad `cartoonish'.  But that doesn't detract from the story itself; as far as it goes, Fr. Reilly gives a strong example of wrestling with his own conscience and choosing the right, even if he might prefer something easier.

The Red Madonna is the first book of a planned trilogy, which is good to know, because there's a lot of `unfinished business' by the end of the book.  Shaughnessy spends a bit of time on the marriage between Adelia and Jim; the twists and turns of the plot pull and tug on their relationship, in both constructive and destructive ways, but by the end of the book, their marriage and its future are still very much up in the air.  So I am left waiting for the next installment; and the one after that.  Well-played on that account, sir. . .

This is a book definitely worth reading, and all the more impressive, given that the author is basically writing in his spare time.

Kindle_Store.reviewText: I wanted to hate this story. It started with cliche word choices, mellow romantic encounters, and underdeveloped characters. That's a book to put on the black list, right? Wrong. I even LOVED Ella's Gifts. After a while, the shortcomings didn't matter anymore because the book was huge fun. Melody Jerva's enthusiasm for her story rubs off on the reader. Impossible to put this book aside, especially once the psychopath enters the scene. If Melody Jerva would have spent more time polishing her work, Ella's Gifts would have been a perfect little book. But, for now, she already has a highly entertaining page-turner to her name.

Among the novels I usually read male authors are a rarity. So the single fact that Quarter Square was written by a man was reason enough to pique my curiosity and make me want to read this novel.

In the first part of the novel Joe (our protagonist) discovers a magic parallel universe which is accessible through the magic door in the century old theatre he's renovating and sleeping in. Through that hole in the wall one enters a Renaissance-fair-like magic version of Plymouth where dwarves dance and juggle, people sit around a bonfire and tell tales, others are singing, dancing having fun. A very colourful and enchanted alternate universe.

However, this haven is threatened by an evil who is after Joe, and the second part of the novel tells the story of Joe and Min (the heroine) being on the run and hiding from the evil werewolf with a neolite tribe, who live in huts in the desert, walk around barechested and loin-clothed.

What is interesting with Quarter Square, is that with this novel I felt the different parts of the novel (plot, writing, etc.) to be quite independent from each other: I found the writing of great quality, it was lyrical and exquisite.

"I rolled onto my back, gave my scalp and beard a good scratch and tried to concentrate on the noises and the smell of dry centuries. I preferred them to the sound of my thoughts and the stink of betrayal."

It set the mood and described the scenes while entertaining all senses of the reader and definitely making use of the reader's imagination:

"The air - heavy with summer smells of beer and cigarette smoke, diesel oil from the harbour, food from every direction and a hundred different perfumes and aftershaves - tasted like life and made me feel like even more of an outsider."

What made me pick up Quarter Square - the fact that its author was a man - didn't let me down. The difference in logic, perception and handling of events was refreshing and authentic. It was wonderful climbing inside the mind of a man and seeing and understanding why he does what he does. It was interesting to see Joe's reasoning behind his hurt of discovering his wife having an affair with his best friend and that it was mostly the sense of betrayal which infuriated him: that he doesn't begrudge his best friend for falling in love with his wife but for lying to him and making him lose his best friend. Reading a story through a man's perspective is fun and liberating: a man narrator is blunter, doesn't overanalyze things (even though he spends a fair time on exploring his emotions it definitely does not come off as mushy), and remains more realistic.

Though I was constantly enchanted by David Bridger's writing style, I didn't connect that well with the plot. I enjoyed the first part of the novel and reading about the "gipsy" circus of the insiders, but from the moment Joe and Min got on the run I felt the story lost most of its colours. (Though I still remember with amazement the description of Joe blending in a tree and David Bridger's description of what it feels like to live and breathe as a tree does.)

Joe is a great character, an ordinary guy next door, and his story is fantastic exactly because of him being so normal. Unfortunately I remained lukewarm and at times even antagonistic towards the heroine, Min. I didn't find her fleshed out enough, and then when she got together with Joe - though I can understand with their background why - it still irritated me that she didn't consider Joe her equal but treated her most of the time almost as a child. When finally Joe couldn't take that anymore and erupted in quite a monologue I read it with great satisfaction. It was good to see him finally step up and assume the role of the responsible man in charge of his own destiny.

Verdict: Quarter Square is very different from the usual urban fantasy novels. I would say it is more on the fantasy side than urban. David Bridger is a very talented and promising new author whose next works I will definitely check out!

ps. I have to spend at least one sentence on the amazing cover. Not only does it look beautiful, it is very atmospheric and portrays the novel and characters wonderfully. A fantastic job, bravo!

And a short quote which gives you a taste of the book:

"Here's the thing. There's magic everywhere in the world. Always has been. But in most of the world it's unknown. People stopped using it, believing in it. (...) It seems that each culture and each generation rejects magic a bit more than the one before. Some cultures more than others, but the general trend is to ignore magic and eventually to forget it."

Well Quarter Square is a magic-preserving community then!

Floating Petals is a collection of 14 short stories inspired by Leela Devi Panikar's eclectic experience of Asia. There is a genuine beauty here, both in the tales themselves and in the language in which they are couched. The author's gentle, positive tone pulls you into the longer, more developed stories, and you quickly find yourself ensconced by the sights, sounds and smells of her world. Everything is vividly described with an economy of language and a light, reassuring humour that keep the narrative moving along nicely.

The author stumbles just a little in her treatment of negative emotions. Characters in frightening situations are never given enough time to convincingly develop their terror -- as if the author herself can't bear to be writing it. This isn't a problem when the main thrust of the plot lies outside of its unpleasant elements in stories like "The Couple" and "Homeless Sparrow". But in tense, gloomy thrillers like "Green" and "The Singeing Shadow" where the point is to evoke sympathetic fear, the result is shallow and abrupt prose that leaves you asking, "Is that it?" However, these stories comprise only a small part of the book, whose real strength is in such stories as "Floating Petals" and "After The Wedding". It's obvious the author is in her element in these tales, getting right to the core of her characters and -- whether intentionally or otherwise -- artfully challenging the reader to re-examine natural prejudices against pain and servitude. I also particularly enjoyed "Love Is All You Need".

With her charmingly optimistic voice, Panikar writes on themes of childhood, love and freedom with an effortless grace. Whatever your taste, I'm sure you'll find something to enjoy. Overall, a great read.

Reviewed by me as a member of Rosie Amber's Review Team

4.5 stars

In this further adventure of the Assassin Without A Name, our hero is recruited by his ex love, Liz, for a special mission.

As with the other books in this series, I felt that its charm lay not so much in the plot itself as in the writing of the incidental parts.  I am not particularly interested in reading long, blow by blow accounts of fights or daring escapes, but I love the bits about the Assassin's life, his thoughts, etc.  I like to picture him in his 'working gear', climbing over his rooftop empire like a cat, unseen by the Black Guard who seek him below, and reading little snippets about his life, like his secret hideout in the deplorable Shambles area of town, where one takes one's life in one's hands simply by entering its streets...

Scott Marlowe has invented a marvellous character, and writes beautifully, with wit and a wonderful turn of phrase.  I'd like to see a novella telling about the Assassin's early life, something that makes more use of the writer's powers of observation, character portrayal and presentation of atmosphere.  Again, this reminded me very much of some of Roald Dahl's stories; the style of writing is very similar.  Good stuff!

Curve Drill is another book in Christa Wick's military series. I really enjoyed it, but I did feel some parts were a little rushed. Over and over Ive attempted to summarize this book, but words fail me. Truthfully, some of it I simply didn't get. What are the flowers growing out of Miels wrists all about? Is this based on some existing myth or superstition that Im not familiar with? Was it simply an unconventional means of making her other in the story so that she and Sam could be outcasts together?And those Bonner girls? It felt a bit like a fairytale whose moral I didn't really grasp. Dont get me wrong. It was interesting, and in no way detracted from the story, it just made me feel like I was missing something. But. Miel and Sam were amazing. The best part of the book for me was Sam wrestling with who he was now vs. who he saw himself being long-term and coming to terms with that. And Miel loving him no matter what form he felt most comfortable with. It is a rare thing, transgender or not, to find someone who loves you unconditionally, who takes you as you are, and loves and supports you without question. At the risk of repeating myself, Im really drawn to stories with LGBTQA themes right now because I simply haven't had a lot of exposure to those stories, and I want to walk awhile in their shoes, to maybe gain a little more insight into what its really like living their lives. The fact that the authors husband is a transgender man lends more authenticity to that part of the story, and I really appreciate that. Perhaps the magical realism isn't quite for me or maybe I really did just miss something. Regardless, its a beautifully written story of love, acceptance, and transformation, and Id definitely recommend it. If, like me, the magical realism isn't for you, I urge you to power through. There is so much more to be gained from this story, it will be worth it. Note: I received this book from the publisher via NetGalley.

This book was interesting in that rather than focusing on one mission that goes horribly wrong, or a series of missions that turn out to be related at the end, it follows the hero on several unrelated missions.

The book makes a big deal about duty vs tradition, but the distinction wasn't terribly clear to me most of the time, nor did I really understand the complaints her superiors had. They seemed more to do with her philosophy than her results.

The action was petty good. I would have liked to see more variety in the weapons/equipment and some more comments on the rules of engagement, instead of this sort of total war approach to every mission.

I thought the "females can't make good warriors" parts were overplayed and trite, considering the group she is fighting for is fully integrated.

This trivia book has a very cool format.  You can choose to have just the questions, or the questions with multiple choice answers, or the quiz with the actual answers.  I liked to take the quiz without any answers first, then look at the multiple choice selections, and then look at the answer.  It was fun that way.  However, I must say that the editing on this book is a mess.  There are missing words or the wrong words, accidentally revealed answers, mixed up quizes.  It was too bad, because the idea for the book was great, and with just a little more effort this would have been a five star book.  You will still be able to enjoy the book, despite the errors.

Selah Davis had grand dreams for her future, none of which included her hometown of Marietta, Montana.  When her high school boyfriend dumped her to move away, her heart was broken and she put Levi Monroe in her past.  12 years later, returning home to cover the yearly Rodeo for her Seattle publication, she has a face to face run in with Levi.  The man who hasn't evaded her thoughts or fantasies even after all these years.  Set on righting a wrong, Selah propositions Levi with a one-night stand.  Sparks ignite and feelings from the past resurface as Selah considers her life in Seattle that isn't all it is cracked up to be and the potential of a future with a cowboy from her past and returning home to run her hometown paper.  A steamy read for sure and who doesn't love a great reunion story?!

They is a quick little story about two couples who get lost in a snow storm while on a trip.

***SPOILERS***  ***SPOILERS***  ***SPOILERS***

They have used most of their gas and can't turn back so they are forced to push on.  The car eventually runs out of gas and the two men decide to bundle up and head off looking for help.  They report back that they see lights up ahead and they are off to find gas and warm beverages for the ladies.

Some time passes and one of the men comes back and he is gravely injured.  The two women get the car running again and drive toward the lights they were told about.  They arrive at a gas station that is overrun by zombies and the other member of their party is being devoured at the store.  You can guess what happens to the surviving charaters at that point.

***END SPOILERS***  ***END SPOILERS***  ***END SPOILERS***

The story is good, the situation is relatable for those of us who don't have roadside assistance or travel outside of our cell phone coverage.  This is a great quick story for zombie lovers.  Check it out!

Darcy proposes at Hunsford and then in anger when she throws all her accusations in his face begins to basically maul her.  And she is half-anger/half-over-heated response in reaction to his kisses and his hands all over her body.  So it continues. Mr. Bennet is rather a smug push-over in granting Darcy not only his consent but in saying how he predicted this and what took them so long.

Others said they were laughing and I have to agree in the fact that this couple would fit well in todays world but neither the Elizabeth nor the Darcy in this novella are anywhere near the people presented to us by Jane Austen.  But you may find it amusingthey certainly did not hold back in each others company.

But if you want to read a little erotica before bedtime  go to it!

Kindle_Store.reviewText:
Never slow dance with a zombie. Sounds like good advice. The kind of good advice youd get from the Dear Abby of the supernatural set. Undeniably wise words to live by. Right up there with never put a campfire out with your face. (Or as a teacher once told me: never put a campfire out with your face. Again.)

Try slow dancing with a zombieparticularly a hungry one with an icky drool face and plump maggots squirming out of its noseand you might find yourself missing a body part afterwards. A face, an arm, maybe even a big toe. Please dear lord, anything but the big toe. No dance is worth an amputation. Even the Macarena.

This is becauseas everyone knowszombies are fearsome and brutal. They eat people like Cheetos, minus the obnoxious cheesy mouth. A good day for a zombie is ripping into some guys chest cavity and snacking on the entrails; the last zombie in getting the colon. It might not be pretty, but its a raison dtre that zombies can call their own.

Unless the zombies are in E. Van Lowes Never Slow Dance with a Zombie, in which case they are essentially non-threatening, non-violent and about as fearsome as a pissed off butterfly. Sure, this is a novel aimed at a young adult audience, but it doesnt mean the zombies cant have a little bite to them. Teens know that zombies snack on faces; in fact, they expect it.

Zombies are the unstoppable killing machine of the monster world, the Great White shark of bogeymen minus the killer John Williams soundtrack, so toning down their violence and eliminating their bloodletting is an odd choice. Using them for a novel in which they have to be toned down is an even odder choice. Like writing a YA book about a serial killer, who never kills anyone.

Lowe takes a different approach in Never Slow Dance with a Zombie, mining the zombies for comedic gold, turning them into a harmless joke. But in making them non-threatening, he eliminates any possibility of dramatic tension in the novel. The main characters Margot and Sybil, who must co-exist with an entire high school filled with zombie classmates, never feel in peril in the book. Never feel like the zombies are a real foil for them. The zombies are just too easily overcome, outsmarted at every turn. Sure outsmarting zombies is difficult, but their overwhelming numbers should balance this equation somewhat.

There is a nice message about the perils of wanting to be popular and its consequences, but Lowe belabors it, addressing it repetitively, repeating it over and over (get the point!) making the book seem like one of those not-very-special After School Specials. Instead of making kids think and challenging them to broaden their perspective, Lowes constant reiteration of his message most likely will eventually turn them off, causing them to feel as if they are being lectured to.

Despite these issues, the story still has its entertaining moments, and there are a few places where its goofy charm shines through. Most of the characters are clichs in the book: the popular girl, the girl who will do anything to be popular, the selfless best friend, and the science club geeks. None of these caricatures are offensive, but neither are they something you haven't seen before. And there is really no reason youd need to experience them here.

So wallflowers rejoice, Never Slow Dance with a Zombie is one slow dance you can miss.
Kindle_Store.summary: One slow dance you can miss

The problem that I have with Alan's writing styles is that its very stream-of-consciousness. The writer needs to learn how to write more densely. I will explain. But overall, Alan needs to start letting most of the content hit-the-cutting-floor. In other words - edit.

His normal approach is to do something like the following: Stone (his lead character) will get called to a meeting. But before Stone even heads to the meeting, Stone starts thinking about the meeting. Sort of. The the reader is accosted by 100 mostly stream-of-consciousness thoughts that run through Stones head, and 99% will not impact the  meeting or Stones response to the meeting - in any way.

So, here are two tools that Alan needs to start applying assiduously, and that includes, after the fact. If he hasn't done this, then he needs to go back and rewrite any section that doesnt have this. Yes. I am giving Alan homework.

1) Multi-Tasking
2) Footsteps

What do I mean by multi-tasking? I mean that every scene needs to accomplish 3 or more things, that 'move the story forward'. And Alan does not get to include "Character Development", "Exposition", or "Establishing" in any of those three. For example, if Stone enters the room, and Alan describes the situation, perhaps this scene will move the story forward by A) revealing a new bit of information that allows the story to move forward, B) have a character say something that reveals what that character is going to do next, and C) mention an object in the room that will serve as a Chekov's Gun component. Thats three things, and a decent reason for that scene to exist. Notice that none of those aspects have anything to do with what is happening inside Stones head.

Granted, I just came up with those three things off the top of my head, and we don't have context for which scene they apply to. But hopefully you (Alan) get the idea. Frankly, I am not in the mood right now, to rewrite one of your scenes. So, I am just making the overall suggestion.

2) Footsteps. I am inventing this term for you. I want you to insert a Footstep every 5 - 10 sentences. And by footsteps, I mean that you have to move the story forward, every 5-10 sentences. So, get out of the characters head, and have him do something, or have something happen. The footstep can be:
A) Someone says something
B) Someone does something
C) Someone decides something
And it always has to be onTopic. Meaning, that if Stone is heading towards a meeting, he is allowed to think about it, for 5 to 10 sentences, but then he actually needs to "GO" to the meeting. If he is then going to the meeting, he is allowed to think about going or about the meeting for 5 to 10 sentences, but then he needs to perhaps, discover something that is relevant to the story. He might see his crew doing something relevant, and it changes his plan for how to deal with the meeting (change). or he runs into someone that walks along with him because they were also called to the meeting. He did not know they were coming, so this is new information. And even better, if he does not want them there, or does not know why they would be a part of the meeting.

"Keep the Heroes thinking processes, focused on the meeting".

Ok. Thats enough instruction for now. Of course, I don't actually expect that Alan will read this diatribe. But  now he knows that this particular reader finds his rambles to be too often, too off-topic, and tooooooo-long.

Move the story forward faster. This does not mean that more will happen, as the story arc can be the same. It will simply mean that the story will be more packed with meaning, instead of the drivel that goes on the the day-dreaming-heroes head. For example, instead of listening to a thousand meaningless thoughts in Stones head that rarely affect the story, Alan would have more room to let us get to know some of the other characters, instead of them all being paper-secondary-characters.

Alan can still have all the insights be coming from the Hero. Just make him more observant about others, so that we can learn about them.

Ok. Thats enough.

Will I read any more Alan Black stories? Maybe, but not enthusiastically.

"Showdown in Durango" was, in some ways, better than I expected. I honestly thought it was going to be terrible but it had some surprisingly sweet and tender moments and some very sexy moments. However, this book was brought down by some pretty heavy handed melodrama. It read much like a soap opera. The twists and turns were too fast and too angst-ridden to come across as realistic. Poor Johnny was just put through the ringer, (who knew they were so many gay men in the wild west!) and just followed along with everything with child-like naivety. In addition, his relationship with Andy seemed strangely thrown together. And OH did it bug me when they called each other "pardner". It was like a gay wild west parody.

I haven't read another gay novel like this one.  It gets points for originality and the fact it's fairly well written, otherwise it would get one star based upon the story itself.  The minuses, at least for me as a reader, is I didn't get the angsty hot coupling I was expecting.  Instead after a short amount of exposition from both lead characters' point of views, they are established as a couple.  The sex scenes weren't hot, and the back story of the experience of the younger man "Ray" with his dad, was a horror story I could have lived without.  And, frankly, whenever someone helpless is abused and a pet tortured or killed, I'm dropping the book like a hot iron.  At least insane "Dad" didn't use one of those!  As for the cowboy lifestyle and ranching, well, the only way we get into that is because Ray is brought back to his former home to work undercover to find out who is responsible for the cattle rustling that might break the ranch's back.  His foster brother or whatever you'd call him is now running the ranch and has used the opporunity to get Ray back on home turf.

I just couldn't. Finish the book.
Spelling and grammar. Very poor.
Choppy phrases pretending to be sentences. Each one a paragraph. So distracting.

If you enjoyed reading my above review, then this is the book for you. I wish authors who believe that this type of writing style helps to convey an emotion would think again. I just wanted to get out my red pen and correct all the mistakes, but my Kindle screen would have been ruined.

Regarding the plot: Fallen woman is rescued by a long-lost friend (by the way, THAT is a complete sentence). There you go, and spare yourself from trying to read this story. Read The Scarlet Letter instead.
Kindle_Store.summary: This book is an example of why a good editor is needed.

*Reviewed on BackPorchReader[dot]com*

***this review contains some mild spoilers***

Sorry, but this wasn't a win for me and I will not be advancing to the next level.

Firstly, I really liked the cover, but in no way is it representative of the character descriptions, including the dog. Thats just a statement and has no bearing on my rating.

The blurbwhen I read it a few weeks ago I was intrigued enough to pre-order the book. Reading it again, after having read the book, it kind of makes me snicker and wonder what I was thinking.

The story felt like trope after trope after trope all dumped in a crock pot. Unfortunately, the flavors didn't blend so well for me. And, spoiler: a crock pot nearly has a starring role.

Theres the snowed in tropeand it was a little bit of a twist from what we normally see, considering this was in an RV that actually moved as opposed to some remote cabin in the woods. I thought that was done relatively well.

Theres the Im stranded and have to get home to a wedding and I gotta have a date or Im a loser. So the RV was handy.

Theres the closeted guy/complete virgin. I had a hard time with the whys of these.

Theres insta-love which I have a really hard time buying into when combined with closeted virgins.

Theres the age gap that was never really addressed, not that it really matters. But it was there.

Theres confrontation with the exwhich, sorry, but was lackluster, felt forced and far too coincidental to be believable.

There's a grand gesture toward the end on Noahs part. Grand Gestures really aren't needed for believable romance.

Im not a gamerand this is a huge undercurrent of the story and the one thing these heroes have in common, along with taste in movies. I wasn't scared of the gaming element, nor did I find it overbearing. Sometimes it got big, and Ill admit I skimmed a few paragraphs to get around it. But for the most part it was fine.

I couldn't get a good bead on Adrian. His sexy tats drew me in some. But beyond thathe was kind of a flake, but really sweet and nurturing at times. I couldn't make sense of him, other than hes just the sort who dances to the beat of his own drum. Nothing wrong with that, but it made it really hard to connect. His family drama seemed to be all in his head because they adored him even when he exasperated them.

Noahand with him Ive got to try really hard not to be judgmental. Hes 35, suuuper closeted, and a complete virgin. I don't judge those thingsexcept the age part, and I REALLY don't want to judge that either. Its just, I never bought into the WHY of it all. Why at 35, and such an intellectual, hes so closeted and inexperienced. And I couldn't buy into it being because of his place of employment because he USED that as a way to hide himself and knew what he was getting into by working there. Hes way far away from familyso getting away was his first chance to be himself. Instead he hid behind religion he didn't fully buy into, what he thought his family would think, and gaining tenure at an ultra-conservative religious college whose tenets he didn't believe in. I get everyones journey is differentbut, the WHYs all piled up fell short for me.

Together, I didn't get the attraction of anything deeper than looks and common interest in video games. The chemistry was lacking and the sexual tension wasmeh.

Their dogs didn't even like each other much in the beginning, and thats usually a sign to run like hell.

Yet, within mere days of a snowy RV journey, they're in love.

Uhhhh okay.

(Not really.)

The rest is them trying to figure it out, deny it, fight against it, fight for it, etc. with lots of boring talk, talk, talk over text and Skype until the aforementioned Grand Gesture.

As the reader, by this point, I didn't care a whole lot.

The One-Year-Later epilogue

*harassed sigh*

I don't think its written in stone that at the end of a romance the people have to get engaged in order to have a believable HEA.

So nopeGame Over.

Well, my impressions of this book are about 50/50 feel good, feel not so good.
The good : The writing is excellent and engaging. I only found one grammatical error on the first read. (I wasn't looking for any, it just kind of jumped out at me).
The neutral : I was kind of puzzled by the fact that Dan felt the need to immerse himself in public self-flagellation over what appeared to be simple, normal,  human regressions on the path of self-discovery. I mean, rather than just notice his perceived missteps and move on, which would be the prescribed/normal behavior for someone engaged in self-realization, meditation, mindfulness. But what is "normal", right? And who am I to assign that moniker to anything or anyone. So I pressed on and kept reading.
The bad (just my perception, of course): Then, after reading the whole "book", I suddenly realized what this really was: just another clever way to get people to buy more copies of his real book. And, I must admit, it really is a very clever way of capitalizing on human nature, combined with the ability to "give" away free books on Amazon. And I, being of the (reluctantly) human persuasion, took the bait. Hook, line, and sinker, as it were. At first, I totally missed the fact that only 17% of this "book" is new material. The rest is just chapter one of the real book: 10% Happier.

I was looking through the Amazon free Kindle books section and came upon Dan's freebie. It intrigued me, not because of the fact that Dan is a well-known newscaster, but because of the title. Dan is not known to me because I stopped following anything media-related since about six years ago. Stopped watching TV, listening to radio, and unsubscribed from all news-related and/or commercial driven feeds on the Internet. With that, slowly but surely, the names of most newscasters kind of slid into the nether regions of my memory. Life is so much more peaceful when we don't allow ourselves to be hyped up and stressed out artificially by things we can do nothing about. But I digress. I got curious because I wanted to know if the author regretted writing a book about becoming 10% happier or, if regret wasn't his issue, what was? So I plunged in and started reading.

As I mentioned before, the "book" is very well written. And engaging. But it's not a book. It starts out with a few pages of Woody-Allenish neurosis and self-flagellation about Dan's perceptions that enjoying his (real) book's success in an excessive way and obsessively watching its rise in the rankings is somehow a failing on his part.

Note to Dan: that's just being human. And while being human often has felt like a failing even to me in the past, I have learned to accept certain aspects of my own and others' humanity too as I grow older, but none the wiser. Being human, and displaying human traits like backsliding on intentions every once in a while, is no more wrong than being a tree and shedding a leaf or more here and there (and sometimes everywhere). Inconvenient, yes - mostly to humans, not so much to the trees. But a subject for blame, no. We learn in bits. And that involves backsliding. Perhaps it even enriches our experience, because we learn from it. We learn to be more aware. And that is what meditation is all about, right?

Which might have been what Dan was trying to do with this "book" - but in a public forum? And with that title? And the way it was presented with just a tiny bit of new material and a whole chapter of the "real" book included? With a Perils of Pauline type of cliffhanger ending? I think not. No. This little "freebie" is really nothing more than a new and innovative way to advertise the book.

I have to admit that I feel kinda conned. Sucked in. Suckered. I would probably be pretty pissed off if I had spent money on this item. But still, I did get pulled into spending time on it. Under false pretenses. I was given the impression that this was a real book that was available free of charge, as many other bona-fide books are available free of charge at one time or another on Amazon. This is not a bona fide book. It's a hook. An advertising hook. And it should be touted as such, just like the preview chapters are on other Amazon books. That way, the reader has a choice and does not come away with a feeling of having been taken for a ride.

Had this been handled properly, I might have bought Dan's real book. But now I no longer feel like it. Maybe later, after I have gotten over feeling victimized. For now, this non-book gets 2 stars from me: 5 stars for writing style and 0 stars for truth in advertising. And 0 stars for taking advantage of the reader.

There are some good tips in here, and some useful ways about thinking about the guitar.  I realize a guitarist of any level might pick up the book, so what is obvious to a veteran might be a revelation to a beginner.  One bit of advice I enjoyed was learn how to play outside by playing only the "bad" notes.  I plan to give that a try and see where it leads.  A few other tidbits worth thinking about too.  But there was also a fair bit of fluff stuff in there.  For example, only watch beneficial Youtube videos and not bad ones.  uh, thanks.  Hack No. 22 was to essentially use brute force to solve your picking technique (brute force is not a hack).  And a few of these hacks had me scratching my head.

 One is his "hack" to avoid using a metronome.  That's just flat bad advice.  Virtually all top players have practiced extensively with a metronome.  Steve Vai used to practice a metronome 10 hours a day.  Petrucci writes all of his solos with a metronome.  On and on.  Bad advice.

Another problem was his misunderstanding of the 10,000 hour rule.  Tippet kind of says it takes 10,000 hours of practice to get "good" and you want to achieve a state of flow in practice.  However, that's NOT what Anders Erickson who created the 10,000 rule says.  Erickson says it takes 10,000 hours of deliberate practice.  He elaborates saying the amount of time spent doesn't really matter much, it is how you spend it.  To put it another way 10,000 hours of flow doesn't do much for you.  You have to spend the time working.

Finally, a couple of his hacks were just plugs for another book.  A plug for a book isn't a hack, it is a plug.
Kindle_Store.summary: A few gems, lots of fluff, and a couple whiffs.

I wanted to like this book. We read this book for our book club and the synopsis was intriguing. The book, however, was not. I kept reading page after page in hopes that a plot would surface. When I got to the last page I was completely disappointed. This book was just a story that followed a small section of a young man's life. In the end I kept thinking, what was this all about? PTSD? Boys becoming men? Horses capable of intelligently interacting with humans? Mental health issues? Verbal abuse? Socioeconomic structure issues? et. al.
I just really was lost, and then irritated that I felt I wasted my time reading the story. The main idea/plot was lost amongst a wave of small ideas and notions. If this story was about the affects of PTSD on a family structure, then it needed to be more about that and less of the angst ridden teen love triangle. If instead it was about a boy becoming a man and facing guy issues, it should have been more about that and less of the mental health/ptsd.
All in all, that's just my two cents on it, you may enjoy reading "Chasing Danny". Don't let my review prevent you from reading the story. One should always make up his/her own mind when reading stories. Reading is a wonderful thing, even when you feel you have lost hours of your time reading drivel, it is still good for your soul.

I'm not a fan of bad reviews because I hate to be negative about the work someone did or in this case didn't do. Let me start off by saying that I really enjoy this series, the characters are fun and the plot is interesting. I think that this is definitely an up and coming new author. However, it was incredibly difficult to look past the atrocious editing. There were a multitude of spelling and grammatical mistakes and the punctuation was very odd in a lot of places. I feel a bit scammed out of the few bucks I paid for this because it isn't a finished product suitable for consumer purchase. I'm going to try the next in the series to see if it's better. If not, I unfortunately won't be purchasing more of Skye's work.

In all honesty, this would be a great series with the proper editing.

If the author ever reads these reviews - if you need a new proofreader, there are plenty of us around!

Kindle_Store.reviewText:
Young tween boy in non stop life or death situations is rather exhausting. No sooner does the main character Ethan sit down then a villain pops up. It starts to become extremely tedious.
This is not an excellently written series. It reads like a poorly edited first attempt at writing
I Have read the first 4 "books";
-The Inventor's Son: The Beginning, expanded .
-The Inventor's Son
-The Scientist's Son
-The Explorer's Son

 So far the writing is a bit  inelegant . Modern phrases are sprinkled about which should have been removed in editing as they don't fit with the era the story is  set in.
 Why did I give this such a low rating ?
1) Ethan is 12/13 and his father pretty much abandons him for most of the series & by book 5 we still don't have a really good reason why.
<there is a reason but to have him not show up at any of the key crises points at all seems to suggest that he's protecting himself & purposely putting his son in harms way. Since the whole series hinges on Ethan trying to find his father, the reason why his father went away needs to be compelling & so far it isn't.>
2)12/13 year old falls for a girl & kisses her. Yes he is certain she's the love of his life & the only one for him forever. Ridiculous plot ploy.
4)"Bitch" is used a good bit. This is a preteen/tween book so totally unnecessary
3) The crazy man's "monster" is VERY horrible...very violent & not only wants to crush children's heads, but has a sexual "thing" for young boys.
EU
5)! totally too far with the blood, guts, gore & pedophile  subject for the target reader.
4) Hero policeman keeps shouting things like "sweet Jesus"....much too often.
5)The main character spends a bit of time contemplating suicide
6) main character comes into acquaintance with prostitutes& mistresses of family members...why so much adult subjects in a kid's book ! ?
7)Evil people who are after Ethan are really violent. People are dismembered, hung, exploded and the like  in detailed description.
8) Main character is told that his mother got pregnant before she was married & had an abortion .
9)torture & assassination
10)Main character is addicted to morphine

so by the end of book 5 you know why everyone is after Ethan, but his father still hasn't shown up.
More importantly, Ethan continues to be unlikable. I actually found myself becoming fond of his cousin Theodore ! I read this because it was free.
Kindle_Store.summary: Main character is whiny & unlikable. Extreme violence, themes of suicide,pedophilia too much for preteen/tween book

I bought this book for my girlfriend for some comedic light-reading, but we both have difficulty finding it funny (it has a few lines that led to laughter).  I think the problem is that my girlfriend and I are both independent professionals, and cannot relate to this book overall.  For example, I don't spend my time blowing my weekly paycheck at the horse track or betting on the Giants, just as my girlfriend doesn't spend her time scrubbing toilets and preparing dinner whilst adorned with an apron and hair scarf.  Frankly speaking, I don't understand why anyone would want to be with a compulsive gambler, or how a relationship could be based on the division of labor dictated by antiquated gender roles rather than mutual respect and pragmatism (e.g., if one partner is a more efficient cook, then that partner should probably play a larger role in cooking, regardless of the partner's gender).  But that is just me, and others can live the way they want within the boundaries of the law defined by our state and federal legislatures.

If you (a man) are a compulsive gambler/alcoholic, lacking any modicum of self-control and financial savvy, and are dating/married to another (a woman) who often has to talk you out of joining in on cockamamie schemes that can quite possibly lead to both physical and financial ruin, or the opposite, then you can probably relate to this book more and find it funny overall.  If not save, the $10 bucks.

I received a free Adobe Digital Editions copy of this book from the publisher through Netgalley, this has not compromised my ability to write an honest and critical review of the book.

28/1 - 1.5 to 2 stars (2 stars for GR because it wasn't completely full of grammatical, punctuational and spelling errors).  While it wasn't full of errors they weren't completely absent.  This sentence is a perfect example: "It has always rankled me that what is best for the gentleman is not always best for the lady yet society seems bent on keeping it these inconvenient methods."  Missing comma and what does "bent on keeping it these inconvenient methods." mean?  Obviously,  Portman is trying to convey something along the lines of 'what's good for the goose should be good for the gander', but those last seven words make absolutely no sense (especially 'inconvenient' as it has nothing to do with the gender differences in those days in this context).

The opening lines state "I am with child, again.  In the unfortunate event I do not recover from this birth, I write my confessions in this diary."  Reading those lines I assumed that Cecelia had experienced previous difficult pregnancies, been warned not to become pregnant again or was in such an abusive relationship that she feared for her life.  But, other than some bad morning sickness with each pregnancy (the possibly deadly pregnancy she's talking about will be her fifth successful birth of five pregnancies - she hasn't lost any children through miscarriage), she suffered no more than any other pregnant woman of the day would have been expected to.  Other than this opening paragraph her fears for her life aren't mentioned again - if she had actually had reasons to fear for her life that might have made the book more interesting.

Cecelia says she's writing this 'diary/confessional' to distract herself from her growing (unfounded) fear and because she wants to explain to 'those she loves' the reasons for the rumours surrounding her marriage to William.  If she's writing to her family members why does she feel the need to 'state that her husband was known to be something of a rake'?  Wouldn't they already know all about his reputation?  To be continued after dinner...

After dinner - Now to the erotica genre this has been placed into.  What the hell?  How can anyone call the sex scenes in this book erotic?  The sex is peppered with sentences like this catastrophe: "Without warning his hand came around and gripped my buttock, he squeezed it hard and the pain flashed through my entire body.  I gasped out aloud.  Despite the grinding weight and heaviness in my womb, a sure indicator of my body's interest in him, I was growing increasingly fearful.
'To the bed with you, good woman,' William cried with gregarious chivalry."I know this because Cecelia herself states earlier that her marriage was arranged very shortly after the start of her first season.  How is "To bed with you, good woman," chivalrous?  I would be more inclined to say it's imperious and domineering.

I think I could safely diagnose Portman with acyrologia (from afar, even), specifically cacozelia - a kind of acyrologia in which one uses newfangled speech or Latinate diction in order to appear learned.  I think learning of this condition is going to be unbelievably useful in writing reviews of this kind - you know, where the book is bad.  I would not recommend this to anyone looking for good erotica, or even erotica at all as not one line of this is erotic.

Kindle_Store.reviewText:
The idea behind this book is quite compelling - build up a bar using a minimal number of bottles required for an increasingly complex array of cocktails.

However, the authors fudge on the 12-bottle rule by having you make your own syrups, infusions, and mixers. (Homemade orgeat syrup? No. Just buy a bottle of amaretto)

They also exclude beer, wine, and cider from the count, even when a drink such as a French 75 must include sparkling wine.

Beyond this, they borrow heavily from other, better books such as The Drunken Botanist by Amy Stewart, and fail to properly include a bibliography.

Also, no tequila! Thus, it fails the basic test of being a reference/recipe book.

Much of the above could be forgiven if it ended up just being a large collection of drink recipies interspersed with colorful anecdotes, but the book fails utterly at being a recipe book, because of the physical printing of the book.

The dense, paperback, glue-spine format means the book absolutely will never lay open unless you break the spine at every recipe you wish to make, and if you do this, the pages begin to fall out.

Finally, very little attention is paid to technique, a far better way of learning good mixology. One would be far better served buying Jeffrey Morgenthaler's, The Bar Book, and looking up recipes on Wikipedia.
Kindle_Store.summary: Poor for math, misleading, and ultimately fails as a recipe book

Kindle_Store.reviewText: This book is a deceitful compilation of the lies and half-truths of the Italian police and prosecutors who wrongfully accused and prosecuted Amanda Knox and Raffaele Sollecito for the murder of Meredith Kercher in Perugia, Italy in 2007. It may add a few of its own fantastical non-truths and misleading interpretations. The truth is that the Italian Supreme Court fully and finally acquitted Knox and Sollecito of the murder and rape of Kercher in March, 2015. There was never any reliable, credible evidence of their involvement. This book may be defamatory, since it appears to claim that despite the Italian Supreme Court full acquittal of Knox and Sollecito, they were guilty. The actual murder and rapist was Rudy Guede, based on the evidence left at the scene of the crime, and who remains the only person convicted of the crime.  The author is merely trying to exploit this case for his own ends.
Kindle_Store.summary: A compilation of lies and half-truths not worth reading.

Now, other than the rushed information that we get, it would've been nice to actually have the parents in the story or maybe have had the book start from the mother's or even grandfather's pov and lead up to this point.

The major problem with this book is that is suddenly suddenly ends. Nik's cousin (who is the main focus of book 2 in this set) comes to help out but leaves when he says he got some possible Intel he must get in person and flies to Tampa. We never how the confirmation between Katya and her uncle go, if her uncle was behind setting up Nik (the uncle is Nik's second in command), we don't know the information Grigori received, if any, in Florida (though maybe it's in his book?), we never learn if Katya takes her place in the family. This story has potential and makes a decent start, but somewhere along the line it feels as if Ms. Kirkpatrick panicked and rushed to get through to the end. When you have such compelling material to work with - a young girl from a broken home, mother working two jobs to keep them on the fringes of the best school system in the neighborhood, a drug dealing relative, and all the privileged, wealthy classmates - it seems to me that the book could have covered consequences and reality a bit better.

When the topic got tough it felt as though we got the dime tour rather than the full price tour. I wish there had been more time spent exploring the familial relationships and the why/how things ended up the way they did. More time was spent on trivial things than on the meat of the story. While I understand that this was written targeting the YA audience, I was disappointed to discover that it dumbed things down for them, not giving them enough credit to handle the darker, more complex side of growing up and of life in general.

Most depressing was the message that it sent, or should I say didn't send. Sure, things could have ended as they did, but odds are they also could have ended drastically differently. The ending just felt false to me, which I find depressing as it could easily influence people to make very poor decisions, believing that they'll walk away without any consequences. It plays directly into the "that will never happen to me" mindset so dominant in our society, and most especially in the younger generations. Heck, it stays with some people their entire lives, however long, or short, they may be.

I'm sorry to say that this is not a book I would recommend for the intended audience. There are simply too many mixed messages and not enough realistic consequences for actions taken.

Yes, almost ALL gaffers tape is black or green screeen green nowdays, but white has some great uses in the cable and electrical department.

Another use for repeating shows is standing marks on the stage floor that come off when you are done without scrubbing. Using 3 pieces you can make arrows to direct motion on the stage floor - visable to the actors, not the audience.  Some hosts have their personal space - mark it with white gaffer's tape and write guests stay behind line.  This also helps with camera placement.

I've even had costume ask to "borrow" (yea right) some to mend a dress - they were amazed it didn't show afterwards and you bet it didn't come off!  I gave them a roll to score some points.  Now if their suspenders fall down they can fix it and think of what a nice guy the sound man was.

Not all gaffer's tape is black.  If you have a few rolls of black, a roll of white, and a roll or two of green depending on your backdrops you'll do fine.  It's adhesive strength is the same no matter the color so you get the effect you are looking for that does not come off until you are wrapped up.

There are similar steamers made by the same manufacturer (Steamfast), including SteamFast brand, McCullough, and it looks like Wagner has the same product design, and I think I came across other brands in my research.
