Electronics.reviewText:
I played my first round with the Garmin Approach G5 today. I was very satisfied.

Strong points:
--finds satellites quickly
--lists golf courses by order of how far you are from them...closest first...makes finding local courses easy (you can also type in names, but I don't see why you'd do it this way)
--automatic hole advance worked flawlessly
--tap-screen feature to zero in on the green and the area around the green (incluing traps and stuff) was very helpful...I used it on most holes
--distances to hazards like traps was very helpful...it's good knowing that you can aim at a trap (because you know you can't reach it)
--tap-screen feature to "place" the flag on the green is very useful...greens can be quite large, and there can be a 1-club difference between hitting to a front flag rather than a rear flag...I credit it with getting me a par on a long par-3 by indicating to use an extra club for a rear pin position
--with July's update, there are 4400 courses mapped out
--all courses are stored in the device, not on your PC
--monthly course updates are free, never(?) a subscription fee nor disabling of courses you've already received...this makes up for the initial high price of the unit, in my opinion
--course downloads are handled by Garmin as a "purchase" of an item that costs $0.00, very straightforward once you understand that's what's happening
--once the unit is registered and you "purchase" this month's course updates, the downloading process itself took only about 5 minutes, which seems remarkable for 4400 courses
--color screen easily visible in bright outdoor light
--very sturdy and waterproof
--only one physical buttton (on-off switch)
--all other functions are handled by the touchscreen, and everything was pretty intuitive
--measuring a shot was easy and fun (I do hit my 3-wood as far as I thought)

A couple of drawbacks:
--I walk and carry my clubs, and was not satisfied with using the belt clip to attach to my bag; I was afraid it would snap off
--Clipping the belt clip to your belt makes the unit hang in an unuseable position...you'd have to keep unclipping it
--It seems a little too big to put in your pocket without noticing it
--So I've ordered the separate slipcase with caribiner clip to hold it to my bag...I think I'll feel more confident with that setup
--Got just one round out of pair of batteries...you'll definitely want to order a couple sets of rechargeable batteries and a recharging device
--Quick-start booklet contains little information...it tells nothing about the initial steps of registering your unit online, how to find the serial number, or how to order course updates
--That said, the website has all the clues you need, although a few were hard to find and not entriely intuitive

Overall, my first impression is very positive. I formerly used a first-generation unit from iGolf, which just gave distances to the green. On this unit, the course map showing the shape of the hole, distances to hazards, closeup of the green, and ability to place the pin anywhere on the green were big improvements.

Does what I hoped for. Now I can see directly behind the car. I don't understand the lines yet. With unit off the mirror is a little dark but perfectly usable. The instructions aren't the greatest (had to use a magnifier to read them) but good enough. There's a red wire on the video feed that is not mentioned. I found on line you can hook it up to the backup light and to the trigger wire instead of going nuts looking under the dash. They must have different rulers in China. The picture doesn't scale 7" no matter how you measure it, but a heck bigger than 4" the others have. No way of telling if the camera is upside down so check before going nuts mounting it. What's with the remote? I guess my battery is weak, I had to hold it 4" away to use it. The mirror is at arms length away, what is the remote for? Haven't tried night yet. The LED's aren't working, have to check that. Same wires as the camera. Oh well, good luck, I'm pretty satisfied.
How about that. You can flip the view with the menu. No need to turn camera around.

The T612 is a great dock/speaker system for the iPhone 3G, though there are a few minor issues that prevent me from giving it a five star review.

As advertised, the device is properly shielded, so there is no signal interference from the phone when it's connected.  The sound quality is quite good for my purposes whether I'm listening to mp3 tracks using the iPhone's iPod functionality or using another audio producing application like Last. FM or Minnesota Public Radio's audio stream application.  The unit itself is quite easy to setup, just open the box, plug it in and away you go.  It also includes support for connecting non-iPod mp3 players via an auxilary jack on the back of the unit.  It even includes the cable for the aux connection which was really nice, I had assumed I'd have to buy one separately.

I only have two complaints about this unit.  First, despite being advertised as iPhone 3G compatible, for optimal functionality with the iPhone 3G, you need the iPhone 3G adapter base which is not included with the unit.  It is however available for free from Altec Lansing.  Another reviewer mentioned that they had to pay shipping when they ordered their 3G adapter, I did not, so I'm not sure if ALS has changed their policies or what.  Unfortunately I received notice that the adapter is currently on back order, so I don't know when I'll receive it.  To be clear though, the unit will work with the 3G iPhone without the specific 3G adapter, you'll just have to fiddle with it to get it properly seated on the connector.

The other minor gripe I have about this unit is that when you plug in the iPhone 3G, the phone displays a message stating that the accessory isn't compatible and asks if you'd like to turn on "airplane mode".  Since the speakers are properly shielded, this isn't necessary, you can just choose "No".  Not a big deal but a bit of a nuisance.

Overall I'm very happy with this unit and from what I can tell, there isn't a better alternative on the market at this time.
Electronics.summary: Great unit, minor issues for iPhone 3G

Electronics.reviewText:
This review is not so much about the SI-2150 as it is about adding another set of front speakers. I added this amplifier (SI-2150) to an Onkyo TX-NR709 to drive the additional pair of front channels.

My Home Theater (HT) system is a Klipsch Reference 7 series:  RF-7 fronts.  RC-7 center.  RS-7 surrounds.  RS-7 back. RSW-15 and an RSW-10 subs.  I had a Sony STR-DA1000ES receiver, or something like that, driving this system, minus the back channels, and it was pretty good.  I upgraded to the Onkyo strictly for the HDMI interface and it didn't seem to have what the Sony had, although they were very close in the wattage output, the Sony being 100 watts per channel (WPC) and the Onkyo 110 WPC, so, I decided to add another set of front speakers to the existing setup.

I had a nice pair of Infinity speakers that weren't being used, so I decided to add them to the mix.  They have a nice warm sound to them in contrast to the Klipschs, which I liked since the Klipschs are a little bright for my taste.  Don't get me wrong.  For movie watching, the Kilpschs are great.  But, they could still use a little warmth.  I used the Onkyo to drive the Infinitys and I used the SI-2150 to drive the Klipschs.  The sound stage, with four front speakers, was totally transformed.  Adding another set of fronts should be a must do on everyone's HT list.  It is very highly recommended.  I haven't watched many movies with the new setup, but the one movie I did use to test it (King Kong, with Jack Black, Academy nominated or winner for best sound effects) was excellent.  I alternated between the two speaker and the four speaker setup and the difference was amazing.

To be totally objective, I did not see much difference in sound quality or quantity between the SI-2150 and the Onkyo.  I was actually expecting to see some difference since the Onkyo is rated at 110 WPC and the SI-2150 at 150 WPC.  That was a bit disappointing.  I was hoping to see a noticable improvement having the Klipschs being driven by a dedicated, more powerful amp.  I am always reading about how a good amplifier is needed to get the Klipschs to perform, so I was expecting to experience some improvement.  Result: Same sound.  Same level of loudness.  And for reference, the gain on the amplifier was set at the midway point.

The physical quality of the unit is good.  Seems to be well made.  Everything seems to be intact and in place.  It came with no defects, although the box had slight damage.  It was double boxed, though.

I am not saying that this amp is no good.  What I'm saying is, don't expect too much.  It's just a means for adding channels.  Maybe that's its intended purpose.  If that's the case, then it has achieved its goal with flying colors.

This amp was not purchased from Amazon but directly from one of Amazon's retailers.

P.S.  I ended up purchasing another one of these amps, this time directly from Amazon, although, it came from the same company from which I ordered the first one. I've been using the ASUS Transformer Infinity for about a month now, and I have to say I really like it. I haven't had a chance to thoroughly use all the features - such as camera and video recording but I have a pretty good sense of the device. The reason I did not give it a five star review is because sometimes there is lag - for example after unlocking - but other than that it is indeed very, very fast, has good hardware materials, and excellent battery life.

Pros:
- Excellent screen resolution - text is very sharp
- Durable hardware materials - aluminum chassis is great, and the champagne color looks awesome
- Upgradeable to Jelly Bean out of the box
- Great amount of storage, and expandable by 32gb micro sd card
- Good price point considering all its features
- Excellent battery life - I tend to lower the brightness significantly due to personal preference
- Watching HD netflix movies on the 10" screen is great - the size is just right
- This depends on personal preference, but I find reading ebooks on it very comfortable. I thought it would be too big and heavy compared to a kindle, but it really works just fine for this function

Cons:
- Sometimes lags after unlocking - probably because it's updating widgets (certainly not a deal breaker)
- On mine the top two corners of glass must not be set completely or completely adhered to the unibody chassis because when I push on them I can feel the glass move a little and here a noise - probably a quality issue. Annoying, but not so much for me to return it (my hands aren't in those areas enough for me to care too much)

Overall - very much worth the money and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a top of the line general purpose Android tablet

At a quarter the price of the Olympus I will keep it. The slide on this is very stiff at first, almost to the point that you feel like you are going to break it. The most disconcerting thing to me was the total lack of smoothness and to actually have to rock back and forth on an uneven plane in the slots to get it to go down. Bottomline, just keep doing this a number of times and it will loosen up and become easier as time goes on as mine has. The bayonet fixture to attach the lens is fine and solid, it's just the sliding aspect that is tough to accept at first. Personally, I would never suggest applying any kind of lubricant to the slots as some have suggested. That's just introducing something you might really regret. I mean some people might be very good at it, but to suggest it to folks in general is, in my opinion, a bad idea. I'm giving this 4 stars as the overall look and effectiveness is just fine. I just wish JJC would do something about the difficult slide. Again, at a quarter the price of the Olympus, I can understand why it's not as good. Hope it hold's up!!

Razor has always been the guy that never seemed to grow up, but I feel in love with him in Smoke Signals. His story and Toris is not a traditional love story, but its beautiful all the same. They meet when she propositions him for sex, and instead of making her feel cheap he marries her instead. The rest of the story is spent watching them wade themselves through their relationship.

I must admit when I realized what her former professional was I wondered how Ms. Gayle would spin this. I shouldnt have worried, because my heart bled for her, and Catherine Gayle truly captured the plight of many women doing sex work. Razor was an amazing person, and exactly what she needed in order to her heal her body, heart, and mind. He was still the same loveable person, but showed a maturity he never quite captured while he was with the Portland Storm. It was always enjoyable to read about the other characters from both series, and the wedding was truly magical. Every book, be it the Portland Storm or the Tulsa Thuderbirds Series seems to get better!

These two work together and for the past two years have been denying the fact that they actually like each other. That is until Beck walks in on Maisie taking a shower at the fire station. Now Beck cannot unsee those beautiful curves that Maisie has been hiding. The chemistry was sizzling hot and their attraction soon started turning into something much more than just lust. Maisie was able to open up with Beck's help and not to mention all the fun times they shared while playing naked Twister.

Im new to Christis work (before this book, Ive only read her Sinful Brides series so far  highly recommended, btw) but it was clear from the start that she is a master of words. However, in The Spy Who Seduced Her, she writes so brilliantly that it is as if youve been whisked away into the story, feeling everything with such an intensity that Victoria and Nathaniel just come to life.

Having once been lovers in their youth, it seemed at first that darling damsel Victoria Tremaine and dashing spy Nathaniel Archer would go down the usual romance novel path, but fate had different plans. Two decades of mourning after her one true love, our now seasoned Victoria Barrett, Viscountess Waters, finds herself face to face with a very much alive Nathaniel Archer, Earl of Exeter and Sovereign of The Brethren of the Lords, when Victorias abominable husband meets a gruesome yet well deserved fate in a den of sin and vice. Nathaniel is tasked with investigating the murder of the late viscount  and the main suspect is none other than the new one, Victorias own son. In a thrilling, page-turning story, youll watch these characters grow in depth and complexity as secrets and heartache resurface during the investigation, in this compelling tale of love lost (but never truly), new beginnings and the utter importance of proper communication.

Make no mistake: this is no ordinary romance. Not only does it feature a mature, hardened pair that have been through more than their share of misfortune (to put it lightly), it does so in such a relatable, vivid way that youll feel the agony, the sorrow, the shock, the anger, the hope, the longing and finally, the blissful joy when they get their oh-so-deserved happily ever after.

For me, its a romantic love story.
Of course its primed in exquisite erotica. An art-form. Lifestyle. Where one-size does not fit all.
We begin at the tragic endkinda
By all appearances, Eli is an atypical submissive; however, appearances are deceiving. He is male sub perfection.
Elis enslavement is sensuous, serious, steeped in tradition & history.
The ending is somewhat predictable, but it ends with a wicked flourish.
I have a library full of books, and within that library I have a list of books I intend to read again. Enslaving Eli, is on that list.
And to think, all this time I thought Artemis was a male. BILLIEROSIEmy new favorite author/tutor.

First of all... this cover is so perfectly Jamie and Jessica.  Not all covers look like the characters do in my head... but that IS Jamie and Jessica.

Second of all... my book reviews for Melissa Foster's books should probably just start being called Melissa Foster author fan-girl crush posts.

I've loved Jamie's character since he was first introduced with his grandmother, Vera.  Before this book begins Foster even notes that "before I started writing this novel, I thought it was going to be difficult to find the perfect woman for Jamie Reed, but the minute I met Jessica Ayers, I realized it wasn't going to be difficult at all".  She was oh so right.  I can say that I was in love with Jessica by page 2.  (Any girl that chucks her phone off her deck after being outbid on ebay is a friend of my.  There are reasons I no longer bid on ebay.)

Jamie and Jessica truly are perfect together.  They're both extremely successful professionally for their ages.  Geniuses at what they do.  But... they've also both decided to take a little break for the summer.  Put their focus a little more on life... or in Jessica's case, finding out what life outside of the orchestra and her mother actually is.  Like the rest of the Seaside Summers couples... the cottages seem to be a place of magical destiny.

(I'm truly happy in my marriage and with my family and life... but boy would I have loved spending a summer at those cottages.  Chunky dunking with the girls while sipping some Middle Sister wines and, again, some margaritas.  And, of course, experiencing a romance that only Melissa Foster seems to be able to create.  I swoon.  Totally swoon.)
Books.summary: Sigh... Melissa Foster has me swooning again.

Books.reviewText: I loved reading this book, but even more I love putting into practice. Neil runs ancient truths through a litmus test of modern science and shows how and why they apply to our everyday lives. I can't think of a more pressing time in history for such a book as this to sink into our collective psyche and inform our thoughts and actions to create a future state that is surely desirable to all. A lot have already been written about the Sabbath but the need far outstrips the supply. What is the Sabbath? What makes this book unique compared to the other books? For author Shelly Miller, the first thing with regard to taking a rest is her mantra: "I Don't Do Guilt." There is no need to be guilty about taking a day off per week, or to rest where needed. Sabbath rest is about receiving a gift and not an excuse for guilt. While the world teaches us to rely on ourselves and our own abilities, taking a rest is in effect an acknowledgement that things will take care of themselves even as we rest. It requires surrender and deep trust. The way forward is not simply an obligation to force a weekly sabbath but to joyfully discover rhythms in which we can rest well. Sabbath is a gift. It is a reflection of God's creativity. It is an opportunity for us to demonstrate to others that rest is not only possible, it is beneficial. Miller goes beyond simply taking a break. Sabbath is a time in which we commune with God in an intentional space. It is an invitation to intimate conversation, unhurried by the hustle and bustle of the world. It is a way in which we say to the world: "You shall have no hold on me."

While the benefits are many, there are also myths and deceptions that threaten to derail our pursuit of Sabbath rest. That is why Miller spends time dispelling myths like doing Church as a form of Sabbath. She writes:

"I tell her that I don't do church anymore. I try to be the church to people. For me, doing church is an illustration in slothful living - not laziness, but mindless busyness, something you check off on a list for your week. The heart can become detached, the ritual commonplace, like a child's piece of art hanging on your refrigerator for month. Initially, it takes the centerpiece of daily activity, but over time the beauty is overlooked, lost in the mundane. Celebrating faith can become a callous responsibility." (69)

Right on.

Just because we do religion or church does not make our doing a restful act. In fact, Sundays can be particularly busy time for believers. Miller believes that belonging precedes believing. She dispels myths:

Needing long periods of quiet and stillness before one can rest well
Needing everything to be done before one can rest well
Becoming mature before one can rest well
Can only be done on Sundays
Using rest as a way of improving productivity
...
The key to true Sabbath is not in the what but in the who. It is not in terms of the activities but in terms of relationships. It is the discipline to stop and to pause without guilt, lest we be forced to stop through physical ailment or other unfortunate circumstances. Rest is a need. We are not created to run 24x7. Muller shows us the need to watch for the arrows of the Lord that direct us toward trust. Signs are there for us to see. From signs of rainbows and weather changes to sipping a cup of coffee leisurely, we avoid the temptation of non-stop action define us. Our identity is not based on what we do but who we are. Sabbath restores this truth. When this happens, we do not feel guilty about "wasting time." When we experience true rest, we see the miraculous among the monotonous; the quest in the question; delighting in playfulness instead of detesting endless chores. In true rest, we find love.

Miller knows that a lot has been written on the Sabbath, and she creatively includes the many poignant observations on the Sabbath from many spiritual writers. From Mark Buchanan, we learn that 'rhythm' is better than 'balance.' From Abraham Heschel, we learn of the Sabbath being the purpose of the other six days and how marriage can be a metaphor for the meaning of the Sabbath. From Matthew Sleeth, we learn of how Sabbath means less doing and more being. From Wayne Muller, we are warned that if we do not make time for Sabbath, something else would, even unpleasant things. From Eugene Peterson, we are reminded of another perspective besides mere progress and constant busyness. Sabbath restores us back to our creativity, instead of perpetual repetitive production activities. There are lots more from individual interviews and sharing. Comprising twelve chapters of fresh observations about the Sabbath and the practical ways to rest, I find myself hard to put this book down. Perhaps, for anyone who do not know where to start with regard to the Sabbath, why not begin with this book?

The single biggest reason to read this book is that it enables us to read not just for information but for inner formation. I like the way Miller flows in and out with stories, illustrations, observations, and Scripture references to show us the fluidity of swimming with the waves, dancing with the wind, and embracing the elements that often come across as problems for the restless world. The reason why there are many who hurry and let stress get to them is because they have failed to understand the benefits of Sabbath rest. That is why the dispelling of myths chapter is so important. Before we can learn the new, the old has to be put aside. We need a paradigm shift. We do not need to do more in order to feel fulfilled. We simply need to establish a gradual rhythm of rest. Miller shows us how and much more. If you are in need of a rest, this book is highly recommended to dispel the myths that often surround us. Do not let the gift of the Sabbath come to us and we leave it unwrapped. Open it and enjoy it.

Shelly Miller leads the Sabbath Society, an online community of people seeking to make rest a priority in this busy world. She lives in London, England with her husband where they work on church planting efforts. Her website is ShellyMillerWriter.com

This book does more than talk about flying in combat, it talks about the build up to war, life in the late 1930's in America and then the training process and the many accidents from young men showing off. His descriptions of combat are there, but not the strongest point.
Given that there are few other books that describe combat in the A-20, this is a valuable book for that alone. I could ask the author a zillion more questions, but this was a pleasant easy read that brought back my father's stories of Pre-WW2 and gives you a feel for life in the front lines of combat/attack aircraft. Heavy on background but a little light on tactics, combat and technical aspects.

Skye and Charlie are such fun characters!  Love reading this tango between Skye and Charlie.  It was like a chase between a cat and mouse.  You have Skye who is like the mouse would be around briefly, have her fun and make a run for it.  Charlie is the cat who loves to have fun and keeps trying to grip his claws onto Skye!

When these two are together, they have so much.  Some of the love scenes are so hot!  Unfortunately, Skye has issues that she does need to overcome both internally and externally.  Charlie does want to be that knight in shining armor to rescue her.  Who wouldn't want this hunky guy to save them?

This was not an extremely long read, but the length of the novel had so much material to keep me entertained.  Just like a good majority of Mimi's books, a lot of humor and steamy, hot moments!  Great job Mimi!

A funny, warm and genuinely moving play which deals with loss and how it affects relationships.  The play, easily Harvey's most theatrical, deals essentially with Danny, a recently deceased 30 year old Liverpudlian, and his relationships with his brother, his best friend and his lover; and their relationship to one another.  The story is told through a mix of fantastical heaven sequences, flash backs and current scenes; and features the usual array of larger than life camp characters, including Julie Andrews ("a chambermaid with exquisite diction") and Beryl (who is also "Judy Garland - Keeper of the Stars).  In short this play should appeal to anyone interest in modern drama, but likes a more romantic, sentimental, not to mention slightly camp, viewpoint

Jon Meacham has tried to go where others have really not gone before - to explore the friendship between President Franklin Roosevelt and his counterpart, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill in his new book Franklin and Winston.
Meacham has done a great job of describing, in intimate detail, the relationship between these two men.  I consider the book to be a true hybrid between a biography and a history because of the style of writing - intermixing details about the individual (the biography part) with situations in which the person played a role (the historical part).  Meacham intertwines these two in remarkable fashion.
This is an important book that truly displays how Roosevelt and Churchill were not only political compadres, but were indeed friends.  I greatly enjoyed how Meacham discussed, with such attention to details, those situations in which both men were involved and played a critical role.  I also appreciated the way in which Meacham explained how those encounters bolstered the friendship between the men - and why.
Although the friendship was rocky at times, with Roosevelt bowing to political necessity in lieu of being true friends, there is no doubt in my mind, based on Meacham's book, that these two men were so much more than just political heavyweights - they were indeed friends.
Books.summary: Half history, half biography, all good!

Books.reviewText:
Wow.  What a fab deck.  I just knew it was going to be beautiful and ordered without even doing my usual hunt on the net to get sneak advance peaks!  (Silly of me really, as there is a site called fairytaletarot.com where you can see loads of cards and read the foreword by Rachel Pollack too!)

Anyway, the artwork is gorgeous, detailed and beautifully coloured.  The colours are perfect - it's not bright, like the inner child cards - nor pastelly - but neither is it dark.  The book gives the tale behind each card - there are some I knew, and many I didn't.  I recommend buying the kit, as the tales give more to the meanings of the cards.

Is this a Rider-Waite clone?  I have no idea.  You'd need to visit one of the many tarot review websites to get their more professional opinion - I'm just a collector of cards with beautiful artwork - not an expert.

The cards are made nicely too - reversible backs, nice stock which should stand up to use.  And the book has an illustration of each card at the beginning of the relevant story, which is a plus for me.

Note:  This is definitely not for use with children, like Inner Child and the other fairytale deck by I can't quite remember who.  It is a deck for adults, as the fairytales here are the real versions, not the expurgated ones normally found in kids's books - and thus much more interesting!

Highly recommended.

This is so beautifully crafted, reading it makes my heart break that the author is not earning royalties.  a LOT of work went into this...I know, because I'm a writer too... A LOT OF WORK went into this gorgeous, layered, rich story.

Why on earth is this free?  I'm not meaning to complain, here. I think it's great that it's free, because if it hadn't been, I most likely would not have found this author.

But ... this is so beautifully done, I stopped several times while I was reading it, just to mourn the fact that it's free.  That's a first for me.

The only thing unfortunate about it is the title, which isn't compelling enough to  adequately represent the haunting, beautiful writing contained in this piece of work.

Who will like this:  readers who liked The Hunger Games, the Pendragon series by D.J. Machale, books by Garth Nix or Terry Brooks; readers who like fantasy with danger and more sophisticated themes will enjoy this.  It's an exploration of the effects of war on society and an individual coming of age story; it's also an examination of the effects of isolation on a person, and what it means to be "outcast," whether by choice or force.

the author is comfortable in the world he's created, so the reader can slip right into it--there aren't so many made-up words and names that you become aware of the writing and are constantly jolted out of immersion in the story.

Snap it up while it's free!

**edited:  it looks like there is an update to this book, I'm assuming it's been edited.  I love authors who do this - they're showing that they care about the quality of their product, and showing respect to the readers as well...another reason to appreciate this author.

Review 7*******

This is a heart warming story, which touched me deeply. This book is not my usual reading material, but I can say with hand on heart that I absolutely LOVED it!

Marissa Lyons is a divorced mother of two, who lives in the suburb of Vista Heights, San Martino near San Francisco. She is a wonderful mother, but when she finds out her high school nemesis, Beatrice Munson is moving in across the street, she's a nervous wreck! However, she takes the bull by the horns and goes to welcome her.
Beatrice Munson is a force to be reckoned with! She is like a whirlwind, bringing new life to the staid suburb. She has a very Zen outlook, and is very colourful in her personality and her dress.
I don't want to say too much and put in spoilers, but it is a fantastic book about friendship, following one's dreams, love, loss, new beginnings and family. The residents of Vista Heights are challenged and changed in ways they never thought possible.
There are some wonderful characters in this book, and my favourite has to be Jeffrey. He is the sweetest, funniest, most glamorous and generous person I have ever come across. His parties are to die for!

Lorena Bathey has written a witty, fast paced story that made me laugh and cry. As I have stated previously, I don't usually read this genre, but I am glad I gave this book a chance. This book is very hard to pigeon hole into any one category, so I highly recommend this book if you love a contemporary book that is highly entertaining. It does have one scene of an attempted rape, so I do not recommend it for younger readers (under 16). I am now a fan of Lorena Bathey's, and I will be on the lookout for more of her books in the future.

I was given this book by the author to read.  I have not been paid for this review.  This is my honest opinion.

I bought this as a gift for my mother, who is an Alzheimer's patient and is not longer able to successfully read, knit, or any of the other hobbies she once enjoyed so much. She uses it every day and I will definitely be looking for more!

I do notice that she is primarily focusing on the images that have large fields to color. The more detailed pictures with tiny leaves, etc. must be hard for her to see and she is skipping over those. I imagine that other residents who have better vision than she does may wind up completing those pages. If your Alzheimer's loved one was once a "doodler" like my Mom, I encourage you to try this as an activity for them.

4.5 stars. I confess that I am a New Adult junkie. In the few weeks since The Deal was released, I have lost count of the number of times someone recommended that I read it. I have to admit that I become nervous about well-hyped books because I worry that they won't live up to my expectations. Fortunately, that was not the case here. The Deal was fantastic read with everything I love wrapped up into one entertaining storyline. The writing was solid and the characters were fun, but more importantly was the fact that I felt everything  the steam, the romance, and the heartbreak.

When I first read the synopsis of this book I remember rubbing my hands together and thinking Here we go! I love the idea of two people who don't particularly like one another having to help each other out in order to get what they want. Hannah was a wonderful heroine. She was intelligent, hardworking, and spunky. There were many times that I wanted to high five her for standing up for herself and being honest with Garrett. I felt horrible for what she had been through and how it had affected her parents, but she was nothing if not strong and resilient.

Garrett was amazing. While he was a bit of a playboy, at least he was clear about the fact that he wasn't interested in a relationship. When Garrett realized that he could have something more with Hannah, I admired how he was willing to go all in. I enjoyed his protective side, but I especially adored how tender and supportive he was of Hannah. Garretts commitment to his teammates was commendable, and I just loved his interactions with them. Those boys were so real and funny. As the book progressed I couldn't decided what I want to do more, hug Garrett or punch his father in the face.

Elle Kennedys writing style was fresh and engaging. There were plenty of romantic moments that made my heart happy and steamy parts that had me fanning myself. However, my absolute favorite aspect of this book was the banter between Hannah and Garrett. This book was genuinely laugh out loud funny. Kennedy did a wonderful job of making The Deal one of the most entertaining stories I have read in a long time. I believe I highlighted a good half of the book and not just the humorous scenes. Bring on Logans story!

As a former combat veteran who's been through the muck of SpecOps, Rob provides valuable insight from both ends of the spectrum in order to guide the readers through their search for solutions to some of life's universal challenges. Immediately, those who choose to embark on this literary endeavor are whisked away by Mr. Dubois' relentless and collective pursuit of personal and international peace keeping. Just as our elite special forces warriors understand that there is no easy operation, readers of this book are reminded early and often of the painstaking and arduous process the element of seeking and keeping peace in order to resolve conflict. A short but powerful read (154 pages) This book is a superb fit for purveyors of policy, educators and generally "doves and hawks" alike.

This is a novel about relationship, relationship between an older and a younger woman, between civilized and wild, the wounded and the healer, the self and all beings. Deena Metzger takes the reader on a journey into a world where these distinctions blur. New meaning, in-sight, emerges in the gap between what the narrator thinks she knows and what she comes to know when sees how porous reality is and learns in the deepest of ways how our wanton killing is not the burden of others but each one of us.

Metzger doesn't write about this abstractly. She takes us on a visceral journey. Just one example:
"Learning from Azul, (the woman) began searching out her own images and her own nightmare geography. The third rail of the subway. Sparks flying. Vast dump sites smoldering. Endless landscapes of twisted fenders, greasy, bent, rusted, unserviceable automobile parts. Miles of cracked plastic tubing. Storm clouds of plastic bags wafted by fierce winds. Mangled rubber hoses. Cities collapsed into endless miles of sewers. The woman was always lost in deserted subway stations, stairs going down and then down again and then down again...."

Only a poet of great power could make a reader see with new eyes. Only a fine storyteller could make us care about the relationship between these two women as they teach each other new ways of being in the world.

I highly recommend this novel.
Books.summary: A novel of transformation that has the power to transform

Books.reviewText: Kate Evans leaves her home in the lower 48 states to become a bush pilot in pre WW II Alaska.  She is the only woman in a group of pilots who fly the area to deliver mail, carry passengers, and deliver freight to the outlying areas.  Kate has a secret about a plane crash that killed her best friend  but she is determined not to let that stop her from her dream of being a bush pilot.  Almost everyone in he new home has a secret from the past also.  Paul, is one of the people that receives mail from her route to a remote area.  She is attracted to him but wants to know about his past.  This is a well-written Christian romance novel with accurate information about bush pilots in Alaska.

Books.reviewText:
Mark Bittman is not vegan, but he spends a good portion of every day eating that way. Bittman refers to his dietary choices as VB6, which is also the title of his new book. VB6: Eat Vegan Before 6:00 outlines what he believes is an ideal balance of healthfor you and for the planetand satisfaction. He outlines the six principles of VB6: eat fruits and vegetables in abundance, eat fewer animal products, eat (almost) no junk food, cook at home as much as possible, consider quality over quantity, and see your weight as just one component of good health. He outlines food that you should eat (and food that should be eating sparingly or not at all), gives ideas for how to make his plan work for you, and even offers a 28-day meal plan to get started, using the recipes considerately provided at the end. But Bittman makes sure to point out that VB6 is not a diet, per say; there are no calories to be counted, no guilt to be felt if you stray for a meal or a day or a week, no temporary rules to follow before returning to the way you eat normally. VB6 is a lifestyle, a long-term change that will make you healthier (Bittman has been eating this way for six years and has lost weight and seen his numbers improve) without making you feel deprived. If you're looking for new ideas for a healthier life, check this out.

This review originally written for Sacramento/San Francisco Book Review.
Books.summary: Be vegan part-time for a healthier life!

Books.reviewText: I received a free advance e-copy of this book and have chosen to write an honest and unbiased review. I have no personal affiliation with the author.  Wow!  Kathy Reichs introduces a new character, Sunday Night.  She is a detective who is flawed and has a dark past that haunts her.  Sunday Night is smart and savvy and she dislikes rules.  As she works to solve the case she continuously has flashbacks from her horrible past.  She works with her brother, Gus.  This is a very well written thriller with a fantastic plot that is full of twists and turns and the action never quits. This is an amazing story that grabbed my attention right from the beginning and didn't let go until the very end.  Kathy Reichs is one of my favorite all time authors and I like Sunday and Gus. This is a keeper and well worth the read.  I look forward to reading more about Sunday and Gus in the future and Im anxious to see how the author develops the characters.

50 Whimical, delightful, adorable drawings of a variety of pets to color. It is a find your favorite animal and get started book. The pig in the bathtub is one of my favorites. Great book to get practice shading and coloring fur and feathers.
If the paper version of the book is purchased you don't have to worry about bleed through to pictures on the back side of the page if you use ink pens or markers The drawings are on one side only. It is still a good idea to place, perhaps, a piece of cardstock under the drawing if you don't like to remove the page from the book to color them.
Drawings are crisp and clean, colorists from beginner to the really experienced will find hours of fun in coloring Pampered Pets.
The author makes this interesting statement It has been said that if we see animals in a peaceful state, it can provide us with an impetus for personal change and healing.

I love this book, I enjoy just looking at the drawings as well as coloring the pictures. I received a free copy for reading it and doing an honest review.

I was diagnosed with a very dangerous type of cancer almost four years ago.  It had spread and the biopsy showed it to be highly agressive.  I learned that I had about a 10% chance of surviving 5 years.  Today, I am cancer free; I frequently work 14-16 hours a day at a job that I love, with little feeling of lethargy; and I look and feel younger than I did ten years ago.  I credit Denny Waxman's macrobiotic program, which he outlines in this book in a very clear and understandable way.  This book is engaging and easy-to-read, and you'll find that you can read it cover to cover in an evening.  I recommend that you do.

I have Melody's smaller yet thick paperback which is all underlined and dogeared, but now so is this one. The photos are phenomenal. The information is intensive, complete, advanced. The index is very helpful. It gives you all you need to know in relation to the hardness of the gem and the information a gemologist would need, but more importantly to me, everything you need to know about the metaphysical and astrological properties of the gemstones. My ONLY complaint, is that it is way too heavy for me to lift, so I have to keep it right next to me where I can just slide it over to my lap, I'm not supposed to lift more than 5 lbs and this sure weighs far more than that. I have over 50 gemstones books, if the house was on fire, I'd put this in a roller bag and take it out and leave all the rest behind!
Books.summary: If you get this, you don't need anything else!

Books.reviewText:
The scope of this book is wider than the story of how people populated Scotland over thousands of years. It's also about all of the British Isles and Europe and Africa, and how various groups, mostly farmers, moved incrementally westward toward Britain. It's full of stories about archaeological evidence of ancient settlers, and place names that have survived from ancient times. DNA sampling reveals areas where Norse, German, French and other settlers dwelt.

One of the most interesting stories to me was about the last Ice Age, when ice was piled high in Scotland and around the northern hemisphere. The water that formed all that ice came from the world's oceans, to the extent that the sea level was low enough that people and animals could walk from Africa and Europe to what is now Britain. Skeletal remains of animals native to Africa have been found in Britain. There was a settlement in what is now the English Channel. The ice melted, and the oceans rose, forming the English Channel. Later migrations to Britain were by boat.

The book has no pretensions of a page-turning plot, but I remained fascinated throughout. I am very happy to know so much more about my ancient ancestors.
Books.summary: The ethnic origins of the people of the British Isles

Books.reviewText:
Shepard's primary goal is to help readers understand how the convergence of native telecommunication technologies and the companies that create them provides the fundamental underpinnings of customer service.
  He addresses three major aspects of telecommunications convergence:
  Technology Convergence - Current telecommunication technologies and how they are evolving and affecting our lives. The book provides excellent and brief descriptions of the myriad of today's telecommunication technologies; IP, Fiber Optics, ATM, SONET, Frame Relay etc., etc., etc...
  Company Convergence - How Telecommunication technology is rewriting the business plans of the companies that manufacture telecommunication equipment, as well as those that provide and receive telecommunication services.
  Services Convergence - The new technology and its rapid evolution requires changes in the way services are delivered and a rigorous anticipation of customer needs. Service providers must look beyond the needs of their customers to the needs of their customer's customer.
  The book includes a comprehensive glossary of industry acronyms and an extensive bibliography of books, articles, and online resources.

Part 2 of A Garden In Paris continues the story of Mary Davis and her daughter Liz. It is also the story of the incredible men who cross their paths. Mary is a widow who, though dedicated to her husband while alive, searches for a future in remnants of the past. Leaving Omaha, she finds herself in Paris.

Liz roots herself in Omaha and all the illusions it holds. When her fiancé asks for more than just continuing her past, to shape their future, Liz balks.

The characters are well developed. I found myself strongly disliking one character, but this person grew as a person to the point I found understanding, acceptance and forgiveness.

This book is a tribute to the author's versatility in moving from historical to contemporary fiction.  Thanks for the gift of story!

Nothing could have prepared me for the astonishment when this book came out of an ordinary brown box.

It's huge. It's heavy. Yet each page immaculately and intimately portrays a superb piece of jewelry with a scholarship that can only come from a life's work, in fact two lives' work. Ethnic Jewellery and Adornment comes from the shared passion of Truus and Joost Daalder for jewelry, history, world cultures, and each other.

This book is like the Sistine Chapel. You can't understand it in pieces. Internet researchers might see an online photograph of a Mongolian headdress with an excellent description and say, "Oh, isn't that interesting," satisfied that they have learned something.

Yes... they have, but the totality of the passion that comes from this book is not there. You have to start at the beginning. Fill yourself with wonder at a collection that darts from antiquity to the present day as easily as it travels the world.

Ethnic Jewellery and Adornment is an extraordinary journey. Take it. When you quote from it, you can be secure the information is correct. That is rare -- anywhere.

I now have to put on my hair ornament in the shape of a round hat from the Tai Lue (Dai) people of Laos and go for a walk. Oh, and I must make sure the characters and flowers that symbolize winter are seen in front, because it is February in Idlewild Park, Reno, Nevada, and the geese will expect me to be correctly attired.

Thank you for writing this book. Thank you for living the lives you did.

BarbaraAnne
BarbaraAnne's Hair Comb Blog

This book was written in 1994 but the questions it asks and answers it gives still apply.  Depending on how the question is viewed it can be seen as trite or provocative. Trite because the answer is obviously yes:  there are Catholic universities and hospitals; there are buildings that house Catholic churches; there are people who call themselves Catholic; and provocative because if the answer is so obviously "yes", then why ask the question?  Because if the answer is "yes" than the further question is What exactly is Catholicism?  There is the Joe Biden brand of Catholicism, which pays lip service to the teachings of the Church but is really seeking something else - popularity, wealth, etc.  And then there is the Catholicism that Fr. Schall espouses - a faith that seeks to follow the teachings of the Church as the institution that was founded by Jesus Christ himself.  The goal is personal sanctity, achieved by self-giving.  Many of the problems that Fr. Schall lists still exist today although some have begun to improve; e.g. there are more bishops and cardinals who are forcefully standing for what the Church teaches; this is no longer left to the Pope only.  This book is not an easy read.  It is written at times in a way that makes it hard to grasp the concepts.  I feel sometimes that this is because the author is trying to teach profound insights that are not easily translatable into accessible language.  For example, one of the recurring themes is that the Church's teachings reflects how things are, that is the nature of things, so that its teaching aligns with reality as it actually is and not as we would want it to be.  Perhaps, the clearest example is on marriage, where natural law (the law of nature) is embedded in the teaching of the Church.  But there are other areas where this is so but that teaching is harder to grasp.  For example, that each and everyone of us has a purpose, guided by Providence.

Fr. Schall is honest and forthright, even taking on John Paul II's encyclical that could be interpreted as demonizing capitalism.  This stance was modified by a later document, but it was a bit jarring to see Fr. Schall so directly criticize the teaching of a pope who he thinks was perhaps the most brilliant man to ever sit on the Chair of Peter.

I didn't think I would love this book as much as I did. But The Alchemists of Loom surprised me in countless ways and I'm already calling it--I'm going to be obsessed with this series.

Arianna is a dragon hunter and, more or less, a thief for hire. Known as the White Wraith, she uses her skills and her partner's weapons to complete heists for the highest payer. During on of these heists, Ari runs into a wounded dragon rider--Cvareh. But instead of killing him and harvesting his organs for the black market, she accepts his deal: a wish in exchange for her getting him to the Alchemists of Loom.

I think the biggest selling point--for me--with this book were the characters. The book is split into four points of view--Arianna, Cvareh, Florence (Ari's partner), and Leona. I loved how Kova wrote her main protagonists; they were fleshed out and underwent amazing development. While my favourite POVs were Ari and Cvareh, Leona's and Florence's were by no means boring. They definitely moved the book along and added their own action to the story, but I was just way more involved with Ari and Cvareh.

This book is wild. The author starts just as Ari is about to start her mission and it certainly gave the book an edge. I was hooked from that moment and it didn't hurt that Ari was a pretty great and sassy character. She takes a lot of risks and has a smart mouth, but she's loyal and caring and she shows this countless times with Florence, someone Ari would die protecting. Although it took some time to find out her full story, Kova wrote it at a steady pace, dropping hints but never dumping too much on the reader. But we are told early on that she's bisexual so that was great! Finding out her story was totally worth it in the end.

I also ADORED Cvareh. I don't even know what it was about him, but I ended up loving him so much, all I want is for him to be safe and happy, two things which probably won't happen any time soon because when do they ever? But anyway, he was both sweet and loyal and despite how Ari treated him in the beginning, he still stood by her and helped her. He also took care of Florence countless times, and I liked that they had a good friendship blossoming.

Ari and Cvareh are complicated. I wasn't sure at first if Kova would pair them up, because it sure as hell wasn't looking like it, but I definitely love how she wrote their partnership. Ari absolutely hates dragons and Cvareh has no reason why. But slow, but surely, they come to slightly be friends, even through their ups and downs. Their back-and-forth turned into thoughtful conversations and at some point, Ari begins to trust him and see Cvareh in a new light, while Cvareh begins to see her as something more.

That isn't to say there's really a romance here. It's totally not the point of the story and it definitely does not take over the plot, but I loved the groundwork of a possible romance. I'm really hoping to see more because these two are my favourite tropes: enemies-to-(possibly)-lovers and sloooooow burn.

Also, I loved the friendship between Florence and Ari. It was clear that they loved each other dearly and Florence would do anything for Ari, while Ari would protect her no matter the cost.

The world Kova wrote is super intricate and intriguing. I loved how she created the guilds that focused on different talents and how she created her dragon race. They lived in the sky and it was super cool how their organs gave them different powers. It's probably one of the most unique magic systems I've ever read about and I'm excited to explore more of the guilds and dragons!

Although there wasn't much of Leona in the book, I liked her as an antagonist! She has an interesting relationship with her dragon king, sometimes which seems obsessive, but she always had her priorities straight and she was straight-up ruthless.

Overall, this was a great book. While I'm sad that book two, The Dragons of Nova, has been pushed back from April to July, I'm still eagerly awaiting it. 4 solid stars for this one!
Books.summary: I'm going to be obsessed with this series.

Books.reviewText: The Brotherhood of War is a story of the US Army Aviation and the US Army Special Forces; the story follows a group of characters from early in their career immediately prior to WWII, through the post war years, into Korea, and finally into Vietnam.  The books reflect the ranks of the key characters; and the changes in responsibilities, and perspective as they progress through the ranks.  Griffin writes from the perspective of the soldier, having been a Marine in WWII.  Start with the Lieutenants and you will find that you want to read all nine of the books in the series.

Ruby is a writer, but when her long term relationship ends she takes a job house sitting with the help of her best friend. However, this job becomes life threatening when people start dying.

It took several pages for me to really get into the plot and grasp what was going on because it was a little confusing, but then it got good. Really good!

The owner of a house contacts a company that deals with the house sitting. The owner, whom Nate and Ruby never meet face to face, becomes a very important part of the story. Though they never meet the elusive man, they discover a lot about the kind of man he is and what it means for Ruby because she is house sitting. Ruby comes to work for Nate, who owns the house sitting company, through a mutual connection. What starts as a convenient working relationship evolves into so much more when Ruby begins to uncover the secrets of the house.

As a writer, Ruby is naturally curious and theres plenty to discover on this assignment. First and foremost is the absentee owner who likes to play with women. And then there are the mysterious deaths.

The characters were for me what made this book special. Nate and Ruby had an instant attraction from the beginning. Though this book is more mystery than romance, I was able to watch their relationship develop and witness them learning to trust each other through the incidents and deaths that occur in the book. Through everything they learn a lot about each other.

The mystery and attraction turned romance is a perfect beach read. The mystery took some time to develop but that time was insightful towards knowing more about Nate and Ruby and their relationship. The climax was the highlight because all of the clues and bits and pieces that Ruby unraveled. It all came together for a realistic and satisfying conclusion.

This is the sequel to last years Fire with Fire, in which Earth had been contacted by aliens and brought to a Convocation of the existing space-traveling races to apply for membership in the Accord that all of them currently belong to. Caine Riordan, a sort of investigative reporter, is the central character, although there are many passages from other points of view. In that Convocation humanitys application is denied, and as this book begins the human base at Barnards Starwhich is the gateway to the other human-settled systemsis attacked by a joint force of the Arat Kur (who look something like giant cockroaches) and HkhRkh (who look something like giant sloths) and most of its fleet wiped out, and shortly thereafter a much larger fleet invades our solar system, takes control of Earth orbits, and lands an invasion force on Java. The rest of the book deals with the human response to this invasion, and I won't say anything about how it comes out other than to say that I expect there will be further books in the series. Good military SF set in the early 22nd century.

I was pleasantly surprised by this book. After reading some excerpts I was not sure if I was going to like the main character. She is a little rough around the edges. A bit too brash for me but Meghan is just what Adrian needs.  The two make a great couple. The banter that they have throughout their story makes for a great read. The attraction the two have simmers until it begins to boil and than the fireworks explode. Alongside their hot sex scenes there is a sweet romance between Meghan and Adrian. I enjoyed watching their relationship grow into so much more than just boss and secretary.

I was given a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

I listened to the audiobook of this novel through Overdrive. It was the first audiobook that I ever listened to and I really enjoyed it.

Book one of the Dr. Thomas Silkstone series is a strong beginning to an interesting main character. An anatomist, Dr. Silkstone, must uncover who killed Sir Edward Crick and why. Placed in the late 1800s, The Anatomist's Apprentice created a fun and enjoyable Victorian-esque crime thriller that I enjoyed.

Tessa Harris provided so many twists and turns along the way that I never knew who was going to be accused of murder next and in the end left me completely surprised at who had killed Edward Crick.

Believeable and entertaining, I will definitely be following along with this character through the next couple books.

Books.reviewText:
I love Sharon Sala's books, in fact I really enjoyed A Field of Poppies.  I found the characters and plot intriguing and well-developed.  I liked that it was a departure from her usual style and genre, but I still felt it was romance-y enough...exactly what I expect from a Sala novel.

This book only earns 4 stars (well, 3.5 if I could offer half-stars) due to the confusion of dates being bandied about in relation to age and birthdays.

You learn early on that Poppy is 20 and a little later that Poppy's mom (Helen) was born July 4, 1962 and died September 12, 2011 (aged 49).

Fast-forward a few chapters, all of a sudden, Helen graduated from high school in 1973 and Poppy was born December 9, 1973, when Helen was 18 (so now she should have been born in 1955).  And should have died at age 38 (1993).

Fast-forward a few more chapters and Poppy is aghast that she forgot her mom's birthday...in OCTOBER!

Sharon, honey, I love your books and look forward to reading them as quickly as they're published, but these types of errors drive me crazy and totally take me out of the moment in the story.  Self-publishing a book does not excuse the lack of copy editing.  However, if a person can look beyond these errors, the book is totally worth it.  Poppy is strong and resilient and everything I wished I'd been at the age of 20.

Grade: B-

This is a book I would never in my life have wanted to read on my own, but I was forced to for an economics class and ended up enjoying it a great deal.
Although the numerous statistics and case studies started to get a little redundant after awhile, I learned a lot about my family's spending habits and what I should do or avoid when I start my own family.  I found out that my parents are stereotypical millionaire UAW's (under-accumulators of wealth).  I've been brought up a hyperconsumer... I hope that the knowledge I gained from this book will help me to reverse my spending-before-earning habits.
Books.summary: This book greatly surpassed my expectations.

Books.reviewText:
Think of megachurch pastors and names like Bill Hybels, Mike Breaux, Rick Warren, and Joel Osteen come to mind. Rarely does one think of Bob Russell. Now that I have had the chance to get to know Bob Russell personally, I bet that doesn't bother him a bit.

Russell was at the helm of Southeast Christian Church in Louisville, KY, one of the largest churches in the nation for more than 40 years. His book, When God Builds a Church: 10 Principles for Growing a Dynamic Church tells the story of Southeast Christian, while distilling principles from Scripture for implementation in other churches.

When God Builds a Church unveils Russell's philosophy about church growth, as much by what it says as by what it doesn't say. It is rare that a pastor can give so much practical, godly counsel without his advice devolving into formulas to be replicated everywhere else.

Russell's principles for a dynamic church begin with Truth (he argues strongly for biblical authority, conservative theology, and a Bible-centured focus) and Worship (he avoids the "worship wars" by calling for selflessness). In the chapter on Leadership, he lays out the biblical case and practical rationale for a plurality of elders.

As one who has frequented Southeast on occasion (and even taught there several times), I appreciated the chapter on Excellence. Say what you may about the mega-church movement. No one can deny that everything at Southeast is done with a spirit of excellence. Would that more churches seek to honor the Lord by offering excellence in every part of church life!

Interspersed throughout the book are Russell's recollections from his forty years of ministry. In the chapter on Faith, he recalls the sacrificial giving of the congregation. In the chapter on Harmony, he tells of tough moments when the church exercised discipline (highly unusual for a megachurch). Two other chapters (Participation and Fellowship) outline practical ways to get members involved.

Perhaps the most unique part of Russell's contribution to church growth is his insistence on preaching the truth, even when it makes people uncomfortable. In the chapter on Stewardship, he argues for more preaching on money, even if people do not want to hear it. Russell constantly cuts against the prevalent megachurch mentality that avoids confrontation at all costs.

In the final chapter, Evangelism, Russell explains that being seeker-sensitive does not mean crafting a worship service with the seeker in mind. Instead, it means we should genuinely worship God and grow in our walk, while welcoming seekers into our midst. Southeast does this by having sermons crafted with Christians in mind, and also by serving Communion and baptizing new converts every Sunday.

All in all, When God Builds a Church is the best book I've read from anyone associated with the megachurch movement. It is practical and full of sound wisdom and its author is one of the godliest men I know.
Books.summary: Practical and Full of Sound Wisdom

Books.reviewText:
The Second Edition of Way Beyond Monochrome goes way beyond just the basics... this dense, 500 plus page book covers every technical aspect of traditional black and white photography including such arcane information as to how to mix your own darkroom chemicals (this might turn out to be quite useful as traditional photography continues become a niche market and the supplies necessary to practice it becomes harder to casually come by).

The first 100 pages of Way Beyond Monochrome focuses on the basics: Visualization, Print Control, and Presentation. The print control and presentations chapters are very strong useful, especially the nearly 50 pages dedicated to the presentation of the end print... an area just as important as getting the print right. As great as this book is, it lost half of the fifth star in this section... only a measly 20 pages or so dedicated to visualization, composition, etc. Yes, there are plenty of books dedicated to this topic, but this book is so committed to every other aspect of black and white photography that another 50 pages on just the process of visualizing the image long before the print.

The next 300 pages are dedicated to the science of black and white photography... Tone Reproduction, Image Capture, Negative Control, and case studies. This is where this book really shines! Every technical aspect of black and white photography and the science behind is covered here, including numerous graphs and charts that will make your head spin. From the Zone System to critical focusing to fine exposure control to creating and maintaining a personal standard... these 300 or so pages will deliver.

The last 100 or so pages cover what you will need in equipment and facilities, and it will provide some invaluable tips, tricks, and tools such as building your tools like a zone ruler, test strip printers.

And, all of this material is supported by some very nice photography as well... a plus for a book like this.

Where else did it loose the half a star? Well, this is 2010 after all and though this second edition does include new material on the digital aspect of black and white photography, it mostly focuses on it as either a bastard step child or as just a tool to be utilized sparingly. And, this is unfortunate. As awesome as traditional photography is, digital cannot be ignored. And, for this book to have been truly great, it would have been more forward looking... It should have taken digital as a standalone technology more seriously; but, it really missed an opportunity to teach the digital photography much more about the photographic science of old and how it correlates to the photographic science of new. Rightly, it points out how much manipulation Ansel Adams did with his photograph, but it missed an opportunity to correlate that to the digital darkroom that so many photographers are now utilizing exclusively.

A Guide to my Book Rating System:

5 stars = This book changed my world in at least some small way.
4 stars = Good book, but not life altering.
3 stars = Wasn't a waste of time, but it was time wasted.
2 stars = Don't bother, clean your bathroom instead.
1 star = The wood pulp would have been better utilized as toilet paper.
Books.summary: The Technical Bible for Traditional Black & White Photography

Books.reviewText:
The Bering Sea Pollock fishery is currently the largest single fishery, by volume, for the U.S. and Russia, which share the Bering Sea.  Kevin Bailey's "Billion-Dollar Fish" tells the history of that fishery and in the process explores the challenges of modern fisheries management.

Bailey takes a meandering path through his topic, mixing personal anecdotes about time at sea in the Bering with almost breathless accounts of the intense commercial competition to exploit the Pollock fishery, and with some careful commentary on the shifting and evolving state of the marine science which has influenced the management of the fishery over the years.  There are well-developed vignettes about some of the colorful and strong characters one can encounter in Alaskan fisheries.  Bailey devotes time and effort to describing the controversial politics of managing the Bering Sea fishery, especially as it has played out in the State of Alaska and in the U.S. Congress.  The processes Bailey describes have led on the one hand to the undoubted disaster of the doughnut hole, still barren of Pollock twenty years after a moratorium ending fishing there, and on the other hand, to the current thriving Bering Sea Pollock fishery, albeit with a challenging future.

This book would likely have benefited from additional editing; those readers not already familiar with the fisheries business may find it hard to follow.  Readers wedded to a particular point of view on the subject of fisheries may be frustrated by Bailey's evenhanded approach.  However, this fisheries analyst and former Alaska resident found much of interest in the book, and appreciated Bailey's willingness to admit the limits of the current science and to explore all sides of a complicated topic.  Recommended.
Books.summary: Interesting path to a challenging subject...

Books.reviewText:
I like the way the author writes.. The book is told from switching POV, Carter and Ari. They have known each other since 4th grade and in between all that's happening, there're snippets of their past which make you "get" them better. Carter is so perfect. Handsome. Rich. Smart. Even good at basketball and oh he's so good in bed. I like their friendship. Like that they know each other so well that they can just call BS all the time.
I was expecting more resistance when they got together. But this work too. And then near the last 20% was the turn in the book. Felt so bad for Carter. Like the ending. And so glad I had "Sincerely, Arizona" at hand to continue reading right after I finished this book.
Missing opening or closing quotation marks or a comma or a full stop here and there.. and wrong pronoun twice prevent me from giving this book a five star.

The recipes in this book are written well and easy to follow.  They are normal recipes, that you can make with normal ingredients.  All you need is a Spiralizer, which you can get right here on good ol Amazon!  I think this book is great in terms of the assortment of recipes provided.  I obviously haven't made all of them, but the 2 that I have made, were easy to make.

2 things I don't like, and 1 of them is a big one for me, is the fact that there is no nutritional information on any of the recipes.  Most books now tell you how many calories, fat, protein, etc, are in each recipe.  This book is completely missing that.  Because of that, I am giving it 4 stars.  I almost gave it 3, but the recipes look really great. I just wish they would have put the nutritional information in here.  That was a huge disappointment when I opened this book.  Not all recipes in this book are low calorie, in fact, many of them are made with butter and high calorie ingredients.

I also don't like that there aren't photos of the finished product.  They wouldn't have to be color photos, even a black and white can show a person what the meal is going to look like.

If the above things don't bug you, then get this book!  Get it anyway, the recipes look great, as long as you don't mind not knowing how many calories are in them.
Books.summary: Great recipes!  Just wish the nutritional information would have been included.

Books.reviewText:
I think that this book is good and that is why I ordered it.
  It tells the continuing saga of what is happening to the malories and their close friends.  It was an excellant read. I would recommend it to anyone who is wanting to update their knowledge of the Malory's.
  Johanna Lindsey is a great writer, her stories always have adventure, action and humor in them.  As you read the story you are joining in the story, instead of just reading along. The characters are very well developed and you find yourself drawn into their lives.
  I have always liked pirates and your get to revisit others characters from other books.  James Malory is one of my favorite characters and he pops up in this book to my delight. I know that I throughly enjoyed this book and would recommend it to others.

For starters: I've never read any McEwan before, and generally do not care for modern writers, but I was absolutely floored by his prose.  The writing is amazing.

His portrayal of naive, pre-teen Briony is dead-on and eerie, and, even though she is far less developed, I could identify some with Cecelia's feelings of being a bit lost and out-of-place at home after the relative independence of college.

I've read a lot of reviews that are impatient with the slow pace, especially of the first part of the novel.  While I agree that it is a novel that immerses the reader fully in descriptions, I think such criticism is a little unfair.  It is not a novel that should be read in anticipation of getting to a juicy ending; it's a novel that should be read with the mindset that getting there is half (most of) the enjoyment.

While I didn't especially *like*, or closely identify with, any of the characters, I thought they were reasonable (I don't like most real, live, people that much, either).  I didn't think Briony was horrible so much as she was ignorant, confused, and self-centered, as are most 13-year-olds; I include myself in that, as embarrassing as it is to remember it.  I thought she was an excellent characterization of an adolescent at an awkward place in life, with an incomplete view and as-yet poor understanding of the world.

The ending was complicated.  No, I don't think anything she did later could actually atone for the mess Briony made.  On the other hand, she was 13 and acting out of ignorance more than viciousness.  And, frankly, I thought the title referred more at her attempt to atone to herself, to lay her conscience to rest, than to actually achieving any sort of atonement in the eyes of the rest of the world.  I think it should not be taken too literally.

There is a lot to like in this book. Douglas Harris does a nice job of describing all of the statisitical cautions associated with using student achievement data for the purposes of evaluating schools and teachers. Great information in and of itself. However, professor Harris' analysis is incomplete. Though he rightfully argues for "advanced value-added" methods of accountability which adjust achievement scores for uncontrollable variables, he neglects the one uncontrollable variable that produces the most variation in student achievement - cognitive ability. For large groups of students of about the same age, say all fifth graders in a state, more than half of the variation observed in achievement test scores is due to differences in cognitive ability. While other variables, such as quality of classroom instruction and home support play important roles in achievement variation, fair comparisons among schools and teachers require that differences in cognitive ability be accounted for and systematically factored out of value-added calculations.

To date, none of the value-added accountbility schemes employed in the United States, including all of the examples described by Professor Harris in his book, have applied controls for cognitive ability thus rendering all of them problematic for high stakes decision-making - such as school sanctions or teacher tenure, compensation, or continued employment decisions.

Value-added measures of schools and teachers are potentially very valuble accountability tools. But basic designs must capture and control all of the most relevent factors affecting student achievement. This book does a good job of informing the design of robust value-added measures. With specific guidance related to controlling for cognitive ability, it could be great.

Offering a kids-eye-view of Grandma and Grandpa's house, "The Hello, Goodbye Window" celebrates the pleasure in simple things, from using a step stool to reach the kitchen sink to getting squirted with the hose. The story is told from the point of view of a little girl, although I would say the child's gender is really interdeterminate, so don't let that stop you from reading this one to those who want "boy" books. With all the precision and detail of a four-year-old, the narrator points out every step in her day, including her nap during which "nothing happens until I get up." The colors and drawing style are hyper and loose, so lively it's almost leaping off the page. If your initial reaction is to reject the artwork for it's very loose style, take another couple of looks as it really grows on you; I did not appreciate (okay, I didn't like *at all*) the illustration until about the 3rd run through. A fun, friendly, full-of-love story that would be good for one-on-one reading with the kindergarten set.  2006 Caldecott Award Winner.

Lauren Willig is all about mixing the genres on mystery, historical fiction and romance. I actually read the second book (The Masque of the Black Tulip) first and only liked it so-so. However, this first one is much better. The author makes the mixing of genres work in this book, where she didn't in the other. The romance wasn't too ridiculous, the characters fun and likable, the historical context appropriate (though ONLY the context is non-fiction, the story is entirely made up) and the mystery remain an undercurrent in the book without the other pieces taking over. Willig remembers each piece of book (romance, mystery and history) and balances them well.
Books.summary: Good Balance of Romance, Mystery and History

Books.reviewText: It took a while for me to get into this book, but once I did I thoroughly enjoyed it. The beginning of the book starts off with the death of Ellery's grandfather. There are events here that are not addressed again throughout the book. I assume they will come up in later books. Ellery comes across as very intelligent and unsure of herself or where she belongs. In many ways as the story unfolds she discovers who she is. I like that part of her discovery includes the ability to address an unresolved relationship from her past and see it more objectively. Good story, I'm completely a fan of Ash and want to see them together.

I really enjoyed reading this book.  The characters were well developed and LIKABLE! I could relate to the thoughts and feelings portrayed and it wasn't over the top... That being said, I have to agree with the reviewers who complained about the editing... lots of typos and such.  The other thing I had issues with, and I'm not a prude, were some of the piercings... I regret to say I googled two of the terms in the book - OMG - I'll never get THOSE images out of my head! LOL!  The end result? I'll be reading future books from this author - she has the potential to be AMAZING!

So I just finished this novel last night by an author I've never heard of before and the experience has left me with more questions then answers. That's the only reason this novel falls short. Let me explain:

 Chris Neilson is a successful writer and father of three married to his wife Ann for over 20 years. One fateful night, Chris gets into a fatal car crash and finds himself dead in a purgatory-like state. When he finally accepts the fact that he is dead, he is transported to Summerland, (a fanciful way of saying "heaven") where he meets a long dead friend named Albert who teaches him lessons about his life and his purpose.
