Chris is deadlocked with indecision and dread however because he loves and misses his wife and can't bare eternity without her. To make a long story short, he finds out she killed herself because of her grief and is now residing in hell for an ungodly (no pun intended) length of time. Chris leaves the comforts of Summerland and travels with Albert into hell where he braves demons, mental torture, and physical pain all in the name of love.  I won't go on further as I believe it will spoil the rest of the story, but suffice it to say the author goes on and on about death, indefinite immortality, reincarnation, good and evil, e.t.c. And what makes me give this only four stars is the way all this information contradicts each other multiple times throughout the story. I won't go into exactly where it can be found since it, again, will spoil the story, but the instances are there, and yeah- a lot of unanswered questions there. I guess if you're not as analytical a person as me, you won't even care and will consider this a well-written, carefully-reserached novel offering both adventure and philosophy.
Books.summary: Good heavens, what a good story

Books.reviewText: One of the best parts of this book is that the author gives you some tips on baking bread, making certain homemade medicines, and talks a lot about the meals she prepares with her emergency reserves.  I thought some of the plot line was believable and clever.  The only thing that I did not like about the book is that the lead female character was the masculine one in her romantic relationship in the book.  I think the author wanted to portray a strong female - but I just found the character to be a bit too dominant with her man.  All and all though, I thought it was a good read.  Light on violence, and long on prepping psychology and tips to the readers.
Books.summary: One of the best parts of this book is that the author gives ...

Books.reviewText:
The Mote in Gods Eye is a good old space opera, written decades ago, but which easily translates to sci-fi readers today. It is a good first contact novel, with a space opera setting, an untested captain too young for his post, a human empire spanning most of known space complete with aristocracy. The details of the first contact are what really drive the book. The cultural nuances humans and the aliens must come to terms with. This is what makes good sci-fi, the human element, not other details like the science and future science.

Modern readers often comment that comparisons between this book and a certain famous scifi television series are annoying or too perceptible. I on the other hand don't mind the comparisons since these authors actually wrote some of the episodes and later movies. I actually kind of like the parallels. I loved that show, and this book has the same tone. Not surprising that I love this book too.

Some books I tear through. And some just lag. For me, this book was engaging and entertaining enough that I was not quite tearing through it, but, had problems putting it down.

While I was reading Othello with my tubby custard in one hand and the book held at a 90 degree angel in the other I thought, I'm reading a play and eating a custard from and outlawed children's show how bizare. However, life is filled with such suprises. Kind of like the suprises in the Bard's play Othello.  Othello is a man who should have had it all.  He had friends, a loving wife, and an army at his command.  The play follows Othello through a conspiracy of his villanous friend, Iago, not the parrot from Aladin, but Shakespeare's greatest villan.  Iago was disgrunteled by the fact that he was passed up on a raise and there fore plots everyone's downfall. Making this a great read for the guy at the bottom of totum pole who is doing fries and wants to move up to salads. Iago in the openion of this reader is the true comic genius.  He plays Othello and others like they have the mental capacity of tree stumps.  He convinces Othello that Desdemona, his wife, is having an afair. Iago narrates most of the play and you here a lot of what he is thinking and planing to do.  Which brings me to jello nobody cares what Bill Cosby is thinking or that he is still trying to salvage a carrier. This play is by far one of the best of Shakespeares in terms of great characters, surprises, and monologes. The readers are beautifully captivated by the play with the genius use of dramatic irony.  Nobody knows what will happen and at anytime a surprise is waiting to happen.
Books.summary: Othello is O good read O! Makes me think of Jell-o! Really.

Books.reviewText:
3.5 stars

This book took me so long to get into, and quite frankly, Im not sure why I stuck with it. But I am really glad I did, as I ended up enjoying it. I adored Vaughn and his easygoing, and at times, boyish nature. He was so honest and kind, just the sort of guy youd want in your circle of friends. I love that he was so willing to just go with the flow. He wasn't one to question why life was the way it was. It just was, and he was going with it. Jonah, on the other hand, was Vaughns complete opposite. I felt like he went with the flow, but it was a deliberate choice instead of being part of his nature. Jonah spent his life trying to appear normal, but I get the feeling that he was really looking for lovein all the wrong places, as they say. This book gives a new meaning to slow build, and Im sure that was intentional and directly related to Vaughns indifference (or possibly aversion) to sex.

Now, I loved the friendship portion of this story. I like that Jonah found Vaughn intriguing enough that he was willing to stop bringing sex into their relationship and try to be buddies. But the part where they actually do decide to delve into relationship territory and make the choices that would work best for them was a bit dicey for me. I didn't understand the haste behind their decisions, and why there weren't different things they could try. But Im going to be honest  after this book, I don't think I have a grasp on what asexuality is at all, and while I don't understand their choices, I don't think the credibility of them depends on me getting it. So while Im not totally sold on the way things ended up, I did appreciate this story.

The mystery behind the missing paintings was predictable, but that was fine with me, because that was just the catalyst for what brought Jonah and Vaughn together. I don't think it was really meant to be suspenseful or a whodunnit. I think the pacing of this one was OK; if it had been a bit tighter, maybe the story would have gripped me from the beginning. The highlight of this book for me was the drunk scene. It was quite possibly the best drunk scene I have ever read, and it left me in stitches. Just when I thought Vaughn couldn't get any more adorable, he goes and turns into the giddiest drunk ever and proved me wrong!

When Blank Spaces finally pulled me in, it pulled me all the way in, and I ended up loving this story. If you're a fan of quirky characters and hard won relationships, this book is right up your alley.

ARC from Netgalley.

This review was originally posted on Books & Beauty Are My Bag.

I was excited to receive Buried Secrets, the first in the Men of Valor series, by Irene Hannon. I loved the cover and the title begged me to stop everything and read the book.

The prologue begins with a bang. It was meant to be a joyride. No one was supposed to die. As soon as I read these words, I knew I was in for a great read.

Years after the event described in the prologue, police chief Lisa Grant and detective and former Navy-Seal Mac McGregor join forces to investigate the discovery of a buried skeleton in an unmarked grave. The plot is well thought out, and the story is well told. As a result of the prologue, it is pretty obvious who the culprits are, and it's only a matter of the detectives solving their case.

I admit to being a bit disappointed with this book. The suspense was there, the story gripping, but I found the romance angle overplayed. Instead of being a thriller with a touch of romance, I felt it was more a romance story with a touch of suspense.

It is great to have strong Christians as characters, but the attraction between the two main character was too "in your face" for my liking. Despite a promising "bad start" when they first meet, they almost immediately find the other to be irresistable. I would have preferred this to be less obvious, especially in the beginning, and their relationship to have faced more of a challenge.

Despite these short-comings (which are my own opinion) the book is a good read and I would recommend it to others who enjoy Christian romance in a suspenseful setting. I've given it four stars.

** I received a free advanced digital copy of this novel from the publisher through the "Revell Reads" program in exchange for my unbiased opinion. Thank you to them and to Net-Galley for making it available.

4.5 STARS!

Stuart and Mariska. I love that the author decided to give us readers a glimpse into their ever after. Now engaged, Stuart and Mariska are now looking forward to the rest of their lives. Stuart wants nothing more than to make a home with Mariska, but he faces some choices when it comes to his uncles ranch. His home is with Mariska and he knows it. But what if home is also at the ranch? Can he live his dream while making Mariska happy? We witness his internal struggle as he tries to balance both. When an unfortunate event occurs, Stuart is left in despair and full of guilt. He spirals down and old habits come to the surface. Can Stuart and Mariska survive this?

I don't want to give too much away, but my heart hurt so much for these two. The situation they are left to deal with is such a sensitive, relevant, and important issue. I think the author gracefully deals with everything that Stuart and Mariska go through. It was dealt with in such a realistic manner. Whether you have been in their situation or not, you WILL feel for them. Understand their pain and grief. Why they react the way they did. But one thing that never faltered was their love. Their love remained constant.
Unwavering. Stuart and Mariska truly demonstrate such growth in their relationship and as individuals. No matter what happens, they always believe in their love.

I found myself lost in this story from beginning to the end. Oh Stuart, my sexy cowboy how I've missed you so! Stuart is his usual alpha self, always ready to protect his love, Mariska. He loves so deeply. Fiercely. It felt in not only his words, but how he looks at her as if she is his whole life.

One To Take adds another amazing layer to this series. I am once again reminded on why each couple is such a vital part to this entire series. And these two are no different. Stuart and Mariska found each other through darkness and despair. And once again, darkness threatens them. But their love? Even in the face of tragedy, their love shines. No matter what shakes them to their core, their love is always felt. Their love is powerful. Their love overcomes. Their story isn't an easy one, but its theirs. While this can be read as a standalone, I highly recommend the entire series as it remains as one of my favorites. The author is a brilliant storyteller in that with each addition to the series, the characters easily embed themselves into your heart. Its like a family that you never want to part with.
Books.summary: Loved every moment with these two!

Books.reviewText: Four gentle Amish reads to lighten up any day. A Legacy of Love by Amy Clipston Leon let Susie go several years when he could not make the promise to marry her on day. Now Susie is engaged and has asked Leon to restore her grandparents' rocking chairs for her new home. Can rocking chairs by the tie that binds? The Cedar Chest by Beth Wiseman Catherine is struggling in her marriage and has turned to her mother for comfort but does not reveal what is happening. Catherine finds her great grandmother's chest in her parents basement and convinces her mom, Emma, to open it. They discover family love letters. Will the letters bring Catherine and Emma closer so Catherine can share her fears with her mom? The Treasured Book by Kathleen Fuller Shane met Lucy when he was restoring his house in Iowa and ever since then Shane has wanted to join the Amish faith to further his relationship with God. He is staying with his Amish friend in Ohio to learn more about the faith when he runs into Lucy. Lucy is taking care of a family member who has become ill. Lucy joins Shane on a trip to a local antique market where Shane buys a Bible. Will the contents within strengthen their bond? The Midwifes Dream by Kelly Irvin The district's midwife, Iris, wants a family of her own but has yet to find the love she is seeking. Mahon brings two English teenagers to her house when they stopped at his family farm asking for help as the girl was in labor. During the night Iris realizes Mahon is not just her best friend's brother. Could he be the love she has been praying for all along? I received a complimentary copy of this book from Zondervan through NetGalley. Opinions expressed in this review are completely my own.
Books.summary: Four gentle Amish reads to lighten up any day

Books.reviewText: I used this book to pray throughout my pregnancy and let me tell you it was a true blessing. The prayers cover every situation that is relevant in pregnancy for instance there are prayers for the health of mother and baby, appropriate bible readings and space for you to record your own thoughts. This is good as it would reveal to your child all your prayers, hopes and dreams for him or her. I would have given it five stars except that it could be packaged better and it needs a lot of editing as there are many typos including grammatical errors etc. I would urge the author and publishers to correct the mistakes and to make the book more attractive. I would then urge expectant mothers who want to pray throughout their pregnancy to buy it as despite its packaging and errors it is worth it.

I found this "book" listed under audiobooks, and ordered it for a disabled friend who cannot read specifically because it was an audiobook. There is nothing in the description to dispel the idea that this is an audiobook, and no reviews to tip me off. What I received was an unmarked Staples brand CD in a torn sleeve, sealed with a sticker stating "This CD contains a PDF file." Yes, a PDF file, and it further states "This CD is nonreturnable," which pretty much violates the Amazon policy of universal returnability. Amazon, take note! Buyers beware! This is just the kind of scam you might learn working for 30 years in the prison system.
Books.summary: Stop! This is NOT an audiobook!

Books.reviewText:
Tempted by the cover and the promise of a hot read I picked up No Surrender...Only to be bitterly disappointed.
This is not a book I can or want to recommend to any reader of quality romance novels.
Some might buy this for its many sex scenes, but please DON'T! They are not hot. They are violent, cruel and humiliating. They are unpleasant and not exiting!
The rest of the book is not much better. The main characters were forced to have sex with each other. The sex turned out to be so good that they fell in love and didn't forget it for the years they were separated. Okay, it's a romance novel. But why does the heroine need to be so stupid? When her hero returns she doesn't welcome him with open arms, but hides their child from him and tells him lies after lies. Too many misunderstanding and constant anger and mistrust force them then into scenes of sex, sex, sex. Unbelievable.
Nope, I really didn't like this book. What a shame as I wanted it to be entertaining and sexy.

How very sad. I've been an admirer of Kate's work since I discovered it in about 1985, and I was hoping this book would offer some fresh insights to her life, work, thoughts, and creative methods. Instead, I found a grotty little mishmash. "Waiting for Kate Bush"  doesn't know what it wants to be -- music bio or fan fiction? It veers annoyingly between the two instead, doing neither very well, leaving me very irritated that I spent so much to get this, and all the way from the UK to boot (before it was available in the US). I found the brief overview of Kate's career the more interesting part, but this seems to be mainly a by-the-numbers clip job that anyone could have put together from UK press archives, previous Bush bios, videos of TV shows, or fan magazines. I learned very little I didn't already know about Kate -- a real shame, since the author is in a position to give us so much more, or so I would have thought. This reporting is delivered in the patented snarky snarl that  exemplifies the worst sort of music journalism practiced the UK: breezy, opinionated, terminally cynical, openly contemptuous at whim, and insufferably self-absorbed. As for the framing "story", which really is the dominant part of the book, I couldn't even get through it all. I found it more or less loathsome and unpleasant, full of repellent characters and oppressive surroundings and situations.  No wonder Kate prefers to stay apart from all of this and all these "fans"! This book made made me feel depressed and unclean -- I suppose it may hold a certain fascination for some disturbed souls, and I guess I'll keep it on my shelves as another curio/collectible, but I truly disliked it and wouldn't recommend it to anyone but those who enjoy wallowing in sordid and unappetizing realities.
Books.summary: Dreadful; neither fish nor fowl, but foul enough

Books.reviewText:
For the life of me, I will never understand why Americans who try their hand at "Troubles fiction" don't have their scripts proofread by someone who's actually from Ireland.  These books are always full of authenticity-shredding mistakes and this one is no exception!  In fact, just about every category of mistake can be found here, for example:

HISTORICAL/CHRONOLOGICAL ERRORS: One character's parents are killed in a car bomb years before car bombs came into use.  Another's parents both die in a prison riot - at a male-only prison.  Children are made into "Troubles orphans" well before the "Troubles" even began.

TERMINOLOGY: IRA members use terms ("Londonderry", "Northern Ireland") which no Irish republican would EVER use.  Irish and English characters use American terms ("brogue", "subway", "blocks") which Irish and English people do not actually use, at least not in these ways.  "Sinn Fein" is twice misspelled as "Sein Fein" and on one occasion preceded by a completely inappropriate "the".

NAMES: Several of the characters have names which sound like an American's idea of an Irish name (Erin, Meaghan, McGlaughlin)

REDUCTION OF CONFLICT TO NARROW SECTARIANISM: IRA members set off bombs in the shape of a cross, never refer to their opposite paramilitaries as "loyalists" or "unionists" but only as "the Prods"

"OIRISH" SPEECH: When the characters aren't talking like Americans, they're talking the way that Americans think Irish people talk ("Be you Provo?")

AND OF COURSE: a woman at the centre of the story with red hair and brilliant green eyes (actually very uncommon in Ireland, but Americans can't seem to write an "Irish" book without this woman!).

I could go on, but in truth, the book doesn't seem to have been proofread by anyone. It's full of clumsy sentences, misused words, typos, sometimes hilarious misspellings ("Rory was a lost sole") - it's just bad writing, apart from its other shortcomings.

The story itself is not gripping, and is so thoroughly unbelievable I just found it impossible to get interested in.  If I had known nothing about the conflict in Ireland I still do not think I would have enjoyed this book, but as someone who reads a lot on the subject I can honestly say that this ranks down there with the WORST Irish-themed books I have ever read.
Books.summary: Awful - Don't read if you're Irish or want to understand the Troubles

Books.reviewText:
First let me say: I detest survival novels where the characters just "magically" happen to have every single thing they're ever going to need to survive the breakdown of society/technology. There's little to no drama, bravery or gallantry involved if you just happen to have enough preserved food, gallons of gasoline, medicines and all the warm clothing/boots/gloves and camping gear you'll need to get you through.

The beginning of this book reads like an inventory. The man and his family have just been through a [literally] earth-shattering experience and he's taking inventory. And smug. This character is so very, very smug in his absolute certainty that his Christian values and hard work have led him to purchase all the things that he and his family will need to survive. Within a couple chapters I didn't like him. After five or six, I actively detested him.

The main character, Rick Drummond, is overbearing, obnoxious and condescending. The wife is a cipher. The daughter is there only for Rick to have his "heh heh, teen girls are so self-centered" moments and apparently his son is only there so Rick can demonstrate "manly men doing manly things"...oh, and the son is apparently there to tote and carry on order. Rick Drummond makes a point of telling us that only a fool lives "paycheck to paycheck" when he magnanimously goes over to help his neighbors, a young couple with small children...despite the fact that most young couples live "paycheck to paycheck" when they're starting out. The author never explains how this family -- who appear to be an average middle class family -- has managed to accumulate several hundred grand worth of tools, equipment, food, gasoline, vehicles for every purpose, camping gear and trailers, etc.

This is pure male fantasy -- he saves the day over and over because of his ultra-preparedness and his planning...this reads like a survivalist's manual in parts. I quit about halfway into the book. Save your brain cells and don't start. I'd have given it 0 stars if Amazon would let me.

I must admit I enjoyed reading Brain Rules, but the book has at least two serious problems. First, Dr. Medina claims that he is a stickler for insisting all his "rules" are backed by solid research. However, at least one chapter about the 10 minute attention span, is based on almost no research whatsoever. Quite simply, there appears to be no empirical published data that supports this rule. It's almost as if Dr. Medina made it up. So then I wonder, how much rigor has been put into the remaining chapters. The other issue I have is that the teaching advice given at the end of each chapter is very superficial. It is clear that Dr. Medina has never taught in a K-12 environment. I think the premise of the book is excellent - combining neuroscience and education. Perhaps in edition number 2, Dr. Medina could team up with an experienced educator. Bottom line: it is critical to make sure the facts are accurate and making statements like "we know our attention span is 10 minutes" is misleading and almost unethical, simply because Dr. Medina presents himself as an authority.

I purchased this book as a text for a Java class.  It is one of the all-time worst textbooks I have ever read.  I stopped using this book half-way through the course as I found it made simple concepts grossly complicated.  I used two other texts to clear the cobwebs: Holzner's Java Black Book combined with the exceptional OO book Java Objects by Barker. There are many problems with the book.  The typeface makes the book visually unreadable: the authors insist on bolding all keywords, datatypes, methods, classnames, and code examples such that half the text on each page is bold.  At least for the first half of the book, almost all of the coding takes place in the class constructors and main (with absolutely no discussion of why this is good programming practice).  There is no sense of creating any type of OO programming hierarchy.  Each chapter has redundant confusing explanations that don't reinforce the topic at hand.  The chapters appear to have been written like a bill passing through Congress; everyone insists on adding their two cents worth, and at the end some completely unrelated topic is tacked on with no explanation of how this relates to the primary intent of the chapter.  The sphagetti-code nature of the text makes it difficult to understand what exactly is going on and makes the book useless as a reference. Save your receipt and don't write your name in this one - you'll want a full refund.

I received Red Sox Century expecting a comprehensive, fair look at the tumultuous history of my favorite team.  Instead, I received a book written by New Yorkers, ostensibly for New Yorkers.  The chapter on Harry Frazee and the sale of Ruth manages to fail in a completely unique way: by somehow ignoring Frazee's destruction of the Red Sox.

The writers continually gloss over the ramifications of the deals, failing to explain how poorly they turned out for his own team.  In an objective book, I'd imagine the trade of one of the best hitting catchers in baseball and  a 20 year old future hall of famer for 4 journeyman would merit a mention.  Not so here.

Any baseball book that passes off honest criticism as anti-semitism is not worth getting.  Save your money.

I chose First Cut because it was a Literary Guild Selection.  It turned out to be a disappointing choice for me.  The author is obviously knowledgable about hospitals and medical terminology, but it was overdone  and overwritten.  The pace was frantic and I doubt any human could  realistically continue to function as our protagonist, Ev, did in thise  book.  She is a resident who is a combination flawless physician, marvelous  teacher, excellent detective, and sexually appealing to all men in this  book.  That is just too much woman for me.  I began skimming about l/3 way  through this tome and was relieved to finish.  The lengthly explanation by  our heroine of how, why and by whom the crimes were committed was just more  (pun intended) overkill.
Books.summary: Killer on Loose in NY Hospital

Books.reviewText:
This book was so bad I got rid of it the next day.  I was able to get through the first 75 pages but then the book lost me, totally lost me, when court transcripts were used instead of "real" writing.  These court documents were all in capitals, making reading so hard, As someone who's been a lifelong reader and a computer user, using ALLCAPS is like screaming. It's also incredibly hard to follow. The book showed the Q & A from the witnesses court statements.  This made for really jerky writing, making the reader so lost so quickly.  Trying to follow the train of thought just continuously showed that the train crashed pages ago.  About 5-10 pages into this impossible to read, literally, that I no longer had empathy from the writer.

I am from Utah and have lived in South west Salt Lake Valley where many polygamists lived. In fact I live around the corner from the employment where the author worked. I used to work next to the Allread (AUB) temple, had former polygamists as part of my daily life whether at work or my outside family activities. Being around and seeing polygamists were a part of my everything life here in Utah.  I'm not Latter Day Saints (LDS) but as a non-LDS in a highly concentrated LDS town, I know what it's like to be an outsider as I watched the "normal" LDS mothers stare scornfully at the two polygamist mothers (non-FLDS and non-AUB) mothers who were at our school as part of a family supporting our kids in their school activities. The local LDS culture is to ignore the polygamists  (if you don't see it, it doesn't exist) but to not tolerate in any way.

The book started out trying to lay things out from a LDS point of view with the Doctrine and Covenants 132 (D&C) section that was created supporting polygamy or celestial marriage as they call it.  I had to skip that part of the book just to get the background story.  The Book of Mormon (BOM) is a dry read any way  Back to this book after trying to read more, the court case seems to be focused on the legal right of who owned the land in West Jordan and who had life residency on them. The court case tried to show the "slave-like" conditions the author had under her polygamist husband but failed miserably.  By this time, I had well given up on the book and with some 30 pages left, I closed the book and said, "that's it."

If you are interested in a well written book about life in the FLDS, I refer you to read "Under the Banner of Heaven" by Jon Krakauer, then Carol Jessop book, "Escape." These both will give you a good idea of what life was and is like for polygamy families living in groups splintered off from the main LDS religion.
Books.summary: Seeking insight into Morman polygamy? Look elsewhere

Books.reviewText: Let me give you a taste for what you are in for if you decide to believe the hype and buy this book. "If you must take risks these days, better the preacher than the whore; eschew Monsieur Breakbone, known in Florence as the Neapolitan Fever, and in Naples, no doubt, as Florence Rot."...um, What?!  I reread this sentence three times, thought about googling all of these phrases to get a glimmer of understanding and then decided I didn't care.  I had not read an engaging word since chapter one.  Then I came to amazon to see if I was the only person in the world who thinks this book is unreadable.  As it turns out I should have listened to my fellow readers and not the aliens that give out book awards. Why oh why did I buy this book in hardback no less?!
Books.summary: The emperor isn't wearing any clothes

Books.reviewText: I saw an ad for this book in a magazine and I thought that it sounded great, I love dark and disturbing stories so I thought a collection of these would be right down my alley. Boy, was I wrong! This book is horrible! I barely made it half way through it. I had to read the first story twice before I figured out the writing style. It switches between characters' thoughts so often without punctuation or any other indication that I couldn't follow the stories. Each story, even after you figure out the writer, is worst than the last. I wish I could get a refund. This a waste of time and money.
Books.summary: Why did i waste my money on this?

Books.reviewText: The writer has completely destroyed all of the work put into the development of Ms Marvel by creating a new character. The comic is written for children and not the majority of fans it has accrued over the years. This is NOT an interesting series anymore, it is boring and has clearly become a social drama rather than an action based story. The artwork is grotesque with no effort put into any semblance of accuracy. I have zero tolerance for religious bias and zero tolerance for religious promotion. This is obviously an effort to promote the Muslim faith rather than continue the character development of a persona that was very specific to Ms Marvel. I have no desire to read a comic that is based on any religion or one that has such a horrendous writer and artist.

Let's start this one off with a quiz for married women: Think back to the last time you corrected or criticized your husband. Why did you do this? A. He was wrong B. I'm smarter than him so I always tell him how to do things C. Both or D. Other

Laura Doyle writes this book from the fatally flawed position that, because as a "strong and controlling feminist woman" she would have been likely to answer "B", that means that all the rest of us would too. She seems to think that because her husband was finally able to catch HIS breath when she quit her nagging, that simply means you can apply a blanket salve that will solve all marital problems with one simple action: shut the hell up, and stay shut the hell up. In one rather extreme example, Doyle advises us:

"Respect means when he takes the wrong freeway exit you don't correct him by telling him where to turn. It means that if he keeps going in the wrong direction you will go past the state line and still not correct what he is doing. In fact, no matter what your husband does, you will not try to teach, improve, or correct him."

Imagine applying this to your household finances or parenting. What if a man is spending all of a family's money before the bills can be paid? What if your husband says it's okay for your teenage daughter to have sex with her boyfriend, and you deeply believe that she isn't ready? A family outing ruined by getting lost is a pain, but it's the least of the problems you're going to have to worry about if you take a consistent policy of never pointing out when your husband is about to make a really big mistake. She also leaves out the part about the ugly fight that will result when the husband realizes that his passive-aggressive, Laura-Doyle-game-playing wife has allowed him to drive 200 miles past their putative destination because she "respects" him too much to tell him, "It's this exit right here."

This is just one example of how this book is a self-contradicting mess - Doyle chides women for treating their husbands "like another one of your children" but apparently doesn't consider allowing someone to go on being disastrously wrong about something because the truth would hurt their pride too much to be treating them like a child. How is allowing a man his illusions and clamming the hell up when he's about to screw up royally "respecting" that man by any definition? Doyle seems to have confused respect with fear.

Put yourself in the husband's shoes while reading this book. You'll probably be insulted by Doyle's insistence on making a blanket characterization of all men as so at the mercy of their tender egos, so fragile in their self-esteem, that they need a wife to handle them with constant emotional kid gloves and never provide them with any kind of advice or counsel!

Laura Doyle seems to think marriage as an institution can never be a union of two equals; one spouse has to be the parent and the other has to willingly assume the role of a child. Since she's already established that it's bad for the husband's psyche to be that child...guess what option that leaves you, the wife, with?

I might be a little prejudiced here; Helen Smith's book that essentially says the same crap as this one does was still leaving a bad taste in my mouth when I read this, and quite frankly I nearly destroyed my own marriage and health by acting as Doyle advises us is the correct way in this book. Speaking up when your husband is wrong is not disrespect. It's part of loving someone to foster, nurture, and teach them. Not all of us are inclined to be screeching harpies like Laura Doyle apparently was; advice, counsel and correction can all be conveyed without disrespect.

If you really love someone and want to spend the rest of your life with them, following the advice in this book will indeed transform you. It will transform you into someone who will likely at some point grow to hate your spouse and quietly start crossing your fingers that they die first so you can have some peace.
Books.summary: You Have GOT To Be F'n Kidding, Lady

Books.reviewText: I will be totally honest and say that I did not purchase For the Love Of  Money but opted to instead borrow it from the library. I am certainly glad  that I did. I could not get past the first two chapters. It is hard to put  into words exactly why this book did not interest me suffice to say that it  just did not. Omar, I think very highly of you as a person since I have had  the opportunity to speak with you on several different occasions, however,  all of your books of late have not been anything worthwhile reading perhaps  with the exception of Single Mom. Maybe instead of writing so many books so  quickly take your time and develop your story line and characters more  completely. Also, enlist the assistance of some readers perhaps from  bookclubs like mine, BusaraNayo, to get a feel for how the story will be  received by the public. I hope you take all of this criticism in stride and  in turn do some introspection and resign yourself to publishing more  intriguing novels in the future and hopefully in the process win back a  legion of readers that you seem to have lost.

To be honest, I am shocked at all the positive reviews.

While the author doesn't have amateur grammatical errors typically found in self published works, his story is pretty much on par with others. There is a lack of depth that engages the reader and has them wanting to read more. Instead, the unrealistic dialogue prevents the reader from truly enjoying the story.

Another problem I had is you are supposed to overlook some serious plot holes in the tale and each turn in the story was painfully predictable. Nothing original is brought to the table. This makes for a tiresome read.

Thankfully, it was only a .99 tale. Although, it is money that wasn't well spent. Pass this one and stick to the professionals.  I'll be skipping the sequel.

WARNING:  The paperback edition is not the same as the hardback edition.  They really shouldn't be listed together.  The paperback edition has a big sign on the back of the book stating, "This is a special version of a textbook widely used by universities throughout the world.  Pearson published this edition for the benefit of students outside the United States and Canada.  If you purchased this book within the United States or Canada it has been imported without the approval or permission of the Publisher, and it does not include all of the same Problems."  The Amazon product description did not disclose these important differences, and none of the third-party sellers seem to disclose this difference.  As a result, I purchased the book, and it turned out my son couldn't use it for his class because, according to his Physics teacher, eight of the problem sets are different.  Argh.
Books.summary: WARNING:  The paperback edition is different from the hardback edition (the problem sets are different)!

Books.reviewText:
You know what the REALLY disturbing thing is?  Look one layer deeper.  Past the mice and littlepeople, past the maze and the cheese stations.  I don't think anybody's called this little nugget out yet: you know what I see?

WE are the cheese.  Your leadership thinks so, if this book has landed in your possession.  Imagine all those middle managers as factory workers, and all the rank-and-file employees as little trinkets and widgets that come down the conveyor belt.  You show up like mana from heaven, they hammer you for a while and then when you are without form and void, you go away, to be replaced with fresh meat.  Tell me I'm wrong.  In the following excerpt, substitute the word "employee" for the word "cheese" and tell me how it reads to you.  For even more fun, think of substitutes for the word "change" - how about "enlightenment" or "employees figuring out your sick game".  Think conveyor belts.  Now it all takes on an entirely different, even more sinister meaning, doesn't it?  Mmm hmm.  NOW how do you feel?  Bitter little pill, ain't it?  All jagged and spiky going down.  Better update that resume, champion.  Meat grinder indeed.

  Change Happens
  They Keep Moving The Cheese

  Anticipate Change
  Get Ready For The Cheese To Move

  Monitor Change
  Smell The Cheese Often So You Know When It Is Getting Old

  Adapt To Change Quickly
  The Quicker You Let Go Of Old Cheese, The Sooner You Can Enjoy New Cheese

  Change
  Move With The Cheese

  Enjoy Change!
  Savor The Adventure And Enjoy The Taste Of New Cheese!

  They Keep Moving The Cheese.
  Be Ready To Change Quickly And Enjoy It Again

Still like the book, copper-top?  Go ahead and nibble that blue pill.  Nibble it!  Now...DOWN THE HATCH!!!  HAHAHAHA!!!!!  Num num num...
Books.summary: A Red Pill for your consideration...

Books.reviewText:
I threw away my "one book a month" Kindle lending library entry on this dismal story. Yes, I knew it was a "teen pyscho" story, and yes I gleaned from the previous reviews that it had an "unhappy" ending. Those facts did not raise my ire. I found the book hard to read because of the stilted writing style. That was the "disturbing" part of the "thriller". If you like simple, to the point sentences such as "he rode his bike", "he wondered how it felt" this may be for you. Even the premise of the story - stupid small town cops, the high school heavy, etc, shout stereotypical teen angst writing. If you want a peek into a true "disturbing psychological thriller" involving a teen pyscho, try We Need To Talk About Kevin. That one is beautifully written, and will keep your attention to the end.

I want my book of the month back!
Books.summary: I want my lending library book back!

Books.reviewText:
From the synopsis: While cautioning against viewing biblical teaching as "the last word on sexual ethics," he stresses the need for accurate understanding of what the biblical "facts" are and concludes that "the Bible supplies no real basis for the condemnation of homosexuality."

A fundamental platform of what Christians believe is that the Bible IS the inerrant LAST word on ALL morality and ethics.

The description of the book attempts to claim that homosexuality "as we know it" was a concept lost on the ancient world. COME ON!!! Are you KIDDING me??? Where do you think we got it?? That same sex relationships just sprung up out of nowhere in the last 1000 years??

I'm sure this book makes a lot of people feel good about their struggle with reconciling what the Bible says with homosexuality. The only problem is you have to completely ignore what the Bible ACTUALLY says to swallow it.

Sad. Misleading. If you want to know what the Bible really says about homosexuality, just read it. It means what is says. It says what it means. Period.

I tried and tried to get into this book, only made it about 4 chapters in. I am a fan of the 19th century, I've read Dickens and loads of historical memoirs and original correspondence etc etc. so the level of detail/language was not the issue. This book was thankless and impenetrable. The characters were dull and/or irritating, and the few 'twists' I came across thus far were predictable and mediocre. I admire what the author was going for, but felt the story was needlessly complicated and bogged down in too many "clever" details with a lot of gleeful rubbing of wicked hands in shadowy corners, but by that time no one cared. I also did not like any of the characters-- the mother was vain and insipid and chose doom time and again, the wicked were moustache-twirling and greedy, the poor were country yet noble etc etc. Drove me crazy.

Shame, I was looking forward to this book but after slogging through several thankless chapters, I gave up and donated it. I'd try again with something else this author has written, but not a fan of this one.

(This review refers to the third edition)  This books attempts to cover 300 years of Italian history in fewer than 400 pages (not counting a 68-page bibliographical essay at the end). This overly-ambitious work skips rather quickly through the rich history of Italy, from the Enlightenment, through the Unification, the World Wars, and beyond, devoting only 10 to 20 pages to each era; only two topics seem more worthy of the authors attention, as he spends 30 pages on both "Cavour and the Piedmontese Solution" and "Mussolini's Italy". While the Italians as a people are still ashamed of the period of Fascism, the author tries to put a positive spin on the ideology of the Fascist Party. By contrast, the author uses fewer than 20 pages per chapter to describe Italy's experiences in each of the World Wars.

By focusing so strongly on the political changes in Italy, the author seems to discount the many other factors that make Italy a beautiful and fascinating place, both to visit in the present and to study in its history. The people of this country have played pivotal roles in shaping Italy, its culture, and its history. The Italians are very proud of their ability to rebuild their devastated country after World War II, and yet the author's absolute focus on the political machines nearly obviates the will and determination of the Italian people.

I was hoping to learn more about Italian history from the this book, and I was disappointed. I am sorry I bought it.
Books.summary: So much history - too few pages

Books.reviewText: The author of this book is a fabulous public speaker, and is superb at making highly technical subjects accessible to lay audiences.  Unfortunately, this book is exhaustingly detailed, contains hundreds, if not thousands, of names, and has a non-well-defined structure.  Had she laid out a priori the steps required to realize a goal of manned space flight and then addressed only the seminal events along this path, the book would have had value.  Instead it reads like a telephone book, with no unifying theme.  I have two doctorate degrees in science and engineering, nevertheless the minutia of the dialog left me puzzled.  This is, quite simply, a bad book.

Friends, I have read all and re-read some of the books in this series.  Goodkind has a stack of great books.  This is not his finest hour.  I know you have read the other reviews like I have.  I tossed this book in the trash about page 400.  I really tried to like this book.  It literaly ground to a halt.  I came to the decision that no matter where the author took it, I didn't care anymore.  It is a shame because I have invested a great deal in Richard and Kahlan like many of you have.  The characters have become flat.  The plots are predictable and series stale.  Wait for the reviews before you buy the next one and skip this effort.  I can't say it any more plainly.  I will buy the next one because of Goodkind's body of work and not the last book in the series.

I read about 40 pages before giving up.  The hero is a Harley-riding Harvard Law School graduate, a tenured law professor who sports long hair, tee shirts, jeans, and boots. He rides a Harley, of course, and saves a wrongly convicted felon from a life sentence. Oh, and he has successfully argued two cases before the US Supreme Court. His Constitutional Law class is populated by students who apparently never made it through high school.  His faculty colleagues are caricatures of mindless, knee-jerk liberals, as imagined by Rush Limbaugh.  I never got far enough to determine whether there is a plot.

The intended audience for this appears to be 12-year-old Fox News fans.
Books.summary: The silliest piece of junk I have read in years

Books.reviewText: I have really enjoyed the "In Death" series 'til now. BUT this one, well...The plot was sheer science fiction and I found it somewhat entertaining -- which is what it is supposed to be but...I really disliked Eve Dallas here. I found her hard, rude, self-willed -- not a tough cop (with a heart underneath all that toughness) -- which is how I have seen her, up to now... Here she is a real a**hole, a creep, a nasty piece of work ..."a little Hitler." Couldn't quite swallow Roarke loving her in this one. All her supposed heroine-ism in this one doesn't, can't, make up or compensate for her meanness and harshness. When she is sooooo nasty to Mira I almost quit on the whole thing. But I managed to put up with her through to the end. She never redeemed herself in my estimation. The most interesting, sympathetic, admirable and truly heroic characters were the "clones."
Books.summary: Nazis + Battlestar Galactica + The Matrix = A Mess

Books.reviewText:
The Bible has been my favorite book since childhood. I find the more I read it, the more it explains itself quite well. While there is much to learn and room for growth, I am open to books about the Bible that add to understanding.

That's why I got this book. Sad to say, it didn't measure up. All the quotations and footnotes seemed to indicate a lopsided unbalanced reliance on modern professionals to tell me what to believe and how the Bible should be properly interpreted. Why should any inquiring person need Mr. Wink or Mr. Willard or Mr. McLaren or Mr. Wright to show us the correct way to understand Jesus and his message? Can't Jesus and his disciples in the new testament get their point across just fine without all the "latest research" and scholarly theories?

To me, the Bible is like a download from the mind and heart of God Himself put in language we can relate to by hand-picked writers who used their own style, personality and eyewitness factfinding to reveal heavenly truth in earthly terminology.

This has been quite sufficient for over 2000 years to get God's point across and what the kingdom-gospel is all about. Now along comes this author and others like him who claim to have more figured out than the rest of us. It's his calling to enlighten us and point us in the right direction after we got it wrong. That sort of prideful know-it-all-ism really bugs me.

The Bible has its own built-in assumptions about how it was written and intended to be understood. I have my own assumptions as does Mr. McLaren. My feeling after having read Secret Message is that his assumptions and the Bible's originally intended ones are poles apart. Because he relies so heavily on Mr. Wink and catholic theologians/missionaries as well as Buddhist philosopher Ken Wilber (per the notes in Generous Orthodoxy) and anti-conservative thinkers almost exclusively, Mr. McLaren's preconceptions and mindset he brings to the Bible skews things to his personal cultural worldview and educational background. He is the religious product of his reading outside the Bible which colors and distorts Jesus' Main Message of who he is and why he came.

Every book that claims to tell you what the Bible REALLY means is nothing but a human lens or filter. It is no better than the quality of what the lens or filter is made of and the degree of scratching, smudging, fogging, clouding, imperfections and flaws in the material and design, or pre-etched patterning that overlays between the viewer and the Bible itself. For me, anyway, I want as clear and uncorrected a view of what God wants to show me in his Book. This Secret Messaging tends to overcorrect and gives me only the writer's personal slant based on the prescription in his lenses and frames and what fits his vision deficiences. I'll use my own two eyes rather than someone who professes to see Jesus and his uncovered truth way better than the rest of us can.  -Larra
Books.summary: I Believe the Bible Doesn't Need Innovative Interpretations For a New World Order

Books.reviewText:
Got from library, which made me happy--didn't pay for it. I don't mind sex and violence but this was a good idea for a story ruined by gratuitous (mostly) sexual violence and the portrayal of unnamed characters (preciously and pretentiously called only by their ARTISTIC careers: "writer," "poet," "painter," "photographer," "filmmaker," as in, Heaven forfend we should read about ORDINARY, non-gifted, inartistic people) from America who rescue a young girl from the violence of war ONLY to save on of their own, the mega-depressed writer. It felt like an "Emperor's New Clothes" of a story: every reference was artificially heightened to shock the reader and with trite images: if there's a wild animal, it's gotta be a wolf chewing its leg off from a trap. I wasn't shocked, just depressed: sex? A privileged woman watching two other women paid have violent sex ("fisting") for her enjoyment. A painter painting with his own semen (scarcely a novel concept) and blood. It disintegrated into a platform for the author's political and social beliefs from time-to-time but without the slightest attempt at artistry in writing or weaving into the story line. If I want that, I can read the comment section of any article about upcoming elections. The writer didn't even do her research: having a young girl have a mediastinal parathyroid cyst in the brain. The mediastinum is the central area of the chest where the heart, trachea and great vessels lie. The parathyroids are in the neck on the thyroid. I can't abide laziness.

(BTW: if you think I didn't get that it can be a long metaphor for the narcissism of the "creative," you're wrong.)

I had hoped this would be an in-depth exploration of
the inner workings and motivations of Presidents Truman
and "Ike" -what I discovered was a poorly researched, boring
book.  It's almost as if Mr. Neal assumed putting both
names on the book's cover would make it a seller.  Buyer
beware.  You can find more in-depth material on these
men and their times right here on the internet.  Also,
it turns out, Mr. Neal received monies from a Truman
Foundation, which is a poor ethical choice on his part, in
presenting a history that the reader assumes is unbiased.
If you like to see pictures of "Harry & Ike" -many which
have been printed elsewhere, you may enjoy "Harry & Ike"
the book.  Quite a letdown as to what I expected.
Books.summary: Very light reading about two powerful men.

Books.reviewText: I usually love this genre, but I couldn't even Finish this book!  I only got through a few chapters and although the gore factor high, the book had no intensity, no flair.  I understand that it was written as a journal from the sick and demented mind of the main character, Edgar.  I guess Edgar is supposed to be stupid and barely literate as well... he couldn't even write a sentence (or was that just the author?... Hmmmm...)  It was as if the author, in a desperate attempt to call himself a REAL writer, just put together the grossest bunch of crap he could think of.  I kinda feel sorry for him, because this was his first book, and I can't imagine how he'll ever be published again after this bunch of hoohaah!!
Books.summary: Can't be dumbed down... it's a dumb as it can get...

Books.reviewText: Alpert knows his physics, and he always makes it interesting. Unfortunately he could have done a lot more with his basic premise about Einstein's lost "unified field" theory, it's almost a shame to have wasted such a good idea on this ultimately slight and forgettable thriller. The book is also marred by its puerile politics. It's OK to portray Cheney and Rumsfeld as evil, but presenting them as cartoon stick figures undermines the plot's already thin credibility. Having the FBI villain casually murder a muckraking New York Times journalist and then drive away listening to Rush Limbaugh might have made a funny Saturday Night Live sketch, but here it comes off as just plain dumb. The descriptions of the military are simply inept - the Black Hawk helicopters that ferry around Delta carry multi-barrel miniguns, not M240 machine guns, and anyway the M240 doesn't fire an "8 mm round". Obviously Alpert didn't care enough about the subject to get those details right. The description of hardware and procedures at the Fermilab particle accelerator, on the other hand, has the ring of authenticity. But Alpert's real problem is that he doesn't like people very much (a problem for a novelist). Nearly every character in the book who is not an academic turns out to be an evil moron of one sort or another. I'm torn between hoping he returns to science journalism and wishing that he would try his hand at a physics thriller one more time, but take things a little more seriously.
Books.summary: Great premise, could have done more with it

Books.reviewText: I wanted a romance but one well written, so what better guide than the writer of the Thorn Birds, a book that rends me even in the remembering, twenty years later?  The Ladies of Missalonghi, with the occasional illustration (who does this anymore?!) is an afternoon's delight, like the fairy cakes its characters concoct and consume with relish.  I admit towards the second half, it felt more low brow than high fiction, but the eponymous protagonist is just dowdy enough to lull, bright enough to change, and downtrodden enough to gratify when she stands up and grows into her own.  Add a dash of mystery, and the prospect of romance, all set in a lushly described small town valley in Australia.  An afternoon well spent, IMHO.

I think Tracy Brogan is a good writer with the potential to be a great writer.
Her characters are 3-D and some of her writing is L.O.L. funny.
This book starts off Funny and Fantastic. Unfortunately, it slows to a crawl about midway and becomes very predictable in some parts. (not to mention: The more I read about the lead character, I wondered if someone so "ridged" had 2 kids via osmosis).
Keep writing Tracy!
But surprise your readers with twists and turns. Also, try spicing it up with a more sex and laughs.
If you do, I think you have the potential to be in the same class as Jennifer Crusie.
Books.summary: Good writer-Great Characters-Story needs a re-write

Books.reviewText:
it shows a guideline how to launch your business from zero.  for people with limited business experience it could be a quick guide to read.  however, this guidelines could be told effectively in one fifth of this book.  the remaining 80% is repeating, wasting time to go over and over again on the same idea and some not-very-useful examples.  The author keep telling you the formula work work work only.

And because the author have lot of paid lectures and this book is considered to be a infomercial to promote his core business and capture your email too.  well, I don't really like this intention.

all in all, the guideline is good for beginner as a reference, but with too much unnecessary repeats and infomercial.
Books.summary: simple guideline for beginner but with lots of infomercial.

Books.reviewText:
I didn't like this one so much, the triplets were really annoying and bratty and it took away from the overall enjoyment of the story. I listened to this as an audiobook and was really surprised that in this one Prilla somehow had a really thick British accent and sounded much older than the Prilla in the Quest of the Fairy Egg book. Actually, most of the accents and voices the reader did were pretty off. It will probably be confusing to your child trying to explain how come Tinkerbell and all the other fairies sound so different. It would be nice if the directors encouraged the voice actresses to listen to each other's recordings before taping a new book, the only fairy that sounded like herself was Vidia.

The story itself was okay but definitely not in my top 5 compared to all the other Disney Fairy stories...

Condition said "good" and definitely should have been "acceptable" which I likely wouldn't have bought. Cover, spine, and pages were all pretty worn and there is a decent amount of highlighting and marking in it though all of the text is still legible. Only reason I didn't do two stars is because I only paid $23 for it, though it is 3 years old and some of the material is outdated. No idea why my teacher had us get an old book. The main problem I have with the book however is that 8 pages in the middle of the book just started falling out when I got to it and the binding is noticeably messed up there. I take good care of my books too as well the fact that I hardly opened the thing until midterms so I'm pretty positive the binding and pages were on the brink before I got it. I understand they were still attached when it was sold to me but I looked up the condition descriptions for books and even before the pages fell out the book falls under "acceptable" considering the wear and amount of highlighting. I am pretty late getting to this review and I have filled all of my science requirements now so I won't need another textbook but the point I want to make is Mr. Tillery please be more thoughtful and/or honest with your condition ratings. I would assume you don't heavily rely on selling $23 used textbooks for income so please be more careful with it. For what I did read of it I thought was well written and engaging for science being my least favorite subject but I don't like buying really worn down books so Mr. Tillery expend a little more energy and do more work on your objects by looking through them harder before you sell them.
Books.summary: and pages were all pretty worn and there is a decent amount of highlighting ...

Books.reviewText:
I haven't read a James Patterson book in years. For a long time I read his books as soon as they were released. When I saw this book is part of a new series featuring Detective Harriet Blue, I wanted to get in on it from the start. I loved Pattersons Womens Murder Club and thought this might be similar. Its not as good, but its still an interesting book.

This is true edge-of-your-seat reading. You cant take a breath and relax with this one. I couldn't put this book down, but it still wasn't a favorite of mine. I really couldn't warm up to the main character, Harriet Blue. Sometimes that happens with first books though. You have to get to know the characters a bit more before you can really like them.

The book does keep you guessing. Towards the end you realize what is going on and you fear for the characters. There, also, is a continuing storyline involving Harrys brother. So, its two storylines in one  the main storyline which is completed in this book, then the storyline with Harrys brother which I guess will be continued through the series. Im interested in learning more about that one.

A side note: There is violence, so if thats not your thing, you probably shouldnt read this.

Doomsday and the end of the world have never been my favorite topics. This is because I do not have a firm opinion on the subject. I have been reluctant to form my own opinion because I have not taken the time to educate myself on the different ways that the end of the world might possibly occur. But today I have taken the first step to offer my view on the subject: I read someone else's opinion of what might happen. Raymond C. Hundley's Will the World End in 2012 is a collection of ten theories, from the Mayan calendar to Web bots, as to why the world will end in 2012. Hundley has explained, given the science (or the lack thereof), and counterarguments for each of the ten speculations. While Hundley's book was informative, I still do not feel as though I will engage in any conversation about the end of the earth and when it will happen. Not because I am uninformed, but because I am apathetic about the subject.

Can two people with two different opinions and very different opinions at that ever fall in love ? Can they ever find a common ground in order to sustain a happy romance with each other ? Core Attraction by Ashlinn Craven is that type of story where opposites really do attract as we meet Dr. Declan MacCarthy aka our Dr McDreamy and Fiona Halpin. Fiona Halpin dreams of having the perfect life with a great house , an awesome job and a perfect husband but she never dreamed that she would find her perfect man this way as Fiona currently works for a power plant as the Public Relations officer and her job is about to get a lot harder when Declan MacCarthy turns up from his holiday and life in Japan to settle back down in his hometown in Ireland - yes, he even has that swoonworthy Irish accent, where he has settled into helping Cancer patients and right now the town is in an uproar due to the power plant as the radiation is causing nasty effects on the cancer patients . So Declan decides to join in on the campaign to shut it down which of course includes numerous pamphlet drops and protests, this is where Fiona comes in as it's her job to do damage control and soften the impact from the protestors and it's not going to be easy as she falls for Declan and vice versa, but Fiona is not one to go down without a fight ? Can the pair of them work things out or will their company rivalry be enough to tear what inkling of romance and core attraction they have for each other ?

Find out in this lovely romance read , which is perfect as I am in Winter for those cold nights where you just want to curl up in bed with a cup of tea and a lovely sweet romantic read to keep your heart warm and toasty.
Books.summary: A Lovely sweet romantic read to keep your heart warm and toasty.

Books.reviewText:
You know I've read some of the Bachman books and with them I was astounded. my favorite: The Long Walk. Some say its not good, but what I love is how King developed such a strong relationship between the characters in a rather short amount of space.

So this is another early work. Came after Bachman died. and I'm not very impressed. I think what King did was got a great idea, an idea that would attract people because it sounded like such a good storyline, and just ran with it. Gave it his all. But it simply just didn't live up to the high expectations such a great idea would receive.

When I first read the synopsis, I figured it would be a lot like Secret Window (remember in the movie, if you've seen it, that all the bad things that were going on in Depp's life was actually being caused by him, his alter-ego that he created?) Well this wasn't that. Instead the alter-ego became an actual human. While I was, truthfully, a bit disappointed that that was the way the story would go (it was too unrealistic for my liking) I still thought it had great potential. I thought "HOW is he going to prove that a man that never existed is causing all this chaos and not him!?" It had the making of being a story that would be a tough fix to end happily.

But it did end happily. Mainly because it ended ABRUPTLY. We never found out how Thad (the main character) dealt with the rest of his problems, where in everyone's eyes HE was still the one who had did all the damage. Its not a new story that King does that though, so I won't elaborate on how much I wish the story would've continued a few pages to tie up the loose ends.

Another thing I didn't like were the letdowns where there was supposed to be a climatic element added to the story. I.E. when the sheriff finally got a hold of the doctor and the doctor told him about the operation where he extracted the "tumor" which was actually Thad's unabsorbed twin. at the beginning of the story, it was mentioned that sometimes in the case of twins, the stronger one absorbs the weaker ones. so when the big "revelation" was revealed towards the end of the story, it was something that was simply repeated to those of us who paid attention. it wasn't shocking because we knew that already!

So as a conclusion: I loved the idea, thought it had great potential, and the ending was pretty good to me.
However, the book was very drawn out (it was hard to get through towards the end), failed to excite you at important details that were supposed to add the climax, left many open questions at the end. And personally, PERSONALLY, the characters were rather annoying to me. Thad was a nerdy, boringly plain weakling (who never seemed really afraid at the fact he might be blamed for countless murders. that should scare anyone), Liz was a strong but annoying woman who talked to much. The sheriff, who IS a key character, was probably my favorite throughout the story.

Not the absolute worst, but nowhere near as good as King is possible of getting when it comes to great stories, even for his early days.

There really isn't much distance between Hope & Despair... The towns of Hope & Despair in America's mid west aren't very far apart, geographically but sociologically these two towns couldn't be more distant. Hope is friendly & welcoming, a nice place to visit but when Reacher decides to check out its neighbour, Despair, he is made to feel utterly unwelcome... Why??? Is it because Jack is a large, well built & intimidating man? He thinks maybe not, generally speaking people don't normally try to physically remove him from anywhere he wants to be... its a free country after all, unless they have something sinister to hide.

Lots of seemingly unnecessary toing & froing that doesn't make much sense until about 3/4 of the way through the book. Then the thing starts to take shape. Lee seems to have taken his time to get into step with this one but your patience will be well rewarded.
Books.summary: It's just a short trip from Hope to Despair.

Books.reviewText:
"Adventures of the Karaoke King" is one of those books that's probably an acquired taste. The most obvious parallel for me are the books by Christopher Moore, which have a zany, comic, lusty tone to them, with flawed characters tilting at windmills. In this book, it's Guy Watanabe, a 30-something loser whose life revolves largely around his impressive karaoke skills. He gets entangled in a sinister corporate plot to take over the mom-and-pop karaoke bars, through his mistress, the fiance of the Chinese CEO behind the plot. From there, it's a cross-country adventure, with a set of increasingly bizarre characters who continue to show up in Guy's life through remarkable coincidences.

In some other ways, Harold Taw's writing reminded me of Michael Chabon's -- I've long admired Chabon's ability to turn really neat phrases, but for some reason, I haven't really enjoyed reading any of Chabon's books. I did sort of enjoy "Karaoke King," but it's not necessarily something that I think I would have picked up on my own.
Books.summary: Quirky voice, kind of like (but not as good) as Christopher Moore

Books.reviewText:
Mr. Eicher recalls the days of his youth of the time when his Amish family moved to Honduras together. He lived there for nine years during his pre-teen and teen years. He shared several stories, both serious and humorous about the people he interacted with on a daily basis and the community that he shared as well as how God took hold of his own life while he lived there. It wasn't bad, it just seemed to me that his writing style at times functioned poorly. I loved learnig about his bouts with chickens, his stuttering issues, learning about his family (though I feel like a lot of that was vague other than when recalling his grandfather), and his own testimony of faith. I don't think I have ever heard of mission work done by the Amish, so this intrigued me most about his family! My biggest qualms with the Amish is the lack of going out on the mission field, so this story shut me up a bit (in a good sense).

His family were honestly a bit more Old-Order Mennonite to me even though he was Old-Order Amish, but his family got away with various things that the Ordnung seemed to be against, so that was definitely different. His family used electricity and tools that normally aren't used by the Amish. However, the Anabaptist roots are what stuck the most and being a New-Order Mennonite, I appreciated hearing how those in the Amish community where he lived put out those non-resistance teachings to practice.

I hoped to have read this a little faster, but it was a bit slow in the beginning and in some other parts too at times.
Books.summary: It wasn't bad, it just seemed to me that his writing ...

Books.reviewText:
A disclaimer: I was offered a copy of the book to read and review on CCB in exchange for my honest opinion. I was not required to have a positive review.

This book has lovely pictures.  The pages and the artwork are very nice.  The story is how the attitude that you surround yourself with will result in positive or negative experiences for you.
The part of the book that most concerned me was that the mother in this story encouraged them to leave the cruise ship, where they lived, and go out and explore Auckland.
Not only that, but when these children were out exploring the city they met up with two people they didn't know before and matched up with them for more travel experiences in Auckland.  This could lead to a disastrous ending.

This REALLY disturbs me!  Encouraging two children to leave their home and explore a new city on their own.  YIKES!  I tremble to think that children would think this was an OK thing to do.  This is a frightening thought.

Among all the reviewers, I don't think I saw anyone else pick up on this message.  To me this is a serious error in this book.
After researching further I found where the author has placed a comment at the very front of the book that says "Maya and Filippo may seem young but they are old enough to travel on their own.  Always get permission from your parents or caregivers before leaving the house or ship."
This information really belongs in the body of the story where it will be seen by the juvenile reader, not on the front page with the copyright information etc.

Parents, just be cautious about the children who may be influenced by that information that it might be okay to venture out in a new environment by themselves without an adult companion and not only that but to not connect up with people they don't even know.
My mother stressed not taking rides from strangers when I was little.  Safety, safety, safety.  Children are precious and innocent.  Even at the ages of the children in this story.

The book was slowing moving and to me not as intense as the other books have been. Though I love the story with Gideon and Eva it lacking a little of the passion and fire they usually have. The ending was a bit anticlimactic, you're hoping for the happy "fairy tale" ending but to me it was a little bland. Not that I makes a big difference but for all the sex they had she NEVeR ended up pregnant, to me I found that a bit strange. I was almost hoping she would I would've like that ending a bit better. Don't get me wrong I LoVE the books and would read them again and again. I was just hoping for a little more excitement....
Books.summary: Though I love the story with Gideon and Eva it lacking a ...

Books.reviewText: 2 1/2 - 3 stars on this one. I have read and very much enjoyed this author's earlier releases. This one, despite  some credibility issues, was an entertaining read most of the way. I don't know what happened when he tried to wrap it up though, because it just did not work. Maybe the publisher was on his back to get it out by a certain due date, hard to say. All I know was the ending was rushed, shallow and disappointing. His fans know he can do better, and I for one hope he takes his time to write a complete novel the next go round.
Books.summary: Early promise, not up to expectations

Books.reviewText:
** spoiler alert ** I considered giving this book a lower rating, but the story was sound at least, and moved forward logically and was generally well written and interesting, so I felt it deserved kudos for that, at least. However, there were a few elements in particular that really bothered me. I get the feeling the climax was supposed to be a big surprise. It wasn't to me; I figured out it was going to go that way when Ivy tried to convince Lia that they could make friends with the Watchers. So their involvement was expected.
The next thing that really bothered me was the reappearance of the love triangle in a major way. Nothing irks me more than a heroine who makes protestations of love to two men almost simultaneously. Yes, they are both men with good and bad points, but please, can we have a clear tendency one way and leave it at that for good?
But the main thing I had problems with was the use of shock tactics. Sure, why not have someone declare their feelings in a way that's going to bring happiness to a pitiable character and then kill that person off? Bring happiness only to shatter it almost instantaneously. Not only that, I didn't think it was done convincingly. I find it hard to believe that any long term resident of the Frost conveniently forgets to have snow blossoms on them just at the particular time they're going to meet a Watcher that kills them. Fancy that. Basing a callous death on an unlikely coincidence does not make for a convincing plot development. It reminded me of the many frustrations I experienced when reading the poorly written Allegiant, which swore me off the Divergent trilogy entirely. These developments in Bluewing may be the end of my interest in the Frost Chronicles, because I don't want to become emotionally involved in something if this is the kind of development I can expect in the future.

Rachel Sexton works for the NRO - an intelligence agency located just outside of DC.  Its Director is a vocal opponent to NASA because of its security leaks.  Her father is running for President against the incumbant and has hinged his entire platform on the concept of NASA overspending the taxpayers money.  She abhors her father and finds herself in the middle of a scientific discovery that will change the world and her father's ruthless campaign that will be toppled by the discovery.  Add meteorites and murderous Delta Forces, and you have Deception Point.

Does this description sound convoluted and ridiculous?  That's pretty much how Dan Brown's novel reads.  It's mindless entertainment, and the plot is just not very good.  Often I found myself saying, "Ok, please get to the point."  This novel is not the "fast paced thriller" some of the reviews advertise, but it is not all bad.  Do not pick it up expecting an award winner, but instead something to read on the beach.  Angels and Demons and DaVinci Code are much better despite being "beach reads" themselves.

I was disappointed with portions of this book.  But again, it was not written by a historian.
In the first few chapters, Reynolds calls Harriet Beecher Stowe an adamant colonizationalist, without noting where the information came from.  She did mention it in "Uncle Tom's Cabin," but stated afterward she was not supportive of it, although her father was.
It is obvious he is very sympathetic to John Brown.  But he did do a very good job of portraying John Brown as the family man he was.  John Brown's letters supports this.  John Brown was also for equal rights for African Americans and women.  This is supported by his statements, letters, and other documents.
But I would read other books, such as Stephen Oates, before I would use this one as reference.

I do wonder why archaeological discoveries like this have never been widely spoken of. If giant skeletons had been discovered in the Middle East, it would have been spoke of ad nauseum. Are there religious reason for not wanting it known they were in north America possibly earlier than when they were known to exist over there? It is awe-inspiring to know that people, some of Caucasian descent, and up to 12 feet tall actually existed in America in prehistoric times. The book is a wonderful read and I do recommend it. The downside is that I saw many things repeated, sometimes several times, as if the author did not trust the reader to understand it the first time. But, that is not enough to keep me from recommending it as worth the price and time to read.

In theory, the diet was excellent. Heavily restricted calorie diet using nothing but power foods. However, the lack of flexibility really killed me. To be specific, the first breakfast meal recommended grapefruit and plain oatmeal. I HATE grapefruit. Hate, hate, hate. So, needless to say, it was difficult to eat half of one every day for 10 days. Not really happening, no matter how good they are for you. I subbed with an orange, but I know I missed out on some nutritional benefits.

Aside from some less-than-pleasant meals, the exercise routine was a little unrealistic unless you're already in shape. The run-jog-walk part in particular assumed that you already could do what it was asking you to do (which I couldn't). All in all, I would recommend this to someone who is already in shape and healthy who wants a quick boost or kickstart. Not for out-of-shapers!
