When these ladies deliver their full album I'll be there to buy it and support them all the way! Don't forget to tour Denver, Saint Louis or Chicago soon so I can see you, ladies. Big Love!!!
Digital_Music.summary: This is the awesome music that we have to search a bit to ...

Digital_Music.reviewText: this is a very good CD to own.  It's not available as a download and it's only a private issue. Sawyer Ward is or was ( I don't know which) a yoga instructor from Ruidoso NM.  She uses a harmonium and a backup percussion but the chants are great and her rendition of Amazing Grace is powerful.  This is not a polished studio performance, which to me is all the better.  This is a heartfelt rendition of spiritual works in an Eastern tradition. All I can say is that I hope at some point, someone makes these available for downloading.  Sawyer Ward deserves to be heard.
Digital_Music.summary: If you are into yoga or meditation

Digital_Music.reviewText:
I was worried, a little, that Chicago might just recycle some sounds and call them new OR come out with a completely new sound.  They did neither.  If you are familiar with the band this music will seem like a long lost friend.  IF you are new to them it will seem like a wonderful discovery.

Already gone reminded me of KOOL AND THE GANG when I first heard it.

I was a little disappointed that there's no Keith Howland led vocals but DANG there is so much to like that is not a problem.

The only thing I didn't like, and IMHO, it is USELESS is the "HOTSINGLE" cut of Feel.  It's the same song a little shorter with no horns in it AT ALL!  Whoever made that decesion should be taken out and dealt with on the South Side.  CHICAGO IS a rock band with a horn section playing jazz and blues influenced music.  Take away the horns and you have just another pop band.

I downloaded it as soon as I could from ITUNES and bought the CD too!

A Chinese friend recommended this artist to me and I am very happy I followed their advice. Some of these songs rock out, some are balllady, some have a fair amount of western influence and others sound very distinctly Chinese, although clearly contemporary.  There are some excellent duets with a female vocalist.  My Chinese reading and Mandarin listening skills are extremely rudimentary  and although it's nice to be able to read some of the titles and catch a few lines of lyrics, I believe it would be very listenable to someone with no knowledge of Chinese.  In China, especially the Sichuan region, he is hugely popular.  If you are planning a trip, you'll definitely impress folks if you can learn to even hum
a few lines of a song or two.
Digital_Music.summary: Beautiful mix of contemporary Chinese songs.

Digital_Music.reviewText: This last album for Capitol Records is a fine piece of history. Judy Garland was one of the best singers of the 20th century and is in excellent voice throughout this CD. She shines on so many songs on this CD that it is hard to pinpoint which are better than the rest. "I Happen To Like New York" and "Judy At The Palace Medly" are superb. It is obvious that after so many years, she still has the appeal. Great vocalist leave a mark. Frank Sinatra once commented on Garland saying "Time will forget most of us.......not Judy Garland.....Never Judy" He was right. There are generations that embrace her every year!!

My definition of Believe is peace,love,and happiness. I've had Believe since 2000 and 9 of the 10 songs are perfect. Especially Takin' Back My Heart. It sounds very romantic and full of love. We All Sleep Alone sounds very attractive and danceable. Taxi,Taxi sounds like a duplicate of We All Sleep Alone. Runaway is very deep,low, and relaxing-just listen to Cher's voice. Love Is The Groove is very peaceful. Believe,The Power,All Or Nothing,Strong Enough are just full of happiness. Through it all peace,love,and happiness fits Believe perfectly. You go Cher.

One Republic's memorable song "Secrets" by this time is no secret but every time I hear it, the extremely powerful lyrics and melody never escapes the mind.  The opening drone of the cello that begins the song sweeps the doors open for the listener to a lyrical rendering of dramatic proportions that lead singer Ryan Tedder meticulously performs along with the rest of the band members.

"Secrets" possesses a very creative and poetic narration that lends itself to interpretation that only the songwriter is able to completely understand that is dependent on the circumstance.  But for the average listener, the precise instrumentation of the pounding drums and string arrangement as well as Tedder's strong vocals show much intimacy of  the dilemmas that are written within each word of the song.  But what tends to ring out are the lyrics that convey and reveal much about betrayal and misunderstandings and the eventual chanting and giving all the secrets away.

Indeed, a song that may be played more than once and may be placed on the list of the most emotionally charged lyrics.

My children are OBSESSED with Macklemore, our new hometown hero. This is one of the many and best reason why.  (as long as you get the non-explicit versions of some of the songs! Yikes!)  Same Love carries a powerful message that I hope my children always remember.  And it's just a damn awesome song, and I usually don't even like ballad-y songs.
Yeah, Eastside's got your back Macklemore.

I've been searching from time to time on Amazon for more of Marty's (et al) gospel music, so got tears when I realized he had released a new gospel album.  Tried & true, Marty just keeps getting better.  I've been watching his Saturday night show for a couple of years now & have watched The Fabulous Superlatives get better, as well, & the cohesion & ease of the group grow together. An all-around entertainer, ya gotta love Marty cause he loves so much what he does.  He doesn't hog the spotlight either & seems very happy to promote others on his show with Connie Smith, his wife.  Those 2 just personify love for each other & for everyone else & for their craft.  Every show they sing @ least one gospel tune, which is a long held tradition with country artists to remember from whence we came, & hope one day to return.
Digital_Music.summary: Soooo happy to find "Pray The Power Down"

Digital_Music.reviewText: If you think Jan Hammer is only Miami Vice, think again.  Hammer has done wonderful work both on his own as well as with the likes of Mahavishnu Orchestra, Jeff Beck, Billy Cobham and many, many more.  His Minimoog solo work shows off some of the best chops you will ever hear.  This record is different, however.  It is a solo work that is slower paced and much more contemplative and introspective than any of the jazz fusion work he did throughout the 70s.  This is one of my all time favorite recordings.  It is nice to see it available in CD format.  Let's hope some of Hammer's other solo work is released too.  Hammer is a true giant who ended up doing cheesy TV scores.  Sad, but there is much to be discovered in his vast earlier work.

Eddie and Alex VH are on fire! Sure, Dave hits a few bad notes, but VH is not (and never has been) about a stellar vocal performance by DLR...it's about Eddie's blistering guitar riffs and Alex VH pounding the skins! I am sick of all the whining about the vocal prowess of a 61 year old showman (yes, Dave is a showman first and one of the greatest ever). Many of the casual fans of VH never understood what VH is all about and the magic of VH live. Hint: It's never been DLR's vocals. So, if you're buying this live album to hear great vocals, please go buy Journey, Captured. But, if you're looking for a TRUE LIVE ALBUM THAT ROCKS...this is the one!! Bands today wouldn't have the courage to put a live album like this out without massive production, touch ups and showing all the warts. VH is good enough live to do just that and I think it's incredible!! Oh, and for those complaining about Michael Anthony no longer being in the band, just STOP IT!! First, if it was your kid, you would do the exact same thing! Second, Michael Anthony was an OK bass player with OK backing vocals, which in the big picture, doesn't matter anymore. VAN HALEN is and always WILL be the power duo of Eddie and Alex VH, not freakin' Michael Anthony. For anyone to say that VH is not VH without Michael Anthony is just plain ridiculous, ludicrous and asinine!
Digital_Music.summary: Dave hits a few bad notes, but VH is not (and never has ...

This particular version of band is my favorite, when both Pigpen and Keith Godchaux played keyboards, organ and piano respectively. When Jerry played a strat and Bill was the only drummer. At the time of the Europe '72 tour the Grateful Dead hadn't quite reached the levels of jazzy exploration found in late '73 through '74. Instead they played the songs with a bounce and a swagger they never surpassed in later years and jammed with a new found grace that added quite a bit of subtlety to their more psychedelic interludes.

The Grateful Dead came ready to play on this the second date of the Europe '72 tour and second date at Wembley Empire Pool. Every song is very well played, with Cumberland Blues ending up on the original Europe '72 live album. It's clear that Bob Weir, Phil Lesh and all are on for this show. But what sets 04/08 at the Wembley Empire Pool apart from most of the other shows of this very fine tour is the monstrous Dark Star>Sugar Magnolia>Caution suite. For me the gold standard Dark Stars are the "original" one found on Live Dead and the surreal and exploratory one played at the Fillmore on 02/13/70. This one at Wembley is just as good if not better. The Dead go places they'd never before explored in part because of the efforts of then new piano player Keith Godchaux and the sense of jazzy exploration he brought. The Dead's amazing group mind improvisational skills are very much in evidence. After the excursion into the cosmos that is Dark Star, the band segues brilliantly into Sugar Magnolia which provides a welcome bit of sunshine. Following Sugar Magnolia is the most fiercely jammed out Caution of the tour and perhaps of all time. Jerry is on fire spitting out tart notes like a musical machine gun and the rest of the band are right there with him.

Pick this album up you won't be sorry. It's a keeper. The playing is exceptional, the mix is good, everybody's audible and the recording quality is excellent. That group mind thing I talked about is evident on every song, oh and there's Jerry's sublime pedal steel on Looks Like Rain. For me this concert is one of the best of the Europe '72 tour, top five at least.

Other exceptional shows from the Europe '72 tour: 04/11 at Newcastle, 04/14 at Tivoli Concert Hall, 05/03 at Olympia Theatre (my vote for best show of the tour), and the run at the Lyceum Theatre in England. 05/26 being the debatable best. The show on 05/11 at Rotterdam has another amazing Dark Star>Sugar Mag>Caution suite. Bickershaw on 05/07 is also great with Pigpen wailing on organ throughout and is the only show of the tour that has both the Other One and Dark Star. Speaking of Other Ones, the 05/10 show at the Amsterdam Concertgebouw has the best of the tour.
Digital_Music.summary: One of the finest dates of the Europe'72 Tour

Digital_Music.reviewText: I've followed The Choir since 1991 and this album takes me back to those old high school days and their Circle Slide album. With Shadow Weaver, The Choir has returned to the sound that put them on the music map. Gone are the repetitive lyrical phrases found on Kissers and Killers/Speckled Bird albums (though they were great but honestly only truly enjoyed/appreciated by cult Choir lovers). This is The Choir at its best. Old followers will love it and it's a great album to introduce someone new to The Choir.
Digital_Music.summary: The Choir has returned to form....

Digital_Music.reviewText: What a wonderful peaceful piece of music!  With the most clear and brilliant violin leading us along with harp strings and bit by bit drawing upon orchestral power, this lovely offering delivers moments of subtle grace with just a hint of angst.  Like a fine oil painting or a gorgeous scene, at times mesmerizing, at times troubling....depending on the whims of weather and light....this is musical genius!

I bought this knowing it would be good. I kind of expected a few songs to be kind of dull because they're a fairy new band. I was actually happy to be mistaken. It has a good mix of upbeat and mellow songs which doesn't seem repetitive.  Every song is wonderful and you don't need to speak the language to like some of them.  This is a nice and refreshing album from a great set of girls. I recommend this to everyone and can't wait until they go on tour here in the US because a lot of us really love this band.

This compilation is most of Powell's recordings for Vanguard, plus one for Capitol. The latter is from 1947, while the others are from 1953 through 1956,

Since this page has sound samples you can get a good idea of both the musical territory this album covers, as well as the sound quality. I have gone through this album a few times and am still hearing new things on each listen.

Like most of the compilations from this label you get a lot of value, but very little documentation. I have tracked down the source albums and personnel for each and am providing them below. One thing that I love is even though the albums are randomly scattered among the track list, they are out of print, so this is one way to get a large part of Powell's body of work as a leader. And since this is an MP3 album, you can easily reorder the tracks and group them according to album.

Here is what you get:

Tracks 1, 2 and 4 are all but one track from the 1947 album titled Classics In Jazz. The front line is comprised of Jake Porter on trumpet and Bumps Myers on tenor sax. Powell leads the rhythm section that is also comprised of Red Callender on bass and Lee Young on drums. The missing track is There's A Small Hotel.

Tracks 3, 5, 8, 10 through 12, 18, 28, 30, 34, 39, 40 and 41 are the album titled Out on a Limb from 1956. There are two ensembles in this album For tracks 3, 28, 30, 34 and 39 the line up is Ruby Braff fronts on trumpet, backed by Powell, Skeeter Best on guitar, Oscar Pettiford on bass and Bobby Donaldson on drums. The remaining tracks for Out on a Limb feature Al Mattaliano on trumpet, Nick Calazza on tenor sax and Peanuts Hucko on clarinet. The rhythm section is Powell on piano, Tommy Kay on guitar, Arnold Fishkin on bass and Bobby Donaldson on drums.

Tracks 6, 16, 19, 22, 23, 27, 32 and 35 are the 1955 album titled Thigamagig. This is an interesting and unique line up comprised of Ruby Braff on trumpet, Powell on piano and Bobby Donaldson on drums.

Tracks 7, 8, 13, 14 and 41 are the album titled Mel Powell Septet from 1953. The front line is Buck Clayton on trumpet, Henderson Chambers on trombone and Edmund Hall on clarinet. The rhythm section is Powell, Steve Jordan on guitar, Walter Page on bass and Jimmy Crawford on drums.

Tracks 9, 26, 29, 31, 33, 37 and 38 are the 1954 album titled Borderline with another unique trio format featuring Paul Quinichette on tenor sax, Powell on piano and Bobby Donaldson on drums.

Tracks 15, 17, 20, 21, 24, 25 and 36 are the 1956 album titled The Mel Powell Bandstand. The front line is Johnny Glasel on trumpet, Jimmy Buffington on French horn and Chuck Russo on alto and baritone sax, clarinet and bass clarinet. Powell leads the rhythm section comprised of Mundell Lowe on guitar, Joe Kay on bass and Eddie Phyfe on drums. The vocalist is Joan Wile.

This is indie chart staple that some would and do say has been done to death, but it is ruddy great. Opening track `Wreckin bar rar, ra , ra', is a 90 second homage to The Ramones and what a great way to kick off such a joyous album.

All of the tracks could be singles, and sometimes that can be annoying, but they are all so good that it just makes this one album that you don't feel you need to fast forward any tracks at all. The obvious pithy wit, irony and verve that is `Post break up sex' is probably the most stand out track, but only just, a real crowd pleaser and floor filler. Track 5 `Wetsuit'; is slower but still has enough momentum to hook you and take you along for the ride. Personal favourite is `A lack of understanding', as it seems to be about me and I like it when you can instantly empathise with a song. The vocals are great too and are all delivered so clear that a lyric sheet is not needed. I have had this a couple of weeks now and during that time three of my fave bands have brought out new albums; this however has been a constant on my MP3 despite all the other music I have been getting. It just feels like summer, sex, angst and fun all rolled up in a great package that you can dance to (but in my case - not very well).

There is a twelfth track `Somebody else's child that is tucked at the end of track 11 and not available on download, this is the slowest and most reflective number and makes the album approach as opposed to download, probably the better option.

Also not my typical genre, but for indie rock fans who like their music accessible, upbeat, with great lyrics tight playing and some heartfelt humour, then this is indie heaven.

I am a huge David Cook fan. I waited at my computer with anticipation for the release of this single. His voice is amazing - yes, it does seem they over processed the vocals a little too much, but I am used to his voice in the raw from his pre-idol releases.  David Cook is an amazin artist and I cannot wait for his album to see what else he has in store for us!

Every David Cook fan should own this single - it rocks!

This has to be my favorite Digweed Live album he's made. I like all of them but this one has to be at the top for me because of the old progressive house sound it reminds me of. This mix set has such a classic progressive house feel to it with its deep yet energetic melodic sound and the use of tracks that have a classic progressive trance vibe and it all works so well.

If your and old prog house fan from back in the day when Digger and the likes of Sasha, Warren and Seaman were at the top of their prog house game than you'll love this mix. I keep saying classic prog house sound which is true and with how clean tracks of today sound make this one of the standout mixes of the year, heck of the past few years imo.

This is one of those songs that I don't think many people know about.  I say that because I seldom hear anyone speak of it like a lot of other love songs.  But make no mistake about it, this is a beautiful and touching song worthy of all the accolades I don't think it ever received.  It's definitely a song to celebrate love to.  Truly stellar performances by two great artists of a truly gorgeous song.
Digital_Music.summary: One Of The Best Love Songs Ever!

Digital_Music.reviewText: This is an amazing album by an amazing band!!!!  My early favorites are Central Park, Wish, Runaways, Flight, (has been released for awhile but one of my all-time favorites) and One for the Pain.  All of the songs are fantastic and they really have the vintage Lifehouse vibe that Lifehouse fans adore.  There is not one song I don't care for.  The more you listen to the lyrics, the deeper you appreciate and long their songs.  True for this album as well!  You will not regret this album!  One of their best!!!
Digital_Music.summary: This is an amazing album by an amazing band

Digital_Music.reviewText:
It is fortunate the lyrics are printed because KEMBA'S GOT THE CABBAGE MOTH BLUES would take a hard listen to get it. The CD is excellent, Shovels & Rope is an addiction (ya, another one), and it is certainly a good investment to get so much joy from listening to the harmony these two sing.

As with other great artists, it would take a book to write about how good they sound and the beauty of their words.

I have been a Blue October fan for 10 years now, especially Ryan's violin playing; I've always enjoyed their accoustic versions.  I also listen classical music & thought the hybrid would be awesome.  That said, I did not like this CD at all!  I was expecting something interesting, more familiar since Blue October uses the violin from Ryan throughout most songs.  But there is a huge difference between classical & electric violin. I know the notes are the same & you can hear a faint similarity on this CD, but I just don't like it at all.
Digital_Music.summary: LOVE Blue October, love classical music, HATE this CD!

Digital_Music.reviewText:
"25 or 6 to 4," one of the greatest songs ever - right? This is not "25 or 6 to 4;" it's more like "Love me Tomorrow" or "Your the Inspiration."  This is the Chicago that at one point said "You know how our band has an incredible brass section? What if we just used synthesizers instead?" It is that Chicago that made this album; and It is the epitome of Adult Contemporary garbage.

I own thousands of Christmas songs; I make a habit of collecting all sorts because I love listening to Christmas music.  I can not make it through this album to no matter how many times I've tried.  I've actually deleted it off of every playlist I have and have even deleted the album entirely from my hard drive and cloud storage.  Yes.  It's that bad.

Now if you like Adult Contemporary music; and if you could care less about classic-sounding Christmas standards; and if you think that 80s Chicago is better than 70s Chicago, you may love this album.  Though it is brass-heavy (a good thing), it is also cheese-heavy; and I am saddened and a little offended that I came to own this album.
Digital_Music.summary: Chicago is great; this album is horrible

Digital_Music.reviewText:
The only thing I like about the album is the cover. That's it! I was disappointed with all tracks dropped before the release.

"The way of the future" seeks to recreate the intro of "White Trash Millionaire" but results in a slow and dumb pentatonic run. The worst opener. The so-called single "In our dreams" proved my worst expectations that the album wouldn't contain any good songs. Only in "their" dreams indeed. The song starts with four measures of clean guitars and flows (very abruptly and awkwardly) into a riff I can "write" if I don't want to be any creative. I was in their gig in Germany in February. The song just sucked and there was no excitement in the audience whatsoever.

"The Rambler" is cute but nothing more. Live it sucks even worse than other stuff. Haha, I saw people going quickly to the toilet or getting a beer before good stuff came. And I can understand them. If BSC claim the song to be "very personal" to them then they can go sing it to their mommas. They could have made a lot more from this tune by changing the melody (this predictable "up" and "down" in the verses) or adding other instruments as on "Hollywood in Kentucky".

The other thing is soul. I like soul, I like these great girl bands who influenced i.a. The Beatles. But as you don't mix beer with cornflakes, you shouldn't combine fat guitars with heavenly singing female voices either. Things that are good by themselves could produce a final "bad". "Soul Machine", thus, has its good moments, for instance, rhythm guitar in the verses, but all in all there's to much sugar in it.

I liked the atmosphere on "Shaking my cage" due to use of the dobro guitar and there are some interesting fragments here and there. But the overall picture is boring and uninspiring.

I sometimes wonder what people can dislike about BSC's previous albums. It is often a matter of taste. But good or bad, each of the previous LPs has at least two or three mind-blowing tracks. "Kentucky" is a disaster considering songwriting. I kind of think that all this talk about "back to the roots" or "heaviest sound" is merely a fig leaf for lack of songwrtiting ideas.

Ain't worth a penny. Kids, save your money and go stuff your throats with KFC instead.

What an absolutely AWFUL album.  If your a young kid (12 and under) and are looking for a little dance grove beat that your parents will let you listen to, this album is for you.  It is very Hillary Duff/Disney "hip" sounding.  If your anyone else please AVOID this album like the plague.
Years ago Jewel was one of the few writers/singers that actually had talent and something of substance to add to the music industry.  Now she has turned into just another "teen beat".  If she has any desire to stay in the music industry any longer she needs to take a good long listen to her first two albums, "Pieces of Me" and "Spirit" and reflect on what it is that made her great.  She used to write eloquent lyrics and had enchanting music now she is just another pop girl ala Britney Spears.
Her new album is shallow and meaningless.  Her once great ability to write astounding lyrics, like those found in her first two albums, has suddenly become transformed into the type of lyrics I would hear from the Spice Girls.  In fact I have no doubt that is the Spice Girls ever somehow make it back they will be asking jewel to borrow her lyrics and beats from this album.  They are that really contrived.
I understand why people would dub her a "sellout".  I am also having a hard time believing that this transformation was all her doing as well.  I can't see her going from "Pieces of Me" to this without some sort of outside influence pressuring that change.
Avoid this album at all costs.  Though the cover says Jewel what is inside is definitely not.
Digital_Music.summary: OK...Who took over Jewel's body and turned her into this....

Digital_Music.reviewText: Honestly this music feels evil.  I tried to listen to it on a few occassions, but was freaked out by it.  I wasn't even fasting which (of course) is an even more sensitive state.  As an experienced faster (up to 21 days with just water) I can attest that this music is the opposite of the soothing, calm music a faster should be hearing.  All I can say is....what were they thinking?

I ran the versions being sold on Amazon through a digital audio workstation and have concluded that they are all subsantially compressed and loudened to compete with so-called modern songs.

If Amazon does decide to offer the un-remastered ORIGINAL tracks from Graceland I will actually buy them.

Until then, look "elsewhere", or hold on to your original Graceland CDs.

Digital_Music.reviewText:
I've now heard this thing uninterrupted all the way through - the only fair way to consume any new block of music, I believe - twelve times in a bit less than three days. For the record, I really, really wanted to like it, for a whole lot of reasons.

The bad news? It isn't very good. The good news? It isn't as bad as the truly awful "A Momentary Lapse of Reason", and it's probably, on balance, better than the ponderous "The Division Bell" (strictly due to the near-total absence of embarrassingly poor lyrics - more about that later). And although it isn't nearly as horrible as some of today's rather obvious I'd-just-be-shooting-fish-in-a-barrel artificial pop music targets, it's still unnervingly weak and seemingly without purpose. Nothing on this album stands up to anything - anything - released by Pink Floyd up to and including 1983.

For those who have quickly acclaimed this release as "a masterpiece" or some other wild superlative, I have to say, sentimentality & nostalgia aside, I just don't get your enthusiasm. The thing isn't even remotely cohesive. It starts, it stops, it falters, it re-starts. It goes absolutely nowhere. It vaguely promises, but never delivers. No idea or theme is ever fully developed. Not only is no new ground broken, old ground that has already been strip-mined past the bedrock is re-dug and offered up yet again. But, for those who persevere through until the end, the final reward is even worse. The only actual "song" on the album is a real stinker, a genuine crapnugget, complete with cringe-worthy lyrics and more overly familiar tropes. Why this stream of stitched-together twenty-year-old leftovers is getting so much adulation from some fans is beyond me.

I wish that Mr. Gilmour & company had done more, musically & artistically, with the brand name they fought so hard to retain. They didn't, though, and now it's just too late. The franchise has been running on empty for a very long time, though, and now I guess it's time they had a rest. This CD is that rest. The legacy deserved better, I think, but as sad and unfortunate as this release is, I'll probably listen to it just once more, late on another cold November night...and wonder about what could have been...
Digital_Music.summary: Not really "endless", it just seems that way...

Digital_Music.reviewText: Hense the title. Let me begin by saying this. Respectfully, while Oran Juice Jones is a name that will be tied to the 1 hit wonders ("The Rain") of the world, his swagger and potential is what we (critics/consumers) were hoping for. In 2009, its long gone. The highlights of this compilation of disposable music, are very few and between. It starts with the fact that the CD is based around Oran rather than on Oran. In todays playing field, if indeed your name still rings any bell whatsoever, you would want to rejuvinate that with a resounding..."I Still Got It", and capitolize on that. Instead, we are introduced to a family that sounds like a pack of wolves. The Vocal talents displayed here at best are very sub-par. In most cases I couldn't bare to listen to the full track without reaching my fatigued finger from pressing the forward button again, and again. Yes,.. I pressed it alot. The First thing that stands out is the poor mixing. The Vocals pitch over the obvious in-house production, and come off incomplete and muffled. The vocals on some tracks are just simply too loud and in some cases the production is just too hollow. This is not a mainstream/big-budget release, so don't look for high production value or big name producers, but in todays market where you have so many options, and little to no cost for local or regional talent. Putting together a respectable project with current values isn't too hard to come by. Google the word producer and youll likely find 1,000's of hungry producers that will sell you a industry worthy track for scraps or for kudos to say they worked with an artist from the past. (Homage) Production wise, the CD is very flat, and you look for the radio record, and the club anthem, or the ballad, and then you realize your listening pleasure quickly becomes pain. Oran is featured on less than half of the project..?? Outdated sound and inadequate vocals make this CD quickly become a listening session that you will all but forget, once you reach the end. One highlight, is that Oran still has writing ability. Brick Jungle has glimpses of what could have been a worthy record over production from todays standards. Lets hope that Oran will utilize his remaining years to tap into "What Was", and collaborate with "What Is", and aim for a single that would attract todays listeners. Harlem is know for its trend setting and swagger, and we hope that Oran will tap into this being a native. Until then, if you make the mistake of spending any $ on this project, request and refund, an autograph, and a written apology. (1 of 5)
Digital_Music.summary: Fruit..that has a very bitter taste.

Digital_Music.reviewText: The only unfortunate thing about Amazon MP3 downloads is you can't listen to the whole thing before buying it.  10 seconds (or whatever it is) is usually enough to know if that is the version of the song you want, but in this case, it wasn't.  As far as I know, there are two versions of the original Dukes of Hazzard theme from the TV series; one played on a regular guitar, the other on an electric guitar.  This one is neither.  It is played by Waylon Jennings, but he throws in some extra "yeah!" gutterals here and there, and the tone and inflections used are NOT the same as either of the two original themes.  Do not waste your money.  I know it was only 99 cents, but it was still a waste.  You'd be better off holding up a microphone in front of your TV speaker and recording the theme direct from the show (if you're not tech-savvy) or using one of the multiple ways of wiring a straight TV to Computer/recorder to capture the song.

The two other reviewers correctly observe that this this album isn't exactly representative of anywhere near the best of Country singer/guitarist Jacky Ward, born in Groveton, Texas on November 18. 1946 and who registered 25 singles on the Country charts from 1972 to 1988. And one of them also offers the thought that this CD contained "most" of the tracks he did in an album titled "More." In fact, it's an exact reproduction of that album except that track 4 was actually the last track in the B-side of that LP, which came out in 1983 as Premier PR-0156. And not only were all re-makes, 7 of them did not even come close to being among his "greatest hits." In that waning era of the 33 1/3 vinyl album it wasn't uncommon for Country artists to re-record some of their material and have it issued without any indication that they were not the originals.

The only actual hit singles represented here are: Big Blue Diamond, his first which peaked at # 39 in June/July 1972 on Target 0146; his 1977 cover of The Drifters' 1957 R&B hit Fools Fall In Love which wound up at # 9 in September/October on Mercury 55003 (the B-side was a re-recording of Big Blue Diamond); A Lover's Question, his 1978 cover of the 1959 Clyde McPhatter hit A Lover's Question, which finished at # 3  Country and # 106 Billboard Pop Hot 100 Bubble Under in February/March on Mercury 55018 to become his best hit ever; and Rhythm Of The Rain, his 1978 cover of The Cascades hit from 1963, which topped out at # 11 in November/December on Mercury 55047. The rest weren't even the B-sides of his charted singles! And as for being "overlooked by the big guys" it's worth noting that 19 of his 25 charted singles were on the Mercury Records label, hardly an also-ran in the industry. He also recorded several albums there.

Other Top 40 hits of his include: Dance Her By Me (One More Time) - a # 38 in December 1975 on Mercury 73716; I Never Said It Would Be Easy - # 24 in September 1976 on Mercuru 73826; Texas Angel - a # 31 in February 1977 on Mercury 73880; Three Sheets In The Wind - a # 20 in June 1978 and its B-side, I'd Really Love To See You Tonight - a # 20 "follow-along" and both duets with Reeba McEntire on Mercury 55026; I Want To Be In Love - a # 24 in August 1978 on Mercury 55038; Wisdom Of A Fool - a # 8 in February/March 1979 on Mercury 55038; That Makes Two Of Us - a # 26 in July 1979 and another duet with Reba on Mercury 55054; You're My Kind Of Woman - # 14 in October 1979 on Mercury 57004; I'd Do Anything For You - a # 32 in January 1980 on Mercury 57013; Save Your Heart For Me - a # 8 in June 1980 on Mercury 57022; That's The Way A Cowboys Rocks And Rolls - a # 7 in Sept/Oct 1980 on Mercury 57032; Something On The Radio - a # 13 in February/March 1981 on Merecury 57044; and Travelin' Man - his cover of trhe 1961 Ricky nelson hit and a # 32 in April 1982 on Asylum 47424.

None of his other charted sides for Mega, Asylum, Warner and Elektra made it into the Top 40, so clearly his best years (in terms of hits anyway) were at the giant Mercury. Those are the sides that would make a definitive "greatest hits" compilation. Avoid this.
Digital_Music.summary: Avoid This ... Re-Makes And Nowhere Near His "Greatest Hits"

Digital_Music.reviewText: The original "First Family" album was the fastest-selling LP in American history. A million copies moved in a few weeks and an unprecedented 7.5 million within a year. Even Pres. Kennedy, the target of this spoof had the record, claiming in an off-hand press conference remark that Vaughn Meader's imitation sounded more like younger brother Ted than him. Released by CADENCE Records in March of '63, THE FIRST FAMILY VOLUME TWO (CLP-3065/CLP-25065) was almost as popular as the original LP, peaking at #4 on Billboard's 200 Albums chart. Sales of both records plummeted with the 11/22/63 murder of JFK and they were recalled from store shelves. Soon after, CADENCE was shut down by owner Archie Bleyer, due primarily to artist departures and changing public musical tastes. The entire CADENCE catalog was sold to Andy Williams. CAST Vaughn Meader; Naomi Brossart; Norma MacMillan; Stantley Myron Handleman; Earl Doud; Bob Booker; Barry Newman; Joe Silver (and others) ACT I NOTES "First Family Vol. 2" is a larger production than the original, with an added orchestra and chorus that initially appear on Scene 2's musical press coinference. S3) The Kennedys spend part of their 5th wedding anniversary looking at a White House up for rent. S4) A silly blackout sketch. S5) JFK's 67 car motorcade gets arrested for speeding through a small town. S6) Baby John on phone with Nikita K. S7) Snores during Pablo Casals' recital aren't from the president. S8) Caroline sings "First Daughter of the First Family." S9) Therapist blackout. ACT II NOTES S!) Fifty Mile Hike song has a lot of annoyed participants. S2) IRS agent goes over JFK's deductions. S3) The Kennedys at the premiere of CLEOPATRA (1963). S4) JFK interviews a possible escort for Caroline. His name is the punchline. S5) The president's meeting with grumpy old "Nicky." S6) JFK demands that Bobby and Ted get their own voices. S7) In the hindsight of history, this bit about John and Jackie in retirement after both younger brothers served two-term presidencies is quite sad. S8) Meader interviews youngsters at a grammar school. ACT I [0:21] Scene 1: The Announcement [5:42] Scene 2: An Evening With JFK [3:08] Scene 3: 1958 [1:23] Scene 4: The Trial [4:06] Scene 5: The Law [1:40] Scene 6: The Crisis [1:11] Scene 7: The Concert [3:49] Scene 8: The First Daughter [0:51] Scene 9: Biography ACT II [3:04] Scene 1: The First Family March [4:42] Scene 2: Taxes [1:03] Scene 3: The Movie [2:37] Scene 4: Caroline's First Date [1:20] Scene 5: Stop the World [2:39] Scene 6: The Brothers Three [1:54] Scene 7: 1996 [4:07] Scene 8: Equal Time TOTAL TIME: 43:37

As a longtime LadyHawke fan (since her debut), I find myself slightly conflicted about this album as in a way, it doesn't fully resonate with me both musically and on a personal level. Bias aside, I can safely say that she has again captured an incredible sound with tracks like 'A love song', 'Wild things', and 'Sweet fascination'. Overall, the album is a success and I can appreciate to a great degree the apparent 180 she performed in regards to the more jovial signature of this album, as well the the heightened 80's sound.

I've now listened to the album 3 times and begun to have more appreciation for the album as a whole, especially in comparison to the darker 'My Delirium'. I'm sure it represents a drastic change for her personally and I'm glad that she's able to fully and comfortably transpose this persona to her recent outing. Overall, a great album with several standout tracks but can't wait to hear how she evolves this sound, or changes direction again.
Digital_Music.summary: I can safely say that she has again captured an incredible sound with tracks like 'A love song'

Digital_Music.reviewText: I have always been partial to the Air Force Band which is how I came to own this album. It has become one of my favorites due to the excellent variety of music it contains. The album was thoughtfully laid out and each piece has a very distinct character it brings to the compilation. It is hard to know which pieces to single out, but some favorites are the Radetzky-Marsch, Race d'Aiglons and the stately Marche Militaire Francaise. Great introduction to both classical and march pieces if you know someone who is looking for an easy introduction to concert band music.

I picked this on a recommendation, and I'm glad I did.  It's instrumental music that makes a good soundtrack to your day, especially if you are stuck in a cubicle.  The themes on *Hoshi* fall somewhere between electronic/ambient, rock & jazz; they have more of a melodic base than ambient, and are softer than even the mildest EDM, but they also have a dreamy, often adventurous side to them.  My favorite piece is "My Velvet Book."

Sugarland a new act from nashville, they do it as it was meant to be done. They wrote `em play `em and sing `em .Thank there record company for that. Usually when a giant country record company introduces a new act , it allows them only a small measure of input. Sugarland `s label( Giant ) blessed them with more than that. For this 11-song debut they wrote or co-wrote all of the Tracks. Jennifer the cute female singer is a bewitching siren who deserves a wider audience. They enjoy turning good stories of sorrow into tender tunes.the ringing " Tennessee " is by far the best song turns the simple pleasure of joy riding into a simple joyous ride for the listener. The Soaring tight harmonies of jennifer and co are intact and the country edge to their traditional music gives it an attractive glow. This Trio `s album is one of the best in 2005.

I know many Roberta fans are excited to finally have a decent chance to get this 1978 recording on CD. To me, this is one of the finest albums of her career and I didn't understand why Atlantic Records refused to reissue this stateside.  I was very disappointed when they even released a box set on her 70's albums and decided to not include this outstanding title.

"Roberta Flack" was reissued on CD back in the 90's as a Japan-only import and was pressed in very small quantities.  I own the orignal pressing but I always thought they could have done a better job with the remasering.  So now this SHM-CD is released and is supposed to be higher fidelity than normal CDs.  I ordered this new Japan reissue hoping to hear an improvement in the sound quality over the original. I'm disappointed to say, I honestly couldn't tell any difference in sound between this reissue and the original reissue.  So, for those of you who own the original pressing, I say keep it!  It is a rare collector's item.

If you are a Roberta fan and don't already own this gem on CD, I say it's definately worth the investment and I have a feeling this pressing will be Out of Print & rare very soon.  And it is a great improvement over the MP3 download that's available on various sites.

I experienced two problems on my Windows XP 32bit PC.  At purchase, I asked that the mp3 be put on my amazon cloud. Then I downloaded from the cloud and experienced some issues:

PROBLEM:  The name that was used was crazy long, so long that windows media player couldn't play the mp3. After I realized the length of the filename seemed to be the problem, I couldn't even rename the file in windows file explorer, just failed and reported an error.  I'm DOS savvy, so I tried the "dir /X" to get a short name and subsequently rename it.  That caused a catastrophic DOS error and did not rename the file.

SOLUTION: Finally I went to the cloud and renamed it there to "water" - then downloaded again.  That resulted with a file with a reasonable name, I called it water.mp3.  But I soon realized that the folder names the Amazon download utility created had similar crazy long names as well and that was giving me issues as well with windows media player.  Luckily I was was able to use DOS to fix the directory names. I used "dir /X" and was able to execute a "rename" cmd that worked on the directory names.

UPSHOT: Hope Amazon fixes the names of the file/directories so others don't get a headache trying to just use the mp3 file.

My plan was to download this mp3 and play it using a mp3 player in a speaker dock, rather than invest in an expensive single purpose white noise machine.  Once I got the file names worked out, took about 60 minutes to figure out all the issues and download TWICE.  I need to purchase that dock next, and will update this review when I get a chance to try it out.
Digital_Music.summary: windows xp struggles with this mp3 in default cloud download

The title track was her biggest hit of her entire music career.  Other highlights here are "Runaway", "All Or Nothing",  "Strong Enough", and her hit "We All Sleep Alone" from  the 80's remade into dance material. This album is good to work out to as  it has lots of energy. I'll bet her next album will be even better now that  she has found a style of music that is appealing to the new generation.

So this is my second Nero download and I'm growing to like them more and more. I'd stash them into the techno/dance genre but unlike a lot of techno and dance which basically relies on its dance beat and repeats the same 2-3 lines over and over again through out the song, Nero steps it up and *gasp* actually writes lyrics. Shock me shock me with that deviant behavior! I would compare them more to daft punk then probably anyone else and they are just as good. I'll be looking out for this up and coming band. For this download I do have to say for the first few seconds you may go "huh? What am I listening too", but stick with it, it's well worth it.

In a time when rap was just beginning to crossover into the mainstream, Young MC came along and assisted in bridging that gap with Stone Cold Rhymin'.  "Bust a Move" is the obvious choice for the best song here, but Young shows a lot of ability in his delivery and lyrical talent throughout the album.  "Know How" and "I Come Off" show the extent of this ability.  Young displays his humor on "Principal's Office" and the lighthearted "Roll With the Punches."  The only reason for the 4 star rating comes at the end, with the decent yet surprisingly mediocre "Stone Cold Buggin" and "Just Say No."  Yet, in the long run, all of the other tracks stand the test of time, whicxh makes this a truly great album.
Digital_Music.summary: One of the best rap albums of the 80s

Digital_Music.reviewText:
It's not often these days that us `masters of the lowdown' get to step out front but Brian Landrus could change all that. The Landrus Kaleidoscope, the electro-acoustic five-piece led by the New England Conservatory of Music grad and guru of low frequency instruments has made a big splash.

Landrus plays baritone sax, bass flute and bass clarinet on Capsule, his latest release for BlueLand Records that hit the street on October 25.

The first thing that becomes clear when you put the album on is that this is not "Soft Jazz" although it is not overly busy and the tunes are very lyrical, there are no compromises musically. Even the make up of the band is daring to an extent, mixing acoustic instruments and electric instrument and even electric guitar effects not usually so overtly present in a jazz setting. Additionally the tunes have more than a nodding acquaintance with soul, R&B  I kept expecting Marvin Gaye to suddenly burst out of my speakers on "I Promise") and even some Afro-Caribbean and Reggae  structures that are tantalizing to the ear.

But, it stays firmly grounded in jazz and the jazz atmosphere quickly absorbs these other influences thanks in large part to the rhythm section of, firstly - as always I name the bass player first - acoustic bass in the capable hands of Matthew Parish, he of the big round, soulful sound who brings to mind Charlie Mingus and Ray Brown.

His fellow rhythm master, Rudy Royston lays down that steady beat that has such deep pockets that the Artful Dodger and Fagin would be left scratching their heads. The Rutgers University Mason Gross School of the Arts and classically trained percussionist is quickly becoming a much sought after first call drummer, no matter the type of music.

Then things get eclectic. On acoustic piano and Fender Rhodes piano we have Michael Cain - no, not the actor - the U of North Texas grad and classically trained veteran of sessions with Ravi Coltrane, Jackie DeJohnnette, Me'Shell Ndegocello, his own critically acclaimed trio and many more jazz giants. Cain is also  the co-producer of the album, and a mainstay in Landrus' various efforts since he studied with him. He brings that funky spice rack to this effort in a very tasty way.

There's only two guys left to mention making up Kaleidoscope, and one of them is obviously Landrus'. So who is that guy on guitar? Well, Nir Felder just may be the next big sensation in jazz guitar and that's no idle threat. Awarded the 2004 Berklee Billboard Endowed Scholarship Award for outstanding musicianship, he has got big ears for harmony and a very fluid, yet edgy solo approach and is an exciting jazz player on the solid body electric. As young as he is you keep expecting him to break out in some shredding imitation of Hendrix yet he plays with a touch and a feel for the composition that's just really amazing in it's disciplined approach without sacrificing creativity .

Felder is a superstar in the making and as much restraint as he brings to the album, you can feel the tension. But it is a serious, dedication to the music and it is a beautiful and unexpected sound he brings to tunes like track two, "Like The Wind" which opens with an airy, reggae feel run, high up on the fret board. Then he meshes with Landrus' bass flute and the trippy Rhodes piano of Cain to make this nearly psychedelic feeling, wah-wah infused piece that would have felt at home in the  summer of love.

"Like The Wind' fades into "Beauty" a more traditional jazz tune that just pops and simmers thanks to the relentless drumming of Royston who seems to be able to hold a complicated rhythm together into eternity. The man lives inside that beat. Landrus  plays the bass clarinet on this piece and shows off the dirty lowdown beauty of the deep sounds it's capable of. Then comes the soulful "I Promise" which may be my favorite track if I was forced to choose one.

"Capsule", the title track is a Brazilian/Afro-Cuban influenced, tantalizing track that has a heartbeat of it's own featuring the baritone sax work of Landrus on his main instrument.

Then things get dark and menacing with "71 & On The Road" a growly, gritty tune about golden age touring as a musician. You can smell the sweat and cigarette smoke in your shirt and your throat is dry and it's 2 a.m. and you still have to pack your kit when you should be collecting social security. But that's not what you do. The bass work here just makes the tune as it threatens to sneak up on you in the dark. Felder plays some roiling arpeggios that push both the bass and Landrus bari sax. What an evocative tune. I want to make the movie.

The last two songs are really showcases for Landrus' baritone, "Wide Sky" brings to mind late afternoon sunshine playing with the shadows and the piano solo is just everything; playful, flirty, immaculate. "Now" is a slow ballad that opens with a nice figure on the guitar and piano playing off the line, and Landrus taking over with a tone, low and sweet.

Capsule is an excellent and welcome addition to `true' jazz scene and Landrus is making a case for low register players that will romance your ears give your soul a tune up and make you smile.

The Dirty Lowdown
Digital_Music.summary: The Guru Of The Lowdown - Bari Sax, Bass Flute and Clarinet.

This mixed cycle of the six Nielsen symphonies employs two conductors, the newcomer Myung-Whun Chung (Sym. 1-3 and 5) and the veteran Neeme Jarvi (Sym. 4 and 6). The bonus disk of concertos is led by Chung, so he fills three of the four CDs, which is good, since he is the more interesting conductor. BIS took a decade to finish the cycle (release dates were 1983-92), so the sound is variable, although in general the two conductors adhere to their individual styles.

The result compares favorably with two other Nielsen cycles that could be considered front runners in the modern era: Michael Schonwandt on Naxos and Herbert Blomstedt on Decca. For a taste of the Danish way with Nielsen, the Schonwandt was highly praised when first released in 2000 on its original label, Dacapo. It's more direct and vigorous than the polished blomstedt set from San Francisco, which has better playing and sound. But in the three masterpieces, Sym. 3, 4, and 5, Blomstedt isn't at his best, falling well behind Bernstein, whose exuberant readings ignited Nielsen's reputation outside Denmark when they appeared in 1962 and 1965. Karajan added his imprimatur to Sym. 4 "Inextinguishable" when he gave it the grand international treatment from Berlin.

I thought it would be interesting to give a thumbnail sketch of each CD in this set. Generally speaking, BIS's sound is good but with no revelations, and at times, as in Sym. 3, their miking in unbalanced. The Gothenburg Sym. , which vies with the Swedish Radio Sym. In Stockholm as the best in Sweden, is by no means a virtuoso band. Like another often recorded orchestra, the Bournemouth in England, they are proficient and clean without exciting much interest in the individual soloists or the overall sound.

CD 1: Sym. 1, Sym. 2 "The Four Temperaments"
Score: B/B+
Nielsen, born in 1865, the same year as Sibelius, turned out a first symphony that suffers by comparison with Sibelius's first - in his mid-twenties he hadn't year hit upon his signature harmonies and orchestral color. In particular, there's an exuberant joy unique to Nielsen that isn't apparent in this work, which rather dutifully goes through the motions of correct, pleasant Scandinavian style a la Stenhammar. Chung's reading does well with what's at hand, but he doesn't light a fire under the score. His reading is vigorous, balanced, and clean. The recorded sound is ordinary. Blomstedt's Sym. 1 is much to be preferred.
That wonderful rollicking Nielsen sound emerges in Sym. 2, which is programmatic, at least in mood, by devoting one movement to each of the four "humors" or temperaments in medieval medicine. Before science took an analytical look at psychology, it was common to type people as Choleric, Phlegmatic, Sanguine or Melancholy. For me, the best versions of Sym. 2 dramatize these four moods quite sharply, and Chung sails in that direction. I like the way he urges along the Phlegmatic waltz, and the Melancholic slow movement creates a nice doleful mood. Bernstein had a rare miss with this work, but it is one of the strongest in Blomstedt's cycle. (Fans of Stokowski should also check out his 1967 reading in EMI's Great Conductors of the Century series.) Overall, Chung's version is good but without much individual distinction. Another Amazon reviewer found it brash and life-affirming. I think it's truer to say that it is nimble and light-weight. As in Sym. 1, the sound is ordinary.

CD 2: Symphony no. 3 "Sinfonia espansiva," Sym. 5
Score: A/B+
I first became interested in Chung's Nielsen thanks to his reading of the Third Sym. - he leads one of the most convincing versions after Bernstein's. The Danes have monopolized the Nielsen discography, with nods to Finland and Sweden, yet if you set Chung's "Espansiva" next to those from Berglund, Blomstedt, the recent Gilbert, and even the much-lauded Schonwandt, he finds more in the symphony's episodic moods than any of them. The whole work is permeated with a rare joy for a twentieth-century symphony, and Chung captures its bursting-at-the-seams jollity while knowing when to suddenly shift gears into tender, dreamy, and graceful music-making. The only drawback is that the sound is unbalanced, with the microphones stuck down the bells of the trumpets and trombones.
As for the Nielsen Fifth, Bernstein's 1962 recording has dominated the field thanks ot his ability to capture true menace in the first movement and Stanley Drucker's virtuosic clarinet solos. Colin Davis's recent live account with the LSO is the only serious challenger I've heard from a major conductor and orchestra. Surprisingly, given his exuberance in the Third, Chung's read of the Fifth offers a mild first movement in the Fifth that falters when it comes to uncovering the implicit violence in the music - he doesn't take risks or even give much of a sense of threat. That's in keeping with Blomstedt's interpretation, but I think both are missing a crucial dimension in the score, which is abut the clash of chaos and order. Leave WW I out of it, the fifth still radically opposes panicked disorder, even hysteria, with consonance. The rest of Chung's reading is vigorous and vital.

CD 3: Sym. 4 "Inextinguishable," Sym. 6 "Sinfonia semplice"
Score: B+/A
This is the only disc conducted by the veteran Neeme Jarvi, who recorded a complete Nielsen cycle for DG with the same Gothenburg orchestra; they have a long association. Jariv is an all-purpose conductor who applies his robust, no-nonsense style to practically everything. Here it fits Nielsen's Fourth well enough, but it's a shame that we don't get to hear what Chung has to say. Don't expect Karajan's subtlety or the power of the Berliners. The score presents few difficulties until we reach the explosive duel for two timpanists in the finale. Jarvi's pace, quick in every movement, starts off at breakneck speed here, which makes for a thrilling, raucous ride. The timpanists are forced to scramble, and they sound a little muffled, as does the whole recording.

After the triumphant originality of Sym. 3 to 5, it would be gratifying to report that the Nielsen Sixth is a crowning masterpiece, but this "simple symphony" has proved anything but, and opinions range from outright failure to fascinating enigma. A lot depends on what the conductor can do with its unexpected interjections, choppy themes, and lack of an emotional core. The best approach, I think, is to make the most you can form each episode. The Scherzo gives us another vision of a mad toyshop akin to the first movement of the Shostakovich Fifteenth. Jarvi comes through amazingly well, with a fast pace and no reason to hold back. His performance is vivid and entertaining from moment to moment. It's as successful as any I've heard of this rarely scheduled work.

CD 4: Violin Concerto, Flute concerto, Clarinet Concerto
Score: A-/A/A
Chung returns for Nielsen's three concertos, which have been well served on disc, especially the flute and clarinet works, which fill a gap for modern woodwind concertos. They've attracted the best soloists (Simon Rattle is about to release a CD pairing both concertos with the first chairs of the Berlin Phil.), but Chung is so vigorous and his two soloists so ebullient and committed that these readings cap his cycle with great success. There's no similar lack of modern violin concertos, but the Nielsen, if rarely programmed, has enjoyed two superlative recordings from Maxim Vengerov and Cho-Liang Lin. Dong-Suk Kang isn't of their caliber but delivers a very accomplished and sympathetic reading. The best sound is on the violin recording, but the other two are good enough.

Overall, there is so much exuberant music-making here that with a great Nielsen Third, Sixth, and three concertos, this bargain cycle is a strong contender for best buy.
Digital_Music.summary: A five-star Nielsen cycle if you discount Sym. 1 and 2

Digital_Music.reviewText:
The gimmick here is the violin Daniel Sepec plays; it is one the composer once owned, a gift from the famed Prince Lichnowsky about 1800. Made in Salzburg about 1700, it came to Beethoven with a handful of string instruments; it was sold at auction in 1827. Notes in this issue by the curator of the Beethoven House Museum in Bonn tell a tale about how it would up there and in this recording. The booklet that accompanies the CD -- which fits in a slide on the left inside page of the booklet-type device -- shows the violin and describes its differentiation from modern instruments.

Violinist Daniel Sepec was born in 1965 and plays with the German Chamber Philharmonic of Bremen, where he is the leader. The notes credit a solo career with some famous period instrument enthusiasts including Daniel Harding, Trevor Pinnock and Franz Bruggen. He is accomapnied by Andreas Staier, an older and bigger name soloist in the period instrument movement, who plays an 1824 Graf pianoforte. The notes suggest the pair team up in a trio and quartet with some other players, also.

These two sonatas, Opp. 23 (No. 4) and Op. 30 No. 2 (7), are from Beethoven's early period of the 1st and 2nd Symphonies. The back cover calls them "the very embodient of Beethovian elan terrible." Together, they represent the period where Beethoven is busting out of Mozartean classical restraint and soaring headlong into his revolutionary romantic middle period.

The Sonata No. 7 in C minor (same as the 5th Symphony) is most dramatic, with fiery allegros surrounding an adagio and scherzo. The players have little reserve in this piece, bowling us over in the beginning and end. The Sonata No. 4 in A minor is an earlier creation representing  Mozartian development. While Beethoven's handprint is strong -- there is an eloquent fugue and variation in the central movement and fire in the closing allegro -- it lacks the consistent momentum and gravitas of No. 7. The makeweight variations, on a theme from Figaro, divide the pair on the recorded concert. While listening to the variations, stay awake for Staier's keyboard crash around the 7-minute mark or you might tip over your tea waking up! Oddly, Harmonia Mundi programmed the concert in reverse chronological order, with the more mature piece first.

The violin may be the star here but I think it plays second fiddle. While of historical interest to people that follow this sort of thing, the fiddle (or Sepec's playing on same) lacks the might and vigor we take for granted from modern instruments, not to mention the lush tone. Furthermore, Staier does his cohort few favors, regularly outdueling him in allegros and molting much greater at the end of Sonata No. 4 than Sepec. To be blunt, Staier is clearly the better player and the more greatly projected one in the recording. He is the star here, not that ancient instrument.

This is an interesting issue period enthusiasts should investigate with haste. The discussion of the violin alone will be enough for some people and the performances are pretty fair also. The recording is good and you can hear everything in 21st century DDD sound. This is the kind of thing that, if you think you will like it, you probably will. Same for those who don't think they'll go for it, especially PPP haters and people that like a more loving embrace or repose than this pair offers (just about none).

I had hoped this pair would deliver more of the explosive early romance I hear in the cello sonatas by period players Anssi Kartunen (cello) and Tuja Hakkila. These guys pack a wallop in Beethoven's cello music (on the Warner apex label) that Sepec and Staier can't match here. Perhaps there's room for growth in this pair sticks with it and does all the sonatas.
Digital_Music.summary: Three and one half stars: a fiery display with a big catch for period devotees

Digital_Music.reviewText:
INDIE MUSIC STOP
Marc Cancassi wears many different artistic hats including, actor,director, producer, book author and musician. It's as a musician that we've known Marc having reviewed three of his previous releases on our site:Days to Remember,Journey Into Time,and White Stone.

With each new CD it seems like Marc moves his musical style in a new direction. On Turning Point you'll find seven instrumental tracks that are filled with rich layered sounds.

Stylistically the music is a blend of electronic, experimental,and progressive rock. When the first track (FACTORY OF IDOLS)started playing I thought that my stereo was going wacky, until my ears adjusted up to the barrage of unusual electronic sounds and noises that were coming from the speakers.

The remaining songs found on this release go for more of a layered sound picking out a base instrument:guitar(NO RETURN);piano (TURNING POINT)and then layering other parts(CITY SONG)on top of them. You'll also find, repeated notes(MR. H), scale runs, and chord progression used in the songs.

Turning Point is a CD that might not appeal to the masses,but the niche audience that appreciates its style will find themselves very satisfied after listening to it.- CW ROSS/April 09'

Harken back with me to an idealistic time when the burgeoning West Coast scene was sprouting tripped out music everywhere. MGM Records attempted to cultivate an East Coast counterpart in the Boston/Cambridge area. Ultimate Spinach were born of this fertile ground along with such other hopefuls as Orpheus, Beacon Street Union and the more esoteric Pearls Before Swine. Although not quite up to their maiden effort this was nonetheless a very significant Psychedelic relic. The tittle track was/is the standout cut and the last original band offering. Of note, Jeff Baxter from Steely Dan was to launch his career on the less directed third Albumn.

Instrumentalist and songwriter, Shak, has written a very unique love story on his latest album, "Take My Soul." Although it is all instrumental, Shak does an excellent job depicting a couple's blossoming and sometimes tumultuous relationship through song. Listen to "A New Dawn," a track which screams of hope and curiosity, much like any new relationship. Along the way, the couple goes through extreme highs and lows, all documented through the creative mind of Shak. Sometimes the couple's relationship is doing well as heard on "Close to My Heart" and sometimes not, which "I Am Sorry" clearly portrays. Shak does an outstanding job composing his well written emotional feelings through melody and instrumentation about what most average couples all go through. If you are looking for a really interesting CD and you love instrumentals, then you won't be disappointed when you listen to "Take My Soul." Shaun H. and the [...] Reviewer Team [...]

He was very disappointed as to the misleading promo & inflated price, however due to the effort needed to rtn & wait for the "promised" refund, I may just keep the cd & "eat" the loss. The past several years have been more about Beyonce' than any of the other divas. But also, it has been more about her overexposure in the music industry. But also it has been more about things internally that also have hurt her in her personal life. One of them is that her husband Jay-Z cheating on her, and having a child out of wedlock. That same feeling also was said about her father Matthew Knowles that had cheated on her mom Tina, and caused that marriage to end in a abrupt and un-amicable divorce. Honestly, when I had heard Beyonce' Knowles make her album Lemonade, I honestly would have to say not on;y was I unimpressed with her album, but I again felt she really had been lagging in musicality in the way she used to have it when she was a part of Destiny's Child. When I heard her song, Daddy Lessons, I thought it was very interesting to hear her try her hands into a country song with her over-branding in R&B. Well, it has worked for divas like The Pointer Sisters that were the first girl group to perform at The Grand Old Opry. At least it is one of her better songs that she had done in years, but not as good as songs like Listen or Halo were. Still, it is a interesting twist in her career, but not really one that has more of a definitive appeal. Hopefully, she will learn to have better in her voice than what she has had before. Honestly, Hymn For The Weekend with Coldplay is her best song this year, and not from her record Lemonade.

Song: C

Sometimes, not being able to hear the actual lyrics in a song is not such a bad thing. Robin Thicke has a strong career and continues to produce much fine music. Remember Dick Clark's weekly Saturday music/dance show, when teenagers, when asked to rate a new song would say, "It has a strong beat and good melody ..."?  That "standard rating phrase" is the reason for a 3-Star rating - - - there is an "Explicit" warning, and it's there for a reason, (and yes, it does have a great melody).

This album is OK, but nowhere as good as O' Be Joyful. On a whole, the songs are much slower and more melancholy. O Be Joyful was the kind of CD that makes you want to you pop it in (does anyone do that anymore?), turn up the volume, roll down the windows, and go for a drive. Swimmin' Time makes me want to take some pills,  sit down in a dark room in my underwear, and drink bourbon until the tears come. And you know they will come.

Hmmmm......the music is fine.....typical Karunesh, but the selections are perhaps a bit obscure and not really worthy to be on a Best of CD. And then there was the atypical experience I had with Amazon concerning this CD. Due to some poor packing, the CD arrived with a cracked jewel case, and as it turned out upon playing, the CD also has a scratch or defect of some kind which affects playback. To be fair, Amazon did refund the entire purchase price and did not ask for the CD to be returned. One final thought....Amazons CD prices seem to be quite high, but then I haven't purchased CDs for a long time. Maybe the prices are typical?

The track sounds fine but it's not digitally rejiggered so if you're a stickler for a bit of surface noise or you're looking for a crystal clear, studio quality recording to really push those $1,200.00 speaker cables you might want to look elsewhere.

There is clapping over the first 5 seconds and last 7 seconds (which the short Amazon preview doesn't give you).
Digital_Music.summary: Not the best version but it's passable.

I had completely forgotten this song, but knew something like this existed. By whom, I didn't know. When I stumbled across it, I bought it immediately. How did I find it? I stumbled across two covers of this song, one by Carlos Santana and Steve Winwood on YouTube. I knew it had been done by someone else, so I went searching here at Amazon. Then I stumbled upon Sade's version. All three are good, and perhaps Sade's version is best, but the original by Timmy Thomas is the one you want, then the others too. GET IT if you remember it from the late 60s! It is the precursor to Marvin Gaye's album "What's Going On".
Digital_Music.summary: Not great, but important to your collection of Peace Love and Happiness music

Digital_Music.reviewText: There is no doubt that this album sounds very similar to Mark Hoppus's side project +44 than actually sounding like a Blink-182 record. Don't get me wrong, that doesn't mean that there is not some enjoyable songs on here. I honestly though "Bored To Death" was a great single but there are only a couple other songs that are as good like that on this thing. Can I blame Mark and Travis for wanting to find a guy that is willing to show up to their gigs and actually carry the band forward? No, I can't. However, that means this band is always going to get flak for not having Tom til the end of time and all their records are going to sound like +44 albums under the Blink-182 name. There is fun to be had on this album but it only comes in small doses. I wouldn't say this is a true representation of Blink-182's work as a music group.
Digital_Music.summary: Alright But Not A True Representation Of Blink-182's Best Material

Digital_Music.reviewText: I got both Axe To Grind & Soul Survivor on cassettes, which I still have. After a few runs through my stereo they both got old really quick. It's good if you like the pop hair bands from the early late 80's/early 90's era. They weren't so special that I had to get CD re-issue of them. A few tracks on both albums grab me ear, but the rest is probably something I'd just put on as  background music at a cook out. Ken Tamplin is a great musician, and I loved his live show, but his song writing is just to radio friendly and poppy for my tastes.
Digital_Music.summary: unmemorable rdio friendly hair band rock.

Digital_Music.reviewText: I'm a progressive rock fan and was a fan of Dream Theater's 90s music more than anything else.  2013 brought them back into my view, and that album was fantastic.  This album truly is "astonishing" considering many aspects such as its artistry, length, attention to detail, story, etc.  The reason I'm rating this a 3 is because it's just sooooooo long that there's never enough time to listen to it.  It also has so many ballads that it makes me keep wanting more of the progressive movements and such.  It is a fantastic album, but I have only listened to it through once since I purchased it 18 months ago.  Take that into consideration.  Maybe you have more time and like the dramatic.
Digital_Music.summary: and that album was fantastic. This album truly is "astonishing" considering many aspects ...

Digital_Music.reviewText:
Dido had stated that her fourth album "Girl Who Got Away" would be more electronic and I had visions of her collaborations with Faithless, or even her clubby contribution "Everything To Lose" to the "Sex And The City 2" soundtrack.

Alas, we get more of the same stuff which took up much of her "Life For Rent" or "Safe Trip Home" albums. That is great if you loved those albums. The arrangements are largely safe and she still sounds bland and listless for the most part. "No Freedom" and the first third of the album perfectly exemplify this.

The title track is a dull ballad garnished with electronic flourishes, while "Let Us Move On" features rapper Kendrick Lamar and while mildly pleasant, "Stan" it ain't.

"Blackbird" threatens to break out into full synths and break beats. Starting with "End Of Night" (with pulsing synths and stomping beats) the album gets more interesting. In fact, this song is reminiscent of Pet Shop Boys. "Love To Blame" is another synth-driven song with Jazzy horns darting in the background and nice drum rolls and bells. "Go Dreaming" is a dreamy synth number.

Next come a trio of lovely atmospheric ballads; The acoustic "Happy New Year", "Loveless Hearts" (with skittery beats), and the spare spectacular "Day Before We Went To War". Now if only the first third of the album matched the rest, this would be a real winner.
Digital_Music.summary: Girl almost got away with it

Digital_Music.reviewText:
There's a misnomer floating around that Maurice Abravanel's 1963-74 Mahler series with the Utah Symphony was the first-ever to be completed. It wasn't, with Bernstein, Haitink, Kubelik and Solti all having recorded the canonical nine symphonies before Abravanel crossed the finish line. (You could say, however, that Abravanel was the first conductor to record a complete Mahler symphony series with an American orchestra, since Bernstein taped his 1960s Eighth in London rather than in New York.) Regardless, Abravanel was among a handful of "true believers" who kept Mahler's music before the concertgoing public in the decades between the composer's death and the dawn of the ongoing Mahler boom in the 1960s. This cycle, available in various CD incarnations on the Vanguard label, is now reissued at budget price in a no-frills slipcase by Musical Concepts.

Let me start off by saying that the Utah orchestra evinces great enthusiasm and dedication; would that many a more polished ensemble showed the same commitment. Yet the thin-sounding strings and more than occasionally wobbly brass make it clear that Abravanel was coaxing his players to give their all--and that sometimes their all just wasn't enough. And there are blind spots in Abravanel's vision of these scores: the angst, terror and grotesquerie that Bernstein exploited so successfully are little in evidence here. Even so, Abravanel's grasp of these often-unwieldy symphonic edifices proves far more convincing than some better-known maestros can manage, even with world-class orchestras at their service. In short, you can easily find Mahler recordings--whether singly or in complete cycles--that boast greater scale, more precise playing, etc., but you'll have a hard time finding a collection with such clear-eyed devotion to the cause of this composer.
Digital_Music.summary: A pioneering cycle that still has much to say

Digital_Music.reviewText:
An extensive collection of British and American childrens classics. Many of the songs are quite bouncy and lively, with about half sung in chorus (by the Columbia River Players) and half by a single child or adult singer (Big Blue Dog Players). There is a set of six quieter lullabies at the end. Note that most are sung in a British accent.

The effect is rather haphazard and the songs both numerous and varied enough that it makes little sense to play straight through. But the large collection for a reasonable price makes it a good choice for intro'ing children to a range of music. Use for story or nursery-rhyme time, especially pairing with illustrated versions of these songs in print.
